title: Differential impact of dynein pathogenic variants on mitotic spindle organization and cortical organoid growth.
abstract: Mutations in the dynein heavy chain gene (DYNC1H1) cause a spectrum of neurological disorders, including malformations of cortical development (MCD) and spinal muscular atrophy with lower extremity predominance (SMALED). How these mutations differentially affect dynein functions in the nervous system, leading to distinct pathologies, remains unknown. Using patient-derived cortical organoids, we address how MCD- and SMALED-causing dynein mutations alter human cortical development. We show that MCD-associated mutations alter the growth of organoids, but that SMALED organoids are unaffected, consistent with the microcephaly phenotypes of individuals with MCD. These defects are mirrored by a large increase in apoptotic cell death in MCD organoids. MCD mutations - but not SMALED mutations - strongly affect radial glial progenitor divisions, by inducing severe mitotic spindle defects and leading to prolonged mitotic duration. Mitotic checkpoint inhibition alleviates mitotic delay but fails to prevent apoptosis, indicating that mitotic arrest is not the cause of cell death in MCD. These findings reveal how specific dynein mutations can distinctly disrupt cortical development, establishing mitotic spindle dysfunction and apoptosis as central mechanisms underlying dynein-related microcephaly.

title: Motor neuron disease due to a novel PIK3R1 mutation.
abstract: Mutations in PIK3R1, which encodes the regulatory subunit (p85α) of class I phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), are associated with immunologic and developmental disorders, but their effects on the nervous system have not been studied. We identified a novel heterozygous frameshift mutation (PIK3R1 c.1710dup) in a patient with common variable immunodeficiency who developed adult-onset, slowly progressive ALS-like motor-neuron disease. Studies of patient-derived induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) demonstrated PIK3R1 haploinsufficiency with selective AKT activation. Investigation of patient's iPSC-derived motor neurons (iMNs) showed reduced neuronal electrical activity, and markedly increased apoptosis. Single-cell RNA sequencing revealed coordinated up-regulation of differentiation and apoptosis programs across neuronal and glial clusters. Engineering the PIK3R1 c.1710dup mutation into healthy-control iPSCs reproduced the impaired electrical activity, increased apoptosis, and transcriptional vulnerability, confirming the variant's cell-intrinsic pathogenicity. In contrast, introduction of canonical APDS2-associated PIK3R1 splice mutations into the same genetic background did not produce these abnormalities, establishing a variant-class-specific mechanism of PI3K dysfunction. Together, these findings define PIK3R1 c.1710dup as a distinct pathogenic variant that links PI3K-pathway dysregulation to human motor-neuron degeneration and expands the mechanistic spectrum of PIK3R1-associated disease.

title: A Deep Quantitative Proteome Turnover Platform for Human iPSC-Derived Neurons.
abstract: Quantitative evaluation of protein turnover in human neurons is crucial for understanding neuron homeostasis and guiding drug development for neurological diseases. However, measuring protein turnover in postmitotic neurons remains challenging because of the broad dynamic range of neuronal protein half-lives and limited proteome coverage in SILAC (stable isotope labeling by amino acids in cell culture) experiments. Here, we established a comprehensive analytical platform for protein turnover measurements in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons by integrating optimized dynamic SILAC labeling, extensive offline peptide fractionation, data-independent acquisition (DIA) LC-MS/MS, and a streamlined computational workflow with stringent kinetic modeling and filtering criteria. As a result, this platform enabled the quantification of 10,792 apparent protein half-lives from 162,854 unique peptides, substantially expanding the coverage of low-abundance regulatory proteins and therapeutically relevant targets, including 72% of the human kinome, 45% of FDA-approved drug targets, and 72% of potential drug targets. Comparative analyses of glutamatergic cortical neurons and spinal motor neurons revealed globally conserved proteome dynamics alongside subtype-specific differences in protein turnover and abundance. To maximize the accessibility and utility of these datasets, we developed NeuronProfile (https://www.neuronprofile.com/), an interactive resource for exploring protein turnover, abundance, protein copy number, peptide-level kinetics, subcellular localization, and therapeutically relevant proteins in human neurons. Together, this work establishes a robust analytical platform and community resource for quantitative studies of neuronal proteostasis, therapeutic target prioritization, and neurological disease research.

title: Ferroptosis-related molecular signatures in Alzheimer's disease and the neuroprotective effects of allicin: an integrated bioinformatics, peripheral single-cell transcriptomic, and experimental study.
abstract: Ferroptosis is increasingly implicated in Alzheimer's disease (AD), but the relationship between AD-associated transcriptomic changes, peripheral immune alterations, and candidate ferroptosis-modulating compounds remains incompletely defined. This study aimed to identify ferroptosis-related molecular signatures associated with AD and to evaluate whether allicin attenuates ferroptosis-related injury in complementary experimental models. Human hippocampal microarray datasets GSE1297 and GSE28146 were examined with explicit consideration of donor overlap; GSE1297 was treated as the primary subject-level reference dataset, whereas the donor-overlapping GSE28146 dataset was used only as a cross-platform sensitivity source and not as an independent cohort. Ferroptosis-related candidates were prioritized using FerrDb, AD-related annotation, protein-protein interaction analysis, and pathway analysis. Peripheral-blood single-cell RNA-sequencing data (GSE181279) were analyzed to describe immune-cell composition and peripheral distribution of candidate genes without extrapolating these findings to brain-parenchymal cell localization. Candidate-drug prediction and molecular docking were followed by D-galactose/AlCl3 rat experiments and erastin-treated PC12-cell experiments. Histology, ROS, Western blotting, RT-qPCR, and JC-1 assays were used to assess ferroptosis-related molecular and mitochondrial changes. Ferroptosis-focused transcriptomic screening and network prioritization highlighted GPX4, FSP1, SLC7A11, TFRC, and ACSL4 as candidate genes for subsequent analyses. Their expression pattern was compatible with reduced antioxidant defense and increased iron/lipid-peroxidation susceptibility in AD-associated hippocampal transcriptomes. Peripheral single-cell analysis showed heterogeneous expression of these genes across T-cell, B-cell, NK-cell, monocyte, and platelet populations; these results are interpreted as peripheral immune context rather than evidence of brain-cell localization. Molecular docking predicted energetically favorable allicin-protein poses, but does not establish direct target engagement. In the experimental models, allicin attenuated histopathological injury and ROS accumulation, shifted GPX4, FSP1, SLC7A11, TFRC, and ACSL4 expression in an anti-ferroptotic direction, and improved mitochondrial membrane-potential readouts, with changes directionally similar to ferrostatin-1. The combined data support an association between AD-related molecular changes and ferroptosis-regulatory pathways and show that allicin can reduce ferroptosis-related injury in the models used. Because the human datasets include donor overlap, the single-cell dataset is peripheral rather than brain-derived, and direct target-engagement, lipidomic, genetic-rescue, and pharmacokinetic experiments were not performed, the findings should be considered mechanistically suggestive rather than proof that allicin directly targets the five proteins or specifically inhibits AD-associated ferroptosis in humans.

title: An Orthogonal Quantitative NMR-FRET Approach for Integrity-Resolved Analysis of Lipid Vesicle Dynamics.
abstract: While lipid-based vesicles gain increasing attention as biomembrane models, artificial cells, and drug carriers, analytical investigation of their composition and integrity remains a major challenge, particularly for monitoring changes during processing and membrane transport. To address this challenge, we present an orthogonal analytical platform that combines 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) spectroscopy to enable integrity-resolved quantification of lipid vesicles. While 1H NMR provides chemically selective calibration-based quantification of individual lipid species, FRET-based assays enable direct monitoring of intact vesicle translocation across membranes, allowing for discrimination between free lipids and vesicle-associated lipids. We investigated vesicles composed of different phospholipid mixtures, including their formation and integrity as well as their membrane transport, and revealed remarkable composition-dependent differences. While vesicles composed of phosphatidylcholine and cholesterol exhibit instability, compositional loss, and limited membrane transport, inclusion of anionic lipids, such as phosphatidylglycerol and phosphatidylserine, significantly improves structural integrity and increases the fraction of lipids transported in vesicular form. These results demonstrate that orthogonal quantification of free and vesicle-associated lipids provides mechanistic insights into vesicle dynamics during processing and membrane transport, supporting the rational design of vesicular systems for applications in artificial cell research and lipid-based nanomedicines, where vesicle composition directly governs mechanical stability as well as biological interactions.

title: TRIB3 Knockdown Attenuates Post-cardiac Arrest Brain Injury with Suppression of Mitophagy: Involvement of AKT-FOXO3a-BNIP3 Signaling.
abstract: Brain injury after cardiac arrest and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CA-CPR) is a major cause of poor neurological outcomes among survivors, yet effective mechanism-based interventions remain lacking. Mitophagy maintains mitochondrial homeostasis, but whether increased mitophagy contributes to brain injury after CA-CPR and which upstream factors regulate it remain unclear. Transcriptomic analysis of hippocampal tissue from rats subjected to asphyxial CA-CPR identified tribbles pseudokinase 3 (TRIB3) as one of the most strongly upregulated genes, with its expression approximately 68-fold higher than that in sham controls. TRIB3 was knocked down by adeno-associated virus (AAV) injection into the hippocampal CA1 region 4 weeks before CA-CPR and by lentiviral transduction in H19-7 cells before oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R). TRIB3 knockdown improved neurological function and attenuated hippocampal CA1 neuronal injury in CA-CPR rats. It also attenuated mitophagy, alleviated mitochondrial dysfunction, and reduced neuronal apoptosis in vivo and in vitro. Valproic acid partially counteracted these mitochondrial and anti-apoptotic effects in vitro. Mechanistic analyses in OGD/R-treated cells showed that TRIB3 knockdown increased the p-AKT/AKT and p-FOXO3a/FOXO3a ratios, reduced FOXO3a nuclear accumulation and BNIP3 expression, and decreased FOXO3a enrichment at the Bnip3 promoter. Co-immunoprecipitation assays showed increased TRIB3-AKT association and reduced AKT-FOXO3a association after OGD/R. In vivo, TIC10 treatment partially counteracted the improvements in mitochondrial function and neurological outcomes following TRIB3 knockdown. Together, these findings suggest that TRIB3 may act as a previously unrecognized upstream modulator of mitophagy after CA-CPR, implicate AKT-FOXO3a-BNIP3 signaling, and support further evaluation of TRIB3 as a potential neuroprotective target.

title: Thalamocortical vulnerability in autism spectrum disorder: a computational model of CPEB4 mis-splicing.
abstract: Skipping of a neuronal microexon in cytoplasmic polyadenylation element-binding protein 4 (CPEB4) transcripts has been linked to idiopathic autism spectrum disorder, but the most susceptible brain regions and cell types are unknown. We asked whether the balance between the splicing activator serine/arginine repetitive matrix 4 (SRRM4) and the RNA-binding repressors polypyrimidine tract-binding proteins 1 and 2 (PTBP1 and PTBP2) is sufficient to predict regional differences in microexon inclusion, and which predictions withstand uncertainty in unmeasured parameters. We modeled their competitive binding to the intronic motifs flanking the microexon, including destabilization of SRRM4 expression by sustained histone deacetylase inhibition, and applied the model to human brain transcriptomic data from tissue samples, single cells and developmental stages. The thalamus expressed markedly less SRRM4 mRNA than the anterior cingulate cortex, and the model predicted lower microexon inclusion in the thalamus in every draw of the sensitivity analysis, although the size of the difference varied widely and absolute inclusion values were poorly constrained. A larger thalamic effect of histone deacetylase inhibition was not robust: it followed from the assumed regional difference in super-enhancer susceptibility, and the cingulate cortex lost more inclusion when this susceptibility was equal in both regions. The model is not experimentally validated, and microexon inclusion has not been measured in the human thalamus. These results propose regional SRRM4 supply as a testable determinant of CPEB4 microexon splicing and identify the measurements needed to test it: microexon inclusion and SRRM4, PTBP1 and PTBP2 protein in thalamic nuclei and cingulate cortex.

title: Gut microbiota profiles and neurodevelopmental symptoms in children from a prenatal-risk enriched birth cohort: findings from the PREDO study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) and Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) are common neurodevelopmental conditions whose early-life biological correlates remain incompletely understood. Children's gut microbiota may represent a biological pathway through which immune-metabolic and gut-brain signalling links early-life adversity with neurodevelopment. We examined gut microbiota profiles associated with ADHD and ASD symptoms in children from the Prediction and Prevention of Preeclampsia and Intrauterine Growth Restriction (PREDO) birth cohort. METHODS: We analysed data from 323 Finnish children assessed at a mean age of 8.6 years. Stool microbiota composition was profiled using 16S rRNA sequencing and differential taxonomic abundance was assessed using MaAsLin2. ADHD and ASD symptoms were mother-rated using the Conners' Parent Rating Scale-Revised and Autism Spectrum Screening Questionnaire. RESULTS: Clinically relevant ADHD and ASD symptoms were associated with metric-specific reductions in alpha diversity, whereas beta diversity did not differ between groups. Male children with clinically relevant ADHD symptoms showed lower abundance of Lachnospiraceae_FCS020_group, Subdoligranulum, Fusicatenibacter, and Anaerostipes (ps ≤ 0.049). Female children with clinically relevant ADHD symptoms showed a distinct profile, including higher Negativibacillus and Faecalibacterium (p ≤ 0.018). Children with clinically relevant ASD symptoms showed lower abundance of six genera, including Anaerostipes and Lachnospiraceae_ND3007_group (p ≤ 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: In this prenatal-risk enriched cohort, ADHD and ASD symptoms were associated with distinct gut microbiota profiles, including alterations in taxa implicated in short-chain fatty acid metabolism, immune regulation, and gut-brain signalling. These findings support microbiota-immune-brain pathways as a hypothesis-generating framework for future longitudinal and multi-omics research.

title: Maternal gluten diet exacerbates offspring autistic-like behaviors through the gut-brain axis mediated by gut microbial metabolite elaidic acid.
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a heterogeneous group of neurodevelopmental conditions characterized by social deficits and stereotyped behaviors, for which effective treatments remain lacking. Here we investigated whether early-life gluten exposure exacerbates autism-like behaviors in BTBR mice and explored the underlying microbiota-metabolite-brain mechanism. Early-life gluten exposure aggravated social avoidance, anxiety, and repetitive behaviors in BTBR offspring, accompanied by reduced mushroom dendritic spine density and diminished microglial branch complexity in the hippocampus. Microbiota sequencing revealed gut microbial dysbiosis, with increased abundance of Hungatella hathewayi and Eubacterium sp. Marseille-P4003. Consistent with their capacity for lipid transformation, untargeted metabolomics showed enrichment of unsaturated fatty acid metabolism and elevated fecal elaidic acid levels. Clinically, targeted quantification confirmed that fecal elaidic acid was significantly higher in children with ASD than in their healthy siblings. Supporting a causal role, exogenous elaidic acid administration dose-dependently worsened behavioral deficits and induced hippocampal spine loss and amoeboid microglial activation. Mechanistically, intestinal transcriptomics revealed activation of antigen processing and presentation and cytokine signaling pathways, whereas hippocampal transcriptomics showed downregulation of immune negative regulators (Egr2, Egr4) alongside enrichment of MHC-I and TNF pathways, indicating impaired central immune restraint. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that early-life gluten exposure induces gut microbiota dysbiosis that drives elaidic acid accumulation, which in turn activates intestinal immunity and suppresses hippocampal immune negative regulation via the gut-brain axis, ultimately aggravating neuroinflammation and autism-like behaviors.

title: Associations of Blood Metal(loid) Mixture with Autism Spectrum Disorder in Children: A Case-Control Study.
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder influenced by both genetic susceptibility and environmental exposures. Heavy metals and metalloids can cross the blood-brain barrier and disturb neurodevelopment; however, most previous studies focused on single-metal effects rather than real-world mixed co-exposure. This case-control study aimed to evaluate associations between blood metal(loid) mixtures and childhood ASD risk. 30 children with ASD and 30 typically-developing controls aged 2-7 years were enrolled in Guangxi, China. Whole-blood concentrations of lead, mercury, arsenic, cadmium, chromium, and manganese were measured by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). Univariate analyses, multivariable logistic regression, and quantile-based g-computation (qgcomp) were applied to assess individual and joint effects. Univariate results showed higher blood lead and cadmium concentrations in ASD children. After adjusting for covariates, each doubling of blood cadmium concentration was associated with higher odds of ASD (Firth-penalized OR = 18.64, 95% CI: 1.75-315.18; P = 0.014); the maximum-likelihood estimate was similar in direction but wider (OR = 27.96, 95% CI: 2.20-577.77; P = 0.017). Because of the small number of events this estimate is interpreted with caution. In the qgcomp model, a simultaneous one-quartile increase in all six metal(loid)s was associated with higher odds of ASD, although the joint effect was not statistically significant (OR = 1.28, 95% CI: 0.70-2.35; P = 0.422). Cadmium carried the largest positive weight within the mixture (0.43), and manganese the largest negative weight (- 0.31); because the weights are constrained to sum to unity in absolute value and the joint effect was not significant, they are interpreted as descriptive summaries of relative contribution rather than as tests of the effect of each metal(loid). Our findings suggest that blood cadmium concentration may be associated with ASD, but the evidence is limited: the joint effect of the mixture was not statistically significant, the component weights are descriptive rather than tests of individual effects, and the single-metal estimate for cadmium was imprecise. These observations highlight the necessity of mixture-exposure assessment in ASD-related environmental epidemiological research, and require replication in larger samples.

title: Human nasal turbinate derived neural crest stem cells attenuate neuroinflammation and dopaminergic neurodegeneration by suppressing the HMGB1-RAGE-NF-κB axis in Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta and persistent neuroinflammation. Although stem cell-based therapies have shown therapeutic potential, effective control of the inflammatory niche in the diseased brain is critical for improving their therapeutic efficacy. This study investigated whether human nasal turbinate derived neural crest stem cells (hNTSCs) protect dopaminergic neurons by regulating microglia-mediated inflammation through the high mobility group box 1 (HMGB1)-Receptor for advanced glycation end products (RAGE)-nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) signaling pathway. In vitro, hNTSC co-culture reduced 1-methyl-4-phenylpyridinium (MPP+)-induced microglial activation and HMGB1 expression in Human microglial clone 3 (HMC3) cells. Conditioned medium from MPP+-stimulated microglia increased RAGE expression and NF-κB phosphorylation in induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived dopaminergic neurons, whereas conditioned medium from hNTSC-co-cultured microglia attenuated these changes. In 9-month-old male mice with 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP)-induced parkinsonism, hNTSC transplantation reduced microglial activation and HMGB1 expression in the substantia nigra. Treatment also decreased RAGE expression and the p-NF-κB/NF-κB ratio, preserved tyrosine hydroxylase-positive dopaminergic neurons, and improved motor performance in open-field and rotarod tests. These findings indicate that hNTSCs reduce microglia-mediated neuroinflammation and dopaminergic neuronal damage, at least in part, by suppressing the HMGB1-RAGE-NF-κB signaling pathway. hNTSCs may provide a cell-based therapeutic approach for modulating the inflammatory lesion environment in PD.

title: High-throughput screening of patient iPSC-derived neurons identifies the gut microbial metabolites that attenuate Alzheimer's disease pathology.
abstract: Gut microbiota-derived metabolites influence the gut-brain axis and may impact Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathology. However, the microbial metabolites involved in this process and their functional roles are largely unknown. We screened 352 gut metabolites in induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC)-derived neurons from individuals with AD to identify compounds that reduce tau hyperphosphorylation. We identified agmatine as a lead candidate, which decreased hyperphosphorylated tau in neurons and cerebral organoids. In 5xFAD mice, agmatine (100 mg/kg/day) improved cognition, reduced amyloid plaques, lowered neuroinflammation, and increased beneficial gut bacteria, including Agathobacter and Bacteroides. Transcriptomic analysis showed that agmatine downregulated complement and inflammatory genes (C1QB, C2, C3AR1, CCL3, CXCL8, and CXCL6) in patient iPSC-derived cerebral organoids. Agmatine also decreased C3aR and pSTAT3 levels in vivo, mechanistically supporting the reduced tau phosphorylation in iPSC-derived neurons. Altogether, these findings identified the therapeutic potential of gut-derived metabolites and identified agmatine as potential treatment for AD.

title: A unified framework for scalable differential testing for spatial omics.
abstract: A key challenge in spatial omics is identifying features whose values vary depending on both cell type and the surrounding cellular niche. Existing methods designed for spatial transcriptomic data do not generalize well to modalities beyond count-based data and do not scale efficiently to current data volumes. Here we introduce spotGLM, a mixture-aware generalized linear modeling framework for cell-type-specific differential testing across spatial modalities, and SPARROW, a power-preserving data distillation strategy for scalable inference. SpotGLM accommodates diverse data types including count-based gene expression, binomial isoform proportions and continuous chromatin accessibility scores within a unified statistical framework. We demonstrate the framework across spatial omics applications. On Visium HD data of colorectal cancer and mouse kidney, we recover cell-type-specific niche effects with serial-slice cross-platform validation. On long-read spatial RNA-seq data, we resolve cell-type-specific isoform switching in the mouse olfactory bulb. On spatial ATAC-seq data from mouse brain, we recover cell-type-specific spatial variation in regulatory motif accessibility.

title: Aging impairs CX3CL1 neuroprotection in α-synuclein-induced Parkinson's disease pathology.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD), the second most prevalent movement disorder, is pathologically defined by the accumulation of α-synuclein (α-syn), loss of dopaminergic neuron and inflammation in the substantia nigra pars compacta. The neuronally expressed chemokine CX3CL1 (fractalkine, FKN), when delivered as the soluble form (sFKN) via AAV-mediated overexpression, protects dopamine neurons in several animal models of PD. Since aging is a major risk factor for PD, we examined the effects of sFKN overexpression in both young and aged PD models. To model PD, young (3-month) and aged (15-month) male F344 rats received unilateral intracranial injections of recombinant adeno-associated virus serotype 9 (rAAV9) encoding either human wild-type α-synuclein (α-syn) or green fluorescent protein (GFP). Motor performance was evaluated at baseline, 1 month, and 2 months post-injection. Behavioral deficits and neuropathological changes were compared across treatment and age groups. CX3CL1 involvement in PD-related neuroinflammation was assessed using immunohistochemistry and biochemical analyses and bulk RNA-seq was used to characterize transcriptomic changes. We found that sFKN rescued both motor deficits and dopaminergic neuron loss in young PD animals but not in aged animals. Analysis of the transcriptomics revealed age-dependent alterations in inflammatory, immune, and neurogenic signaling in response to sFKN treatment. In conclusion, while sFKN effectively ameliorates behavioral deficits and dopaminergic neurodegeneration in young PD animals, its protective effects are lost in aged animals. These findings emphasize the necessity of rigorous age-inclusive preclinical evaluation and suggest that targeting CX3CL1 signaling alone may be insufficient as a therapeutic strategy in age-related neurodegenerative disease.

title: Time-dependent alterations of the heart-brain axis in rats following a single microwave exposure.
abstract: This study aimed to investigate the time-dependent changes and possible mechanisms of the heart-brain axis in rats following S-band microwave exposure. A single microwave exposure model was established using 8-week-old male Wistar rats (2.856 GHz, 50 mW/cm², 30 min). At Days 1, 3, and 7 post-exposure, we evaluated electrocardiogram, heart rate variability, and electroencephalogram activities, alongside serum biochemical and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay indicators. Integrated transcriptomic and proteomic analyses of the hippocampus and myocardium, combined with real-time quantitative PCR, were utilized to validate key molecular changes. The results showed that following a single exposure, the function of the rat heart-brain axis changed in a time-dependent but outcome-specific manner: neuroendocrine, autonomic, and electroencephalographic alterations were most evident on Day 1, most circulating cardiac and brain injury markers were highest on Day 3, and lactate dehydrogenase increased only on Day 7. These changes were primarily characterized by imbalanced autonomic nervous function and heart rate variability, abnormal electrocardiogram and electroencephalogram activities, and elevated injury-related markers. Integrated multi-omics analysis revealed significant molecular remodeling in both tissues on Day 3. Myocardial differential molecules were primarily enriched in cytochrome P450-mediated metabolism and detoxification pathways, with representative molecules including Adh6 and Cyp4f5. Hippocampal differential molecules mainly involved neuroactive ligand-receptor interactions, neural signal transduction, and synaptic regulation pathways, with representative molecules including Adra2b and Chrna3. These findings suggest that a S-band microwave exposure induces heart-brain axis autonomic regulatory imbalance, electrophysiological abnormalities, and synchronized changes in central neural signaling and peripheral metabolic detoxification. These results provide an experimental basis for risk assessment and protective strategies against high-power microwaves.

title: A minimally invasive protocol for cerebrospinal fluid collection in mice and small-volume proteomics.
abstract: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is a valuable resource for pre-clinical drug discovery, as it can be used to detect biomarkers of neurodegenerative diseases and overall brain health and function. Here, we describe a protocol for collecting CSF from mice. This minimally invasive approach enables serial collections and longitudinal analysis of CSF samples from the same mouse. We also describe steps for quality control and proteomic analysis.

title: Cerebral Inflammation Is Additionally Reduced by Combined Quetiapine and Propranolol After Severe Traumatic Brain Injury.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Pharmacotherapeutics may enhance post traumatic brain injury (TBI) outcomes. While post-TBI quetiapine (QTP) reduces intracranial pressure, propranolol (βB) may blunt neurovascular inflammation and preserve blood brain barrier (BBB) integrity. We hypothesized that post-TBI QTP plus βB additively reduces penumbral leukocyte (LEU) mobilization and enhances neuroclinical recovery. METHODS: Forty-two CD1 male mice underwent severe TBI (controlled cortical impact: injury, I) or sham craniectomy (S) followed by intraperitoneal saline (Placebo), QTP (10 mg/kg), βB (2 mg/kg), or both (QTP + βB) twice a day for 2 d. At 48 h, in vivo pial intravital microscopy assessed BBB endothelial-LEU interactions and microvascular permeability. Cerebral tissue was procured for wet-to-dry (edema) analysis. Weight loss recovery and the Garcia neurological test gauged neuroclinical recovery. RESULTS: In vivo LEU rolling was greatest in I + Placebo and lowest with combined treatments I + QTP+βB. In vivo BBB permeability was greatest in I + Placebo (0.7 ± 0.03%) and similarly reduced by QTP (0.4 ± 0.03%), βB (0.4 ± 0.03%), and I + QTP+βB (0.4 ± 0.02%) (all P < 0.0001 versus I + P). However, whole hemisphere cerebral edema was lowest in I + QTP+βB. Combination therapy (I + QTP+βB) optimized weight loss recovery and normalized Garcia neurological test scores (17.7 ± 0.2 versus I + P:15.3 ± 0.2; P < 0.0001). CONCLUSIONS: Combining post-TBI quetiapine and propranolol additively modulates TBI, reduces BBB leukocyte mobilization and brain edema, and enhances neuroclinical recovery. Dual therapy should be investigated in humans following severe TBI.

title: CellColocDB: a disease-centred resource linking GWAS loci to genes, cell contexts, and fine-mapping evidence.
abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified disease-associated loci, but linking these signals to molecular mechanisms remains difficult because of linkage disequilibrium and context-dependent genetic regulation. CellColocDB is a disease- and window-centred resource integrating GWAS-QTL colocalization across bulk, sorted-cell, and single-cell QTL datasets. The current release includes 2805 GWAS datasets covering 1201 diseases and traits and 40 516 GWAS windows, together with 23 QTL sources, 316 QTL contexts, and 89 842 molecular features. CellColocDB contains 3 572 118 coloc.abf results with PP.H4 > 0.5, including 1 609 418 with PP.H4 ≥ 0.8. Analyses are organized as GWAS dataset × GWAS window × QTL context × molecular feature tasks, allowing contexts and molecular features to be compared within the same GWAS region. coloc.abf is the primary colocalization analysis, with coloc-SuSiE and SMR/HEIDI providing complementary evidence where available. Task-specific ABF top SNPs are linked to CAUSALdb2 fine-mapping results from seven methods. Results are available through disease-, QTL context-, gene-, and locus-level views, with regional association tracks and matched variants, and can be queried by gene, genomic region, or GWAS window ID. CellColocDB is freely available at http://www.mulinlab.org/colocdb/.

title: Neuroprotective effects of metformin on cognition, mTOR, and inflammatory cytokines in a scopolamine-induced cognitive impairment model in ovariectomized rats.
abstract: Metformin, with its antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and neuroprotective properties, exhibits protective activity on the central nervous system (CNS). This study examined metformin's impact on anxiety-related cognitive deficits and hippocampal level of cytokines in Alzheimer's (AD)-like and ovariectomized rats. Eighty female Wistar rats were divided into eight groups: control, sham, ovariectomy (ovx), scopolamine (sco), ovariectomy +scopolamine (ovx + sco), metformin + scopolamine (met + sco), metformin + ovariectomy (met + ovx), and metformin + ovariectomy + scopolamine (met + ovx+sco). Morris Water Maze (MWM), Elevated Plus Maze (EPM) tests, Nissl and Thioflavin staining, ELISA, and Western Blot were used. In all groups, Metformin was administered before intraperitoneal injection of scopolamine and before ovariectomy surgery.MWM behavioral test results showed that metformin improved spatial memory in impaired groups (SCO, OVX + SCO and OVX). The EPM behavioral test indicated that metformin could improve the increased anxiety levels found in the impaired groups. Nissl staining revealed the neuronal damage in the rats of the impaired group. Thioflavin staining showed that metformin reduced the number of beta-amyloid plaques in the treatment groups. ELISA results demonstrated increased the levels of cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6) in the impaired groups, and metformin reduced these levels. Western blot results showed increased mTOR expression in the affected groups, which metformin was able to reduce. The results indicated that metformin administration prior to intraperitoneal scopolamine injection and ovariectomy surgery was associated with improved learning and spatial memory, reduced anxiety and inflammatory cytokine levels and decreased mTOR expression.

title: Astrocytic Hopx Overexpression Ameliorates Amyloid-β Plaque Burden and Cognitive Deficits in Alzheimer's Disease Mouse Models.
abstract: Astrocytic dysfunction is closely associated with nearly all types of neurological diseases. Targeting astrocyte regulation has thus emerged as an important potential therapeutic strategy for neurological disorders. However, mechanisms that induce astrocyte dysfunction under pathological conditions have not been fully elucidated. In this study, we identified that Homeodomain-only protein X (Hopx) is downregulated in astrocytes across inflammatory models, Alzheimer's disease (AD) mouse models, and brain tissues from AD patients. In the brains of AD mice, Hopx-positive astrocytes exhibit efficient β-amyloid (Aβ) plaque clearance. Furthermore, astrocyte-targeted Hopx expression reduces Aβ plaque burden and alters astrocytic subcluster transition in 5×FAD mice. More importantly, astrocytic Hopx overexpression via intrathecal AAV injection significantly improves cognitive function of AD mice. In summary, this study highlights the pivotal role of Hopx in astrocytic function under AD pathological conditions, providing a promising therapeutic target for AD and potentially for other neurological diseases.

title: Microglial SIRT3 restrains maladaptive inflammatory-phagocytic activation and neuronal vulnerability in acute tau models.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Tau pathology is a defining feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD) and related tauopathies. Microglia play important roles in tau uptake, clearance, and propagation, yet the mechanisms that govern their functional responses to tau-associated stress remain incompletely understood. Sirtuin-3 (SIRT3), an NAD+-dependent deacetylase predominantly localized to mitochondria, is a key regulator of mitochondrial integrity and metabolic homeostasis; however, its role in microglial responses to tau pathology remains unclear. METHODS: We employed complementary in vitro and in vivo models to investigate the role of microglial SIRT3 under tau-associated conditions. SIRT3-deficient HMC3 cells and human monocyte-derived microglia-like cells (MDMi) were assessed for mitochondrial integrity, inflammatory activation, tau uptake, and metabolic alterations using transcriptomic and functional metabolic analyses. In vivo, microglia-specific inducible SIRT3 knockout mice were examined in acute tau challenge models using fluorescently labeled and disease-associated tau preparations to assess neuroinflammatory responses, tau accumulation, mitochondrial damage, and neuronal vulnerability. In addition, AD-derived MDMi and postmortem cortical tissues were analyzed to examine microglial SIRT3 expression in relation to tau pathology. RESULTS: SIRT3 deficiency caused marked mitochondrial structural abnormalities and functional impairment in microglia, accompanied by increased ROS production, enhanced migration, inflammatory activation, and increased uptake of tau. Transcriptomic profiling and functional metabolic analyses further demonstrated a shift toward glycolysis-biased metabolism together with activation of stress- and microenvironment-responsive transcriptional programs. In vivo, microglia-specific SIRT3 deletion exacerbated neuroinflammatory responses, tau accumulation, mitochondrial damage, and neuronal vulnerability in acute tau challenge models using fluorescently labeled and disease-associated tau preparations. Notably, SIRT3 expression was increased in AD patient-derived MDMi and in microglia within postmortem cortical regions with high tau burden in AD patients. Consistent with a context-dependent response, tau exposure induced dynamic changes in microglial SIRT3 expression over time. CONCLUSIONS: Microglial SIRT3 functions as a stress-responsive metabolic checkpoint linking mitochondrial homeostasis to inflammatory-phagocytic activation under acute tau-associated stress. SIRT3 deficiency promotes mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammatory activation, glycolysis-biased metabolic remodeling, and altered tau handling, which are associated with increased neuronal vulnerability. These findings identify SIRT3-dependent mitochondrial regulation as an important component of microglial response to tau-associated stress and provide a framework for further investigating how metabolic dysfunction contributes to microglial maladaptation in tau-related neurodegenerative diseases.

title: Markers of Blood-Brain Barrier Integrity and Neurodegeneration Across Alzheimer's and Non-Alzheimer Neurodegenerative Diseases.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Dysfunction of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) is increasingly recognized as an early feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, the relationship between BBB integrity, glial activation, and neuronal injury is not fully understood, particularly in non-Alzheimer's disorders such as frontotemporal dementia (NADD/FTD). This exploratory study investigated the relationships between BBB integrity, astroglial activation, and neuronal and tau-related injury in AD, NDD/FTD, and cognitively healthy controls (HCs). METHODS: Of the 105 individuals who were screened, the final analytic cohort, which was characterized using PET and CSF, comprised 63 participants. These included 34 individuals with AD, 16 HCs, and 13 participants with NADD/FTD. BBB integrity was assessed using platelet-derived growth factor receptor β (PDGFRβ), CSF fibrinogen, and the CSF/serum albumin ratio (QAlb). Plasma glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), neurofilament light chain (NfL), and phosphorylated tau 217 (pTau217) were assessed as markers of astroglial activation, axonal injury and tau pathology, respectively. Exploratory statistical analyses were adjusted for age and sex. RESULTS: Markers of BBB integrity did not significantly distinguish between the diagnostic groups (all p > 0.05). Significant associations were observed across the full cohort between CSF fibrinogen and CSF total tau and QAlb, and between plasma GFAP, NfL, and pTau217 (r = 0.65-0.70, all p < 0.001 for GFAP). In exploratory mediation analyses, neither tested model showed a significant indirect effect. No comparable amyloid-related mediation effects were observed. Exploratory mediation analyses involving other markers of BBB dysfunction likewise showed no significant indirect effects. CONCLUSION: BBB-related markers did not demonstrate consistent associations with astroglial activation and neuronal injury across diagnostic groups within this cross-sectional cohort. While these findings do not exclude a role for BBB alterations in neurodegenerative processes, they do suggest that their biological significance and potential relevance across disease stages remain unclear. Further research is required in the form of larger longitudinal studies to investigate these relationships.

title: Multimodal PET/MR imaging in Alzheimer's disease: A comparative study of structural, metabolic, synaptic and perfusion measures.
abstract: PURPOSE: Structural MRI and 18F-FDG PET are clinically established imaging biomarkers of neuronal injury in Alzheimer's disease (AD). Synaptic density PET (SV2A), arterial spin labelling (ASL, perfusion), and cortical thickness (CTh) can offer additional information, but have not been compared within the same patients. We performed a head-to-head evaluation of these imaging measures for detecting neurodegeneration, discriminating AD from healthy volunteers (HV) and examining their associations with cognition. METHODS: Thirty-six biomarker-confirmed AD patients (71 ± 9 y/o; M/F 17/19) underwent 18F-FDG, 18F-SynVesT-1 PET/MR and neuropsychological evaluation. Patients were classified as MCI-stage (CDR = 0.5, n = 22) or dementia-stage (CDR > 0.5, n = 14). Image processing and analysis was performed in CAT12.9 with partial volume correction for PET. PET and ASL measures were normalized to the whole cerebellum. Classification performance was evaluated with partial least squares discriminant analysis and Firth logistic regression under repeated stratified 5-fold cross-validation. RESULTS: In the MCI-stage, reductions were mainly found in the temporal cortex. In the dementia-stage, reductions for the 5 imaging measures extended to the temporoparietal, precuneal and frontal cortices. 18F-FDG PET, assessed against a separate HV cohort, showed large reductions (Cohen's d up to -2.5) and excellent discriminatory performance (AUC = 0.94). Among the cortical measures evaluated against the same HV, cortical thickness showed the largest reductions (d up to -1.6). Cortical thickness, 18F-SynVesT-1 and volumetry provided similar discriminatory performance (AUC 0.81-0.86). ASL did not show detectable reductions in MCI and had a lower AUC (0.72). Global cognition was associated with widespread atrophy, cortical thinning, and 18F-FDG hypometabolism, whereas domain-specific cognitive measures showed more localized regional associations. 18F-SynVesT-1 and ASL demonstrated weaker and less consistent correlations. CONCLUSION: Multimodal PET and MRI measures showed overlapping yet distinct spatial patterns of neurodegeneration. In MCI, structural, metabolic and synaptic abnormalities were found, whereas perfusion deficits only significantly emerged in dementia-stage AD. Structural and functional measures differentially relate to global and domain-specific cognitive decline. The study was registered on clinicaltrials.gov (NCT05384353) as of 20 May 2022.

title: Lipid regulation of autophagy flux and neurodegeneration.
abstract: Autophagy is a lysosomal degradation pathway crucial for the maintenance of proteostasis, organelle quality control, and stress adaptation. Autophagosomes form from finger-like structures emanating from the recycling endosome, called phagophores, which capture cytoplasmic cargo before closing like a fist. These closed structures are then released from the recycling endosome by dynamin 2 to form autophagosomes that ultimately fuse with lysosomes, where their contents are degraded. In the central nervous system, autophagy protects against the cytoplasmic accumulation of toxic, aggregate-prone proteins and damaged organelles, common features of neurodegenerative diseases such as Huntington's and Alzheimer's disease. Lipids have emerged as crucial mediators of autophagosome biogenesis and have multifaceted effects on autophagic flux. At the edges of the phagophore, coordinated lipid transfer from donor membranes and scramblase activity support appropriate lipid bilayer formation and membrane expansion. In addition, the highly curved, loosely packed lipids at the phagophore edges act as a platform for binding of key autophagy effectors via their amphipathic domains and promote autophagosome maturation. The role of lipids extends beyond structural support in autophagosome formation and includes modulation of upstream signalling pathways, establishment of autophagic membrane identity, and lysosomal maintenance. Autophagy itself contributes to the maintenance of lipid homeostasis via the selective lipid droplet degradation pathway termed lipophagy. Importantly, alterations in lipid composition and metabolism have been demonstrated to impair autophagic flux and contribute to the development of several sporadic and inherited neurological disorders.

title: Proximity-Induced Targeted Degradation of Microtubule-Associated Protein Tau Pre-mRNA Using Small Bifunctional Molecules.
abstract: Dysregulation of RNA processing caused by single-nucleotide mutations can profoundly alter cellular homeostasis and drive disease. A prominent example is the aberrant alternative splicing of the microtubule-associated protein tau (MAPT) gene, which leads to imbalances in 3R and 4R tau isoforms and is associated with multiple tauopathies. In particular, mutations such as the disinhibition-dementia-parkinsonism-amyotrophy complex (DDPAC) variant promote exon 10 inclusion, increasing the 4R/3R ratio and contributing to tau aggregation and neurodegeneration. Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) can reduce MAPT mRNA levels, while small molecules have been developed to modulate MAPT pre-mRNA splicing by targeting regulatory RNA structures. Here, we investigated an alternative approach based on Proximity-Induced Nucleic Acid Degradation (PINAD), in which an RNA-binding ligand is conjugated to an RNA-cleaving warhead. We designed and synthesized a library of 24 bifunctional small molecules derived from a previously reported MAPT pre-mRNA SRE-binding ligand. Screening in SH-SY5Y cells identified PINAD-23, which reduced MAPT mRNA levels in a dose-dependent manner and decreased the expression of both 3R and 4R tau isoforms. Biochemical studies using a model MAPT RNA showed that PINAD-23 binds the target RNA and promotes RNA cleavage. Defined cleavage products detected under metal-free conditions supported a contribution from a base-mediated pathway, while Cu(II) binding by the diimidazole warhead and Cu(II)-dependent RNA cleavage supported the involvement of a copper-dependent pathway. These findings provide a proof of concept for converting a previously characterized MAPT RNA-binding ligand into a bifunctional small molecule capable of inducing target RNA cleavage and reducing downstream tau expression.

title: Engineered autophagy receptors for selective protein clearance in neurodegeneration.
abstract: Engineered autophagy receptors offer a way to direct intracellular degradation toward proteins implicated in neurodegeneration. Guo and colleagues fused cytoplasm-stable antibody fragments to microtubule-associated protein 1A/1B-light chain 3 alpha (LC3A) and delivered the resulting constructs using small extracellular vesicles. Their experiments show reduced pathological tau and cytoplasmic TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) in neuronal cultures and reduced tau pathology in mice. A separate adeno-associated virus experiment reduces TDP-43 pathology and improves motor performance in mice. These findings connect selective cargo recognition with intracellular delivery and raise questions about how engineered autophagy receptors might be adapted to different disease contexts. Here, we discuss which pathological protein assemblies are most accessible to these receptors, how selective clearance interacts with neuronal autophagic capacity, and how intracellular exposure relates to sustained functional benefit. We consider these questions with particular attention to preserving physiological protein function and linking cargo turnover to neuronal outcomes.

title: Mechanism of the lysosomal calcium signaling TRPML1-TFEB axis in Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a prevalent chronic neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive apoptosis of midbrain substantia nigra dopaminergic neurons, striatal dopamine depletion, and α-synuclein (α-syn)-positive Lewy-body formation. Patients exhibit motor deficits (resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, postural instability) plus non-motor manifestations such as cognitive and sleep impairment. PD pathogenesis arises from intertwined mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, defective protein degradation and disrupted calcium homeostasis, whose precise mechanisms remain incompletely defined. As both a degradative organelle and signaling hub, lysosomes govern clearance of proteins and damaged organelles and mediate key neuronal events through calcium-dependent signaling. Transient Receptor Potential Mucolipin 1 (TRPML1), a lysosomal calcium-release channel, and Transcription Factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosome biogenesis and autophagic flux, constitute the conserved TRPML1-TFEB axis that couples lysosomal calcium signaling to transcriptional control of cellular degradation. Physiologically, TRPML1-triggered calcium release activates calcineurin to drive TFEB dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation, one of several convergent routes that maintain neuronal protein and organelle homeostasis; TFEB is likewise engaged by the second lysosomal calcium channel TPC2, by mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) inhibition and by oxidative-stress-dependent phosphatases. Pathological TRPML1 malfunction perturbs lysosomal calcium signaling and suppresses TFEB activity, triggering lysosomal defects, autophagic blockage, α-syn buildup, mitochondrial damage and oxidative stress, which culminate in dopaminergic neuronal death and PD progression. Mounting data identify dysregulation of this axis as a core pathogenic driver bridging lysosomal failure and neurodegeneration across genetic, toxic and ageing-related PD, although for several disease genes the available evidence documents TFEB-dependent lysosomal failure without direct TRPML1 perturbation. This review summarizes this axis' molecular-physiological features, its pathological crosstalk with major PD events, targeted therapeutic progress, research limitations and future directions, offering theoretical clues for PD mechanistic study and novel therapeutic development.

title: Deep Brain Stimulation of the Nucleus Accumbens and Anterior Limb of the Internal Capsule in Severe Autism Spectrum Disorder: Clinical Outcomes and Infralimbic-Accumbens Circuit Involvement.
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder with limited effective treatments. Deep brain stimulation (DBS) has emerged as a potential intervention, yet its efficacy and mechanisms remain poorly understood. We conducted a prospective, single-arm cohort study of nucleus accumbens-anterior limb of the internal capsule (NAc-ALIC) DBS in patients with severe ASD, observing preliminary safety and longitudinal reductions in repetitive-behaviour and social-domain symptom severity during follow-up. Exploratory sweet-spot analysis suggested a candidate medial-ventral NAc region associated with social-domain score reductions. In a maternal immune activation mouse model, NAc-DBS enhanced social novelty preference and reduced repetitive behaviours. NAc-DBS partially normalized aberrant oscillatory activity in the NAc and infralimbic cortex (IL), increased IL neuronal activity, and enhanced cross-frequency coupling. Chemogenetic activation of the IL→NAc projection enhanced social novelty preference, whereas inhibition of IL neurons projecting to the NAc attenuated the DBS-associated social novelty improvement without affecting marble-burying behaviour. NAc-DBS also increased glutamate, AMPA receptor, and brain-derived neurotrophic factor levels, consistent with enhanced synaptic plasticity. Together, these findings provide exploratory clinical evidence of longitudinal reductions in symptom severity during follow-up after NAc-ALIC DBS and suggest that NAc stimulation modulates IL and NAc neural activity, implicates the IL→NAc pathway, and engages plasticity-related processes.

title: Heparan sulfate sulfatases are essential for the patterning of human stem cell-derived midbrain dopaminergic neurons.
abstract: Midbrain dopaminergic neurons (mDA) are selectively lost in Parkinson's disease, driving sustained efforts to generate bona fide mDA neurons from human-induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) for replacement therapy. While morphogen gradients and transcription factors have been extensively studied, extracellular regulators remain largely overlooked. Here, we identify the heparan sulfate-modifying enzymes SULF1 and SULF2 as essential for establishing mDA neuron identity in vitro. Using CRISPR/Cas9-engineered iPSCs, we show that loss of SULF1/2 increases 6-O-sulfated heparan sulfate species and disrupts patterning both at the anteroposterior and dorsoventral axes in human iPSC-derived mDA cultures. Double-knockout cells thus fail to acquire ventral midbrain fates and instead adopt hindbrain, spinal cord and neural crest-like identities as revealed by single-nucleus RNA sequencing. Mechanistically, we partially explain the changed patterning to aberrant FGF signaling and demonstrate that FGF inhibition redirects cells toward midbrain fates, however without restoring ventral identity. These findings establish a critical role for SULF1/2 in mDA neuron in vitro differentiation and uncover a previously unrecognized layer of extracellular control over neural patterning.

title: Proteomic Analysis of Plasma Small Extracellular Vesicles and Targeted Metabolomic Analysis of Plasma From Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder.
abstract: Autism is a neurodevelopmental disorder with deficits in social communication and interaction, restricted and repetitive behaviors, and unusual stereotyped interests or activities. With a lack of molecular information on the etiology of ASD, early diagnosis of this disease remains a challenge. Small extracellular vesicles (sEVs), as extracellular vesicles containing various important biomolecules, have been demonstrated to have a functional impact on physiological processes in the central nervous system. Herein, we profiled the proteome of plasma sEVs collected from preschool children with autism and performed targeted metabolic analysis on their plasma samples. Screening of the differentiated proteins between autistic and healthy children revealed potential biomarkers, including those involved in calcium ion binding, such as MACF1 and CALM3. Bioinformatic investigation further identified 10 outlier proteins, such as EHD1 and ERF3A, strongly associated with autism. Targeted metabolic analysis and IPA prediction suggested the potential involvement of the PI3K-AKT/mTOR signaling pathway. The sEV proteomic and plasma metabolomic analyses were performed in parallel, and pathway-level findings from each dataset were compared descriptively. These results provide insight into the biological mechanism of autism and promise in determining biomarkers for the early diagnosis of ASD. title: An Anti-Adhesive Hydrogel Delivering Ginger-Derived Exosome-Like Nanoparticles Reshapes the Neuroinflammatory Microenvironment After Traumatic Brain Injury.
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) triggers secondary injury involving neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction, highlighting the need for multi-target therapies. Ginger-derived exosome-like nanoparticles (GELNs) offer multi-target therapeutic potential but are limited by insufficient local retention and rapid clearance. TBI-induced brain-skull adhesion may further aggravate the pathological environment. To address these limitations, an anti-adhesive hydrogel (CG) composed of methacrylated chondroitin sulfate and 2-methacryloyloxyethyl phosphorylcholine is loaded with GELNs to form CG-GELNs. CG-GELNs attenuates pathological brain-skull adhesion and provides greater behavioral benefits than free GELNs, including reduced anxiety-like behavior, improved social novelty discrimination, and enhanced spatial memory. At the pathological level, CG-GELNs confers coordinated protection against secondary injury by preserving blood-brain barrier integrity, suppressing pro-inflammatory responses, mitigating mitochondrial damage and oxidative stress, and ultimately preserving synaptic function. Mechanistically, GELNs-associated microRNA-396 (miR-396) suppresses secreted phosphoprotein 1 (SPP1) expression, and functional rescue experiments support the contribution of this miR-396/SPP1 axis to the anti-inflammatory effects of GELNs in microglial cells. Overall, CG-GELNs simultaneously improves localized delivery of GELNs, attenuates pathological brain-skull adhesion, and suppresses neuroinflammation, offering a potentially translatable therapeutic platform for remodeling the neuroinflammatory microenvironment and promoting neurological recovery after TBI.

title: Functional transcriptomic profile of mouse controlled cortical impact model of post-traumatic epilepsy with robust spontaneous recurrent seizures.
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major cause of acquired epilepsy, yet the molecular changes linking the initial injury to post-traumatic epilepsy (PTE) remain incompletely understood. Here, we used a severe controlled cortical impact mouse model that develops robust spontaneous recurrent seizures to characterize the temporal and regional progression of post-traumatic transcriptional responses. Bulk RNA sequencing was performed on the contralateral cortex and hippocampus collected from TBI and time-matched sham mice at 7, 21, and 60 days after injury, corresponding to the acute injury, latent period, and chronic epilepsy phases, respectively. Transcriptomic changes were characterized using differentially expressed gene (DEG) analysis, Gene Ontology and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes gene-set enrichment analyses, and Ingenuity Pathway Analysis. Transcriptomic responses were strongly dependent on brain region and disease phase. At 7 days, the cortex showed enhanced neuronal and structural signaling alongside suppression of immune, metabolic, and cell-cycle processes, whereas the hippocampus showed prominent neuroimmune activation and metabolic stress. By 21 days, before the emergence of spontaneous seizures, the hippocampus shifted toward partial normalization of metabolic pathway enrichment, accompanied by suppression of neurotransmission, synaptic plasticity, and neuronal organization. In contrast, the cortex showed increased enrichment of immune and tissue-remodeling processes. Although relatively few DEGs were detected at 60 days, a selective hippocampal signature persisted after PTE was established. Pathway analyses converged on coordinated changes in neuroimmune, metabolic, lipid-regulatory, and synaptic processes. Upstream Regulator Analysis further identified a temporal reversal in APOE-associated regulatory activity, linking inflammatory and lipid-metabolic responses with later synaptic remodeling. The 21-day post-injury hippocampus represents a critical disease-modification window. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that PTE progression involves phase-specific molecular remodeling that shifts from an early cortical response to sustained hippocampal dysregulation. The latent hippocampal signature identifies a potentially actionable molecular window before recurrent seizure onset.

title: Spatial Transcriptomics Reveals the Macroscale Signatures of Cortical Cell Types on Anatomic Magnetic Resonance Imaging.
abstract: ​Esta​blishing how intensity in magnetic resonance images (MRIs) covaries with molecular factors can help to derive quasi-mechanistic biological insights from neuroimaging. Gray/white matter contrast (GWC) of [Formula: see text]-weighted MRI is an abundantly available phenotype often used to investigate aging and cognition. Despite growing interest in investigating microstructure using GWC, its relationship to cell type-related tissue properties is understudied. We leverage spatially resolved post-mortem transcriptomic data from six donors to identify associations between cell type marker genes and GWC averaged across cognitively normal living adults ([Formula: see text] = 577, mean age = 56.2 years). Astrocyte marker gene transcription is significantly associated with cortical variation in mean GWC, referred to as [Formula: see text]. Additionally, estimated relative astrocyte abundance correlates significantly with [Formula: see text] ([Formula: see text] = 0.409, [Formula: see text] < 0.01). Gene transcription correlations with [Formula: see text] are enriched for oligodendrocyte marker genes only within the frontal lobe, which is known to age fastest. Transcriptions of genes related to iron trafficking and myelination help to identify potential explanations for associations of [Formula: see text] to astrocyte and oligodendrocyte distributions. A multivariate linear model of cell abundances explains 31% ([Formula: see text] = 0.56) of variation in [Formula: see text], of which [Formula: see text]40% is attributable to neurons, ~33% to endothelial cells, and ~15.7% to microglia. Findings are replicated in two additional independent cohorts of cognitive normal adults ([Formula: see text] = 577 in each), indicating that reported associations are not dependent on scanner parameters. Our findings empower interpretation of GWC and its use in studying aging and disease.

title: Ghrelin ameliorates Alzheimer's disease by reversing mitochondrial dysfunction in hippocampal neurons via the GHSR-1α/Sirt1-FOXO1/3 pathway.
abstract: Although ghrelin has been shown to exert neuroprotective effects, whether it can reverse mitochondrial dysfunction in hippocampal neurons in association with specific signaling axes remains unclear. Network pharmacology was employed to predict the potential targets of ghrelin in AD. An Aβ25-35-induced injury model was established in primary cultured mouse hippocampal neurons. An in vitro rescue model was constructed using SIRT1 overexpression plasmid transfection and lentiviral-mediated knockdown. In an AD mouse model established by intracerebroventricular injection of Aβ25-35, ghrelin was administered intraperitoneally and SIRT1 knockdown lentivirus was delivered intranasally. Cognitive behaviors were evaluated using the Morris water maze and open field tests, and pathological changes in brain tissues were assessed by H&E and Nissl staining. Network pharmacology analysis identified 168 potential targets shared between ghrelin and AD, among which the SIRT1-FOXO1/3 signaling pathway was significantly enriched. In vitro experiments showed that Ghrelin significantly upregulated the expression of GHSR-1α, SIRT1, FOXO1, and FOXO3 in Aβ-injured neurons, reduced ROS levels, restored the NAD⁺/NADH ratio, and was associated with enhanced PINK1/Parkin-related autophagic markers. Overexpression of SIRT1 mimicked the protective effects of ghrelin. In vivo experiments further demonstrated that intraperitoneal administration of ghrelin significantly ameliorated cognitive dysfunction in AD mice and alleviated neuronal pathological damage in the hippocampal CA1 region, whereas SIRT1 knockdown reversed these protective effects. Ghrelin treatment was associated with enhanced PINK1/Parkin-related autophagy and improved mitochondrial homeostasis.

title: External validation of a mathematical model of brain health.
abstract: BackgroundUnderstanding the mechanisms underlying brain aging and age-related pathological changes is essential for advancing brain health research. Our group previously developed a mechanistic mathematical model of healthy brain that integrates key biological processes involved in normal aging, from which Alzheimer's disease (AD)-related changes may emerge naturally.ObjectiveTo characterize and validate this brain model by evaluating its sensitivity, calibrating its parameters, and assessing generalizability in independent populations.MethodsThe model represents the evolution of key biological processes associated with brain aging, including amyloid-β (Aβ), tau pathologies, neuroinflammation, and neuronal death. After identifying the 30 most influential parameters, we calibrated the model using cognitively normal participants from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database (n = 211) by minimizing a loss function composed of three outcomes (Aβ plaques, tau tangles, and neuronal density). The calibrated model was then applied to the UK Biobank cohort (n = 35,899) of normal controls (aged 44-82 years). The effects of sex and APOE were evaluated using stratified simulations.ResultsParameter calibration significantly reduced the prediction errors for Aβ and tau. Neuronal density predictions showed strong agreement in the UK Biobank cohort. The variance decomposition identified APOE status as a major contributor to variability in Aβ.ConclusionsOur validated brain health model links mechanistic pathways with population data and reproduces neuronal density patterns in an independent cohort. These findings support its use as a framework for studying brain aging and investigating how AD-related pathological changes may emerge with aging.

title: Phenotypic expansion of TUBGCP6 primary microcephaly: severe cortical malformations without chorioretinopathy and insights into variant interpretation.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Biallelic variants of TUBGCP6 are associated with primary microcephaly, chorioretinopathy, short stature, and intellectual disability (ID). Most reported cases had at least one loss-of-function variant. PURPOSE: : We aimed to refine the phenotypic spectrum associated with novel TUBGCP6 variants in 3 patients, including 2 with biallelic missense variants, and compare them with 13 previously reported cases. METHODS: : Neurological, cognitive, and neuroimaging data were assessed in 3 patients carrying TUBGCP6 variants identified using next-generation sequencing. These 3 patients were recruited through the Microfanc project (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT01565005) or a call for collaboration with the ITHACA European Reference Network. Functional analyses of the fibroblasts from 1 patient included Western blotting, immunofluorescence, and proximity ligation assays. Variants were further characterized using complementary sequence- and structure-based in silico analyses, including structural modeling, stability, conservation, and protein language model-based predictions. RESULTS: : None of the patients had chorioretinopathy or short stature at the last follow-up (age: 7.8, 15, and 17.6 years). Two patients presented with malformations of cortical development, microcephaly, gyral simplification, and focal epilepsy. Cognitive impairment ranged from borderline intelligence quotient to severe ID. Patient 1 carried compound heterozygous missense variants, p.(Val359Ile) and p.(Gly990Arg). TUBGCP6 failed to localize to the centrosome and to interact with γ-tubulin. Patient 2 carried the homozygous missense variant p.(Leu448Pro) predicted to destabilize TUBGCP6. Patient 3 harbored 2 compound heterozygous frameshift variants, p.(Gln1389GlyfsTer13), which was predicted to under gononsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD), and p.(Pro1759AlafsTer68), which may produce an aberrant C-terminal extension, although NMD remains possible. CONCLUSION: : This study expands the phenotypic spectrum of TUBGCP6-related diseases to include malformations of cortical development, microcephaly with or without ID, and the absence of chorioretinopathy. Our combined in vitro and in silico findings suggest that stable but dysfunctional TUBGCP6 may produce a more severe brain phenotype than a complete loss of function, while sparing the retina. However, these mechanistic insights remain preliminary.

title: WFS1 deficiency impacts GnRH neuron development through mechanisms involving ER stress dysregulation.
abstract: Wolfram Syndrome, a rare neurodegenerative disorder caused by biallelic mutations in the WFS1 gene, presents with endocrine and neurological features. Although hypogonadism has been described in Wolfram Syndrome, the role of WFS1 in reproductive development is not well understood. Congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (CHH) is a rare genetic disorder characterized by deficient development or function of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neurons. Through whole-exome sequencing in familial CHH cases, we identified two rare heterozygous missense variants in WFS1. Functional in vitro assays revealed reduced protein levels, activation of endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress and unfolded protein response (UPR). Zebrafish and mouse embryos studies showed WFS1 expression in regions critical for GnRH neuron development. Knockdown of wfs1b in Tg(GnRH3:EGFP) zebrafish embryos disrupted GnRH3 neuronal architecture and downregulated isl1a, a key transcription factor for axon guidance. Our findings support a mechanistic model linking WFS1-mediated ER homeostasis, isl1a expression, and GnRH neuron development. We propose WFS1 as a novel candidate modifier in CHH pathogenesis and provide in vivo evidence that ER stress and isl1a dysregulation impair the formation of GnRH neuronal network.

title: Cross-tissue transcriptome-wide association analyses prioritize the 17q21.31 locus in autism spectrum disorder.
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) has a complex genetic architecture, and the regulatory transcripts underlying common-variant associations with ASD risks remain incompletely resolved. We integrated ASD genome-wide association summary statistics with genetically predicted expression across 29 GTEx v8 tissues using Joint-Tissue Imputation (JTI) and FUSION, followed by summary-data-based Mendelian randomization (SMR), regional conditional/joint analysis, colocalization and comparison with external ASD molecular evidence. All-tissue false-discovery-rate correction identified 264 significant JTI gene-tissue associations representing 64 genes and 561 FUSION associations representing 128 genes, with an overlap of 40 genes between JTI and FUSION and 152 unique genes in the union set. Brain eQTL and mQTL SMR identified 22 and 21 significant probes, respectively, while analyses across 16 non-brain tissues identified 59 significant probe-tissue associations. TWAS signals converged at 17q21.31. Conditional/joint FUSION retained only the Brain Cerebellar Hemisphere MAPT-AS1 model among 353 significant associations in the primary regional analysis, with the same model retained in an extended-window sensitivity analysis. BrainMeta-ASD colocalization was completed for 23 probes; none met the prespecified criterion for strong colocalization, and MAPT showed the highest PP·H4 (0.5052). Among the 152 union genes, 82 were supported by at least one of the Huang, Matoba or Gandal studies and 15 by at least two; MAPT and XRN2 were the only genes supported by all three data sets. MAPT-AS1 was supported by Matoba et al. in H-MAGMA analysis and is classified as a Category 2 gene in SFARI Gene, while Walker et al. provided additional developmental-brain context through prenatal-brain TWAS. These findings prioritize 17q21.31 as an ASD-associated locus supported across multiple genetic and regulatory evidence layers.

title: The niacin receptor HCAR2 alleviates depression-like behaviors by suppressing microglial NLRP3 inflammasome and complement-mediated synaptic pruning.
abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a leading cause of disability, yet current antidepressants are limited by treatment resistance and delayed onset. Neuroimmune inflammation and aberrant synaptic pruning are core pathological drivers, but targeted therapeutics remain scarce. Hydroxycarboxylic acid receptor 2 (HCAR2), a microglia-enriched GPCR and the target of niacin, has shown anti-inflammatory potential, but its role in depression is unknown. Using a chronic unpredictable mild stress mouse model with bidirectional HCAR2 manipulation, we found that chronic stress impaired hippocampal HCAR2 signaling. Niacin robustly alleviated depressive-like behaviors, whereas HCAR2 knockout markedly attenuated these effects and exacerbated stress vulnerability. Mechanistically, HCAR2 activation suppressed hippocampal neuroinflammation and microglial NLRP3 inflammasome activation via a non-canonical, ARRB2-dependent endocytic pathway: activated HCAR2 internalized into microglial endosomes, bound NEK7, and blocked NLRP3 inflammasome assembly. Concurrently, HCAR2 preserved synaptic integrity by inhibiting complement C3/CR3 signaling and attenuating excessive microglial synaptic phagocytosis. In conclusion, HCAR2 acts as an endogenous protective regulator in depression via dual mechanisms: ARRB2-mediated endosomal sequestration of NEK7 to suppress NLRP3 inflammasome, and inhibition of complement-driven synaptic pruning. These findings identify HCAR2 as a promising therapeutic target and provide a rationale for repurposing niacin in MDD treatment.

title: Integrated serum metabolomics and hippocampal transcriptomics reveal metabolic reprogramming associated with BBB impairment and hippocampal injury in HFD-fed mice.
abstract: AIMS: Increasing evidence suggests that high-fat diet (HFD) consumption induces systemic metabolic disturbances and is associated with blood-brain barrier (BBB) dysfunction and hippocampal injury. This study aimed to explore the potential mechanisms linking HFD-induced metabolic disturbances to BBB and hippocampal abnormalities. METHODS: Male C57BL/6J mice were fed an HFD or a normal diet (ND) for 12 weeks. Systemic metabolic and inflammatory status, hepatic lipid accumulation, neurobehavioral performance, hippocampal injury, BBB integrity, and hippocampal inflammatory alterations were systematically assessed. Integrated serum untargeted metabolomics and hippocampal transcriptomics were performed to identify key molecular pathways. RESULTS: HFD-fed mice exhibited systemic metabolic disturbances, increased BBB permeability, hippocampal neuronal injury and inflammation, and impaired motor coordination. Integrated serum metabolomic and hippocampal transcriptomic analyses identified alterations in histidine and glycerophospholipid metabolism. Hippocampal transcriptomic analysis revealed upregulation of carnosine dipeptidase 1 (Cndp1) and phospholipase A2 group IVE (Pla2g4e) and downregulation of diacylglycerol kinase kappa (Dgkk) and ethanolamine-phosphate phospho-lyase (Etnppl), which were further validated by RT-qPCR. Serum metabolomic analysis further revealed decreased serum carnosine levels. Given the reported neuroprotective properties of carnosine, we further investigated its effects in palmitic acid-treated HT22 cells. Carnosine improved cell viability, attenuated oxidative stress and inflammatory responses, and modulated the expression of Cndp1, Pla2g4e, Etnppl, and Dgkk. CONCLUSION: HFD was associated with BBB impairment, hippocampal inflammatory activation, neuronal injury, and behavioral alterations. Integrated metabolomic and transcriptomic analyses implicated histidine and glycerophospholipid metabolism associated with HFD-induced metabolic disturbances and hippocampal injury.

title: Sjögren's Disease Salivary Gland Fibroblast Subsets are Interferon Enriched and Aberrantly Promote Pain.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Fibroblasts are emerging as critical mediators in the pathogenesis of Sjögren's Disease (SjD) onset and progression. This study aimed to define fibroblast subpopulations within salivary glands (SG) and elucidate their functional contributions to SjD pathogenesis. METHODS: We analyzed 3' single-cell RNA sequencing data from minor SG biopsies of individuals with SjD (n = 17; 58,205 cells) and controls (n = 19; 33,584 cells). Data processing and analysis employed Cell Ranger, Seurat, Harmony, DESeq2, ENRICHR, Ingenuity Pathway Analysis, and CellPhoneDB. Key findings were validated using immunofluorescence microscopy of human SG tissue, primary human fibroblasts, mouse dorsal root ganglion cells, in vivo mouse models, and spatial transcriptomics. RESULTS: Salivary glands from SjD patients exhibited an expanded fibroblast compartment enriched for interferon (IFN)-responsive gene expression. Subclustering identified six distinct fibroblast populations. Among these, FMO2+ fibroblasts demonstrated the strongest IFN signature and engaged in disease-specific ligand-receptor interactions with myeloid cells, which spatially co-localized in SjD tissue. A distinct NEGR1 (aka: KILON)+ fibroblast population uniquely expressed nerve- and axon-associated transcripts. Functional studies revealed Kilon treatment sensitized mouse dorsal root ganglia sensory neurons in vitro (p≤0.01) and increased pain sensitivity in vivo (p≤0.01). CONCLUSIONS: This study defines previously unrecognized fibroblast heterogeneity in SjD. FMO2+ fibroblasts exhibit an IFN-enriched transcriptional profile and might communicate with myeloid cells. In contrast, KILON+ fibroblasts represent a novel neuro-associated subset possibly capable of modulating pain. Together, these findings highlight distinct and pathogenic roles for fibroblast subsets in SjD and identify new avenues for therapeutic intervention.
