title: Drp-1 Participates in LPS-Induced Neuroinflammation and Microglia-Neuron Interaction Through mtDNA-cGAS-STING Axis.
abstract: To investigate the role of dynamin-related protein 1 (Drp-1) in the process of LPS-induced microglial injury and its initiated neuroinflammation. C57BL/6J mice or BV2 microglia were challenged with LPS, and the behavioral performance and the cell viability were tested, respectively. The expression of Drp-1, inflammatory factors, and key molecules of the cGAS-STING signaling pathway was measured in the mouse hippocampus or in microglia in vitro, together with the abundance of mtDNA. Moreover, the effect of Drp-1 was further explored by siRNA in vitro and its selective inhibitor Mdivi-1 in vivo. Furthermore, a co-culture system of microglia and neurons was used to observe the potential role of cell-free mtDNA in the microglia-neuron crosstalk. Meanwhile, the plasma levels of cell-free mitochondrial DNA (cf-mtDNA) were detected in patients with major depressive disorder (MDD). In vivo, intraperitoneal injection of LPS could result in anxious-like and depression-like behaviors in mice, together with a significant microglial activation and its related neuroinflammation, mtDNA release, and the imbalanced expression of synaptic plasticity, Drp-1, cGAS, STING, p-STING, and IRF3 in the hippocampus. All these behavioral and neuropathological changes could be reversed by treatment with Mdivi-1. Moreover, LPS-induced behavioral dysfunction and neuropathological injuries were also observed in mice that received hippocampal stereotactic injection of mtDNA. In vitro, besides the detrimental effect of LPS on microglia, our results indicated a crucial role of microglia-derived mtDNA in linking Drp-1-associated mitochondrial dysfunction to LPS-induced microglial injury and neuroinflammation, and in the crosstalk between HT22 and BV2 cells. Additionally, the plasma concentration of cf-mtDNA was increased in MDD patients, with a significant positive correlation with plasma levels of IL-6, IL-1β, TNF-α, and IFN-γ. As a key regulator of mitochondrial fission, the imbalanced expression of Drp-1 participates in LPS-induced microglial injury and neuroinflammation via the Drp-1-mtDNA-cGAS-STING axis.

title: Tangeretin improves Neuro-2a cell survival after oxygen-glucose deprivation via phosphorylation of Akt.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Hypoxic-ischemic brain injury (HIBI) results from insufficient cerebral blood flow and hypoxia and can cause severe damage to the neonatal brain, leading to long term neurological disabilities. In this study, we hypothesized that tangeretin would improve cell survival by modulating mitochondrial potential in Neuro-2a (N2a) cells after oxygen-glucose deprivation (OGD) via Akt phosphorylation. METHODS: N2a cells underwent 3 hours of OGD to mimic HIBI in vitro. Cells were treated with Tangeretin +/- MK2206 (an Akt inhibitor) or vehicle immediately after OGD. Cell survival was quantified by alamarBlue, propidium iodide, and TUNEL assays. Mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP) was determined by JC-1 fluorescence. Protein expression was evaluated using western blotting. RESULTS: Treatment with tangeretin significantly improved N2a cell survival after OGD, which was reversed with co-treatment with MK2206. Specifically, tangeretin improved apoptotic DNA fragmentation in cells as measured by TUNEL assay, which was also attenuated by MK2206. OGD significantly increased the percentage mitochondrial depolarization and reactive oxygen species in N2a cells compared with normoxic groups. Tangeretin treatment significantly diminished this effect. CONCLUSION: Tangeretin provided neuroprotection against OGD in N2a cells by enhancing cell survival, maintaining mitochondrial membrane potential and suppressing apoptosis. Tangeretin deserves further exploration for its neuroprotective effects against HIBI. IMPACT: In Neuro-2a cells injured by oxygen and glucose deprivation (OGD), tangeretin enhances cell survival. Tangeretin-associated cell survival is mediated in part by reduced DNA fragmentation. Tangeretin preserves mitochondrial membrane potential after OGD. The neuroprotective effects of tangeretin are at least partially mediated by Akt phosphorylation. Tangeretin deserves further evaluation for its neuroprotective effects after hypoxic-ischemic brain injury.
authors: Yadav RK, Johnson AO, Peeples ES
overview: BACKGROUND: Hypoxic-ischemic brain injury (HIBI) results from insufficient cerebral blood flow and hypoxia and can cause severe damage to the neonatal brain, leading to long term neurological disabilities.
main: RESULTS: Treatment with tangeretin significantly improved N2a cell survival after OGD, which was reversed with co-treatment with MK2206.

title: Strontium-90 Radiotherapy Suppresses Fibrosis by Attenuating the FAK-RhoA/ROCK-YAP/TAZ Mechanosignaling Axis in Hypertrophic Scars.
abstract: Hypertrophic scar (HTS) fibrosis is sustained by abnormal mechanical signaling, but how strontium-90 (Sr-90) superficial radiotherapy counteracts this process is unclear. We combined primary HTS fibroblasts and a rabbit ear HTS model with atomic force microscopy, molecular and functional assays, histology, and RNA sequencing to examine cell mechanics and FAK-RhoA/ROCK-YAP/TAZ signaling. Sr-90 reduced fibroblast stiffness and stress-fiber organization, inhibited nuclear YAP/TAZ localization, TEAD activity, profibrotic gene expression, migration, adhesion, and collagen-gel contraction, while increasing LATS1/2 phosphorylation and suppressing FAK/Src-RhoA/ROCK-MLC2 signaling. YAP/TAZ overexpression partially reversed these effects, TEAD1/4 silencing diminished the reversal, and non-phosphorylatable YAP-5SA/TAZ-4SA mutants produced stronger rescue than the corresponding wild-type proteins under irradiation. In rabbits, Sr-90 reduced scar pathology, YAP/TAZ-TEAD interaction, and FAK-RhoA signaling and downregulated Hippo- and focal-adhesion-related transcriptional programs. These findings show that Sr-90 suppresses HTS fibrosis by weakening the mechanical-signaling network that converges on YAP/TAZ and by enhancing LATS1/2-dependent YAP/TAZ inactivation.

title: Mycobacterium tuberculosis CpsA interferes with the TBK1-p62 axis to inhibit xenophagy.
abstract: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) survives in macrophages by interfering with host lysosomal trafficking. Previously, we demonstrated that the Mtb protein, CpsA, is critical for bacterial survival in macrophages and infection in mice and that it can inhibit a noncanonical autophagy pathway. We also found that CpsA can interact with NDP52 and TAX1BP1, selective autophagy receptors that recognize cytosolic bacteria and target them for degradation, raising the possibility that CpsA also disrupts canonical autophagy. Here, we show that CpsA binds NDP52 and TAX1BP1 in their SKICH domains, which normally recruit the autophagy initiation machinery and TBK1. We demonstrate that CpsA prevents phagosomal recruitment of FIP200, a component of the autophagy initiation machinery, and blocks TBK1-dependent phosphorylation of p62, leading to impaired xenophagy. Our findings provide mechanistic insight into how Mtb subverts host defenses, revealing that in addition to blocking noncanonical autophagy, CpsA inhibits the TBK1-p62 axis to block xenophagy.

title: Sinomenine attenuates neuroinflammation and neurological deficits following intracerebral hemorrhage: involvement of CaMKIIα-AKT and cAMP-PKA-CREB signaling.
abstract: Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) is a devastating subtype of stroke characterized by high acute mortality and persistent neurological impairment, yet effective pharmacological therapies remain lacking. Sinomenine, a bioactive alkaloid derived from Sinomenium acutum, has shown neuroprotective efficacy across diverse neurological disorders; however, its role in ICH remains insufficiently characterized. To investigate the therapeutic potential and mechanisms of sinomenine against ICH, a combined approach integrating network-based pharmacology, in silico docking, molecular dynamics (MD) simulation, and in vivo experiments was employed in this study. Network analysis identified AKT1, EGFR, GSK3B, MMP9, and mTOR as central candidate targets, while GO and KEGG enrichment analyses identified the PI3K-Akt, cAMP, and NF-κB pathways as potentially key players. In silico docking and subsequent MD simulations revealed stable interaction of sinomenine with AKT1, EGFR, GSK3B, and mTOR. Consistent with these in silico predictions, sinomenine administration significantly ameliorated neurological impairment and attenuated brain edema in a rat model of ICH. Further mechanistic investigations revealed that sinomenine may modulate cAMP-PKA-CREB signaling and the CaMKIIα-AKT axis, accompanied by reduced NF-κB expression, downregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokine production, and upregulation of BDNF. Together, these findings suggest that the protective effects of sinomenine against experimental ICH may involve coordinated changes in inflammatory and neurotrophic signaling pathways. This study provides experimental data supporting sinomenine as a promising multi-target therapeutic agent against ICH.

title: Alisol B attenuates rotenone-induced oxidative injury in SH-SY5Y cells: AKT-associated protection and changes in p38 MAPK phosphorylation.
abstract: Alisol B is a protostane-type triterpenoid whose protective effects against rotenone-induced neuronal cell injury remain unclear. This study investigates Alisol B pretreatment against acute rotenone-induced injury in SH-SY5Y cells and associated AKT and p38 MAPK signaling changes. Network pharmacology, molecular docking, and three independent 300-ns molecular dynamics simulations were used to identify candidate targets and explore predicted protein-ligand interactions. SH-SY5Y cells were pretreated with Alisol B before acute rotenone exposure. Cellular metabolic activity was assessed by CCK-8, ROS-associated fluorescence by DCFH-DA, apoptosis by Annexin V-FITC/PI flow cytometry, and AKT and p38 MAPK phosphorylation by Western blotting. MK-2206 was used to investigate the functional involvement of AKT-associated signaling. A total of 397 overlapping candidate targets were identified, and AKT1 showed the highest degree in the protein-protein interaction network. Docking and molecular dynamics analyses supported the structural plausibility of a predicted Alisol B-AKT1 interaction but did not establish direct target engagement. Alisol B pretreatment partially improved cellular metabolic activity, reduced ROS-associated fluorescence, and decreased apoptosis after rotenone exposure. MK-2206 attenuated the effects of Alisol B on cellular metabolic activity and ROS-associated fluorescence. Alisol B was also associated with increased AKT phosphorylation and decreased p38 MAPK phosphorylation. Alisol B pretreatment provided preliminary protection against acute rotenone-induced injury in SH-SY5Y cells.

main: Docking and molecular dynamics analyses supported the structural plausibility of a predicted Alisol B-AKT1 interaction but did not establish direct target engagement.

title: Ergothioneine in Neuroprotection and Cognitive Function: Implications for Brain Disorders.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are characterised by progressive neuronal loss and continue to be significant health issues worldwide. Oxidative stress is a central and unifying pathway that mediates neurodegeneration by interacting with neuroinflammation, mitochondrial pathophysiology, protein aggregation, excitotoxicity, and neurovascular dysfunction. Existing treatments are mostly symptomatic and do not effectively target the upstream pathological events. Therefore, there is an urgent need for new neuroprotective agents that are more effective and specific for treating these conditions. Ergothioneine (ET), a sulfur-containing amino acid obtained from dietary sources, is a promising neuroprotective candidate because of its distinctive biochemical and pharmacokinetic properties. ET shows unmatched stability and antioxidant behaviour, undergoes selective cellular uptake via OCTN1/SLC22A4, and has been detected in brain tissue in experimental models; however, the extent and mechanism of its delivery across the intact blood-brain barrier, particularly in humans, remain incompletely established. ET has demonstrated multi-targeted neuroprotective potential in preclinical models, including direct scavenging of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species, modulation of endogenous antioxidant systems, metal-ion chelation, preservation of mitochondrial function, regulation of inflammatory responses, and modulation of apoptotic pathways. ET improved cognitive performance and restored redox homeostasis in experimental animal models. Although encouraging, clinical evidence remains limited. To demonstrate the efficacy of ET as a therapeutic and preventive measure for neurodegenerative diseases, future studies should use large-scale clinical trials, dose optimisation, and biomarker-based strategies. Furthermore, ET exhibits several pharmacokinetic and biochemical properties of potential relevance to neuroprotection, including OCTN1- mediated cellular uptake, prolonged tissue retention, and antioxidant activity. Although ET has been detected in brain tissue in experimental models, its transport across the intact blood-brain barrier and the extent of brain exposure in humans remain incompletely established.
authors: Singh M, Kumar M
overview: Neurodegenerative diseases are characterised by progressive neuronal loss and continue to be significant health issues worldwide.
main: ET improved cognitive performance and restored redox homeostasis in experimental animal models.

title: Serum Extracellular Vesicle Proteomics Identifies Candidate Protein Biomarkers for Major Depressive Disorder with a Diagnostic Specificity Assessment against Schizophrenia.
abstract: Diagnosis of major depressive disorder (MDD) relies on subjective criteria and lacks objective biomarkers. Serum extracellular vesicles (EVs) carry stable cargo and can cross the blood-brain barrier, making them attractive biomarker sources. We therefore profiled serum EVs from a discovery cohort of 60 participants (40 healthy controls [HCs], 20 MDD patients) by size-exclusion chromatography and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, and subsequently validated candidate proteins by ELISA in an independent cohort of 60 participants (20 HCs, 20 MDD, 20 patients with schizophrenia [SCZ]). Differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) were defined by |log2 fold change| > 1 and Benjamini-Hochberg FDR-adjusted q < 0.05. Using these criteria, we identified 358 DEPs (235 upregulated, 123 downregulated), which were enriched in complement activation, coagulation, and immune-inflammatory pathways. However, several of the most significant DEPs are abundant circulating plasma proteins that are common co-isolates of serum EVs, so part of this signal may reflect residual soluble serum protein, and-given that EVs were isolated from serum rather than platelet-poor plasma-the pathway enrichment should be interpreted with caution. In the validation cohort, EV-associated TNC and APLP1 were elevated and EV-associated TF was reduced in MDD relative to HCs (P < 0.05), whereas only serum APLP1 was elevated. Notably, EV-associated TNC was also elevated in SCZ, while APLP1 and TF were unchanged; moreover, direct MDD-versus-SCZ comparisons were not significant, indicating that the data do not support MDD-specific alterations. In addition, a logistic-regression model combining EV-associated APLP1, TF and TNC distinguished MDD from HCs with an area under the curve of 0.905 (95% CI 0.812-0.998; 0.830 by leave-one-out cross-validation), outperforming individual proteins (TF 0.725; TNC 0.758; APLP1 0.725). Collectively, these findings define a serum EV-associated proteomic signature in MDD and preliminarily validate TF, TNC and APLP1 as candidate diagnostic biomarkers, implicating immune-inflammatory and complement-related pathways. Nevertheless, the panel remains exploratory and requires validation in larger, multi-center cohorts with diverse psychiatric controls.

title: Dual-modality photoacoustic and optical coherence tomography imaging simultaneously tracks transplanted stem cells and their viability.
abstract: Monitoring transplanted cell viability in vivo, noninvasively remains a considerable challenge. By using multiwavelength photoacoustic microscopy powered by a reactive oxygen species (ROS)-responsive contrast agent, we can relatively and semiquantitatively assess and longitudinally monitor the viability of human-induced pluripotent stem cell-derived retinal pigment epithelium (hiPSC-RPE) cells in vivo. The contrast agent comprises colloidal chain-like gold nanoparticle (CGNP) clusters conjugated with IR775c, a heptamethine cyanine dye that undergoes selective oxidative quenching under elevated ROS conditions associated with cellular death (CGNP-IR775c). Dual-wavelength photoacoustic microscopy at 620 and 775 nanometers provides self-calibrated ratiometric measurements that enable relative viability assessment, distinguishing healthy from nonviable cell populations. In vitro studies demonstrated that CGNP-IR775c exhibited biocompatibility and showed dose-dependent ROS sensitivity across physiologically relevant H2O2 concentrations. hiPSC-RPE cells labeled by CGNP-IR775c were subretinally transplanted into living rabbit eyes and longitudinally monitored for 2 weeks, showing that laser-induced oxidative stress produced measurable photoacoustic signal changes that were consistent with the viability status of the transplanted cells. The imaging technology developed here provides a practical solution for noninvasive, longitudinal, and semiquantitative assessment of the transplanted cell viability in vivo, and may contribute to ophthalmology cell-based therapy in both preclinical and clinical settings.

title: Distinct regulatory logic controls recruitment and membrane dynamics of ESCRT-III subunit Vps60.
abstract: Endosomal Sorting Complexes Required for Transport (ESCRT) machinery drives membrane remodeling and scission events essential for multivesicular body (MVB) biogenesis. The accessory ESCRT-III subunit Vps60 (mammalian CHMP5) shares structural features with the major polymerizing subunit Snf7, including the capacity to form homopolymers in vitro. Here, we demonstrate in Saccharomyces cerevisiae that Vps60 recruitment and polymerization require conditions that permit Snf7 polymer turnover: Vps60 is largely excluded when Snf7 assembly is absent and when Snf7 disassembly is blocked, consistent with recruitment of Vps60 late in the ESCRT-III cycle to Snf7 assemblies that undergo normal turnover. Structure-function analysis reveals that Vps60 regulation diverges fundamentally from core ESCRT-III subunits: while occlusion of the Vps60 C-terminus by a GFP tag drives constitutive membrane association and polymer assembly, C-terminal truncation impairs endosomal recruitment, indicating that the Vps60 C-terminus is required for membrane recruitment, in contrast to the autoinhibitory C-terminal domains of core ESCRT-III subunits. A C-terminally tagged Vps60 that constitutively associates with membranes phenocopies loss of Vps60 function in both intralumenal vesicle (ILV) formation and cargo sorting. These findings indicate that despite structural similarity to Snf7, Vps60 functions as a late-arriving accessory factor whose recruitment and assembly are tightly coupled to Snf7 dynamics.

title: Stem Cell and Extracellular Vesicle Therapies for Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: Pathophysiology, Preclinical Evidence, and Translational Challenges.
abstract: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) remains a devastating neurological condition with high mortality and morbidity, largely due to secondary brain injury mechanisms such as early brain injury (EBI) and secondary white matter injury (SWMI). Conventional surgical and medical interventions have not been sufficient to prevent long-term disability, prompting investigation into novel regenerative strategies. We conducted a narrative review of preclinical and limited clinical evidence on stem cell- and extracellular vesicle/exosome-based therapies for SAH, with emphasis on MSCs and their derivatives. PubMed/MEDLINE and Embase were searched between February and March 2025 for studies examining mechanisms, therapeutic targets, dosing, timing, and routes of administration. Stem cell-based therapies, particularly MSCs and their exosomes, have shown the ability to attenuate neuroinflammation, oxidative stress, excitotoxicity, and BBB disruption. Key mechanisms include modulation of the HMGB1/TLR4/NF-κB axis, polarization of microglia toward an anti-inflammatory phenotype, and secretion of trophic factors such as TSG-6, BDNF, and NT-3. Preclinical studies demonstrate improvements in neurological function, cognitive outcomes, and histological preservation across multiple SAH models. Exosome delivery of microRNAs (e.g., miR-129-5p, miR-193b-3p) has emerged as a potent cell-free strategy. Benefits have been reported after both early and delayed administration; however, differences in experimental models, therapeutic products, dosing methods, routes of administration, and outcome measures prevent direct cross-study comparisons and preclude identification of an optimal treatment window. MSC-derived therapies, hold significant promise for mitigating secondary injury and improving outcomes after SAH. Despite this promise, significant translational challenges concerning optimal dosing, delivery methods, and long-term safety must still be addressed. The path to clinical use requires rigorous validation in large animal models before advancing to human trials. Such validation may support the future clinical development of stem cell-based therapies for SAH.

title: Subfield-specific hippocampal enlargement in high-functioning autism spectrum disorder.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Although previous studies have reported abnormal hippocampal volumes in children and adolescents with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), the specific alterations in hippocampal subfields and their relationships with clinical symptoms in high-functioning ASD (HF-ASD) remain unclear. METHODS: In this study, we analyzed T1-weighted structural MRI data from the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange I (ABIDE-I), including 182 children and adolescents with HF-ASD and 213 age- and sex-matched typically developing controls (TDC). Using a linear mixed-effects model, we compared hippocampal volumes between groups, and examined associations between volumes and clinical measurements. RESULTS: Compared to TDC, the children and adolescents with HF-ASD exhibited significantly increased volumes in the right entire hippocampus, presubiculum, subiculum, and granule cell layer of the dentate gyrus (GC-DG). No significant volumetric differences were observed within the child or adolescent subgroups, nor between these age groups. Notably, presubiculum volume showed a positive correlation with verbal scores and a negative correlation with social scores in the HF-ASD group. CONCLUSIONS: These findings indicate subfield-specific hippocampal overgrowth in children and adolescents with HF-ASD and presubiculum volume alteration may be a potential neuroanatomical correlate underlying verbal and social dysfunctions.

title: Human disease-associated V94M mutation causes partial loss of function by impairing the plasma membrane trafficking of the TRPC5 channel.
abstract: The human transient receptor potential channel canonical 5 (hTRPC5) is a second messenger-gated, Ca2+-permeable cation channel that is abundantly expressed in the brain. Owing to its X-chromosomal localization, TRPC5 variants bear the potential of causing channelopathies in hemizygous males. We identified a valine 94 to methionine (p.(Val94Met)) missense variant in two brothers with a neurodevelopmental disorder. To investigate if this variant affects the protein function, we inserted that variant into the cDNA of hTRPC5, and performed Ca2+ microfluorometry and electrophysiological analyses during channel activation via G-protein coupled receptors or by exposing cells to the direct activator englerin A. In both assays, we found a partial loss of function in hTRPC5(V94M) compared to wild-type hTRPC5. Since V94 is located within the second ankyrin-like repeat, a direct impact on the regulatory voltage sensor-like domain or the central pore domain seemed unlikely. We therefore analyzed whether the assembly of tetrameric channel complex or its integration into the plasma membrane are affected. Confocal microscopy demonstrated that hTRPC5(V94M) is strongly retained in endomembrane compartments with an impaired forward trafficking to the plasma membrane and sub-plasmalemmal punctae. Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) measurements revealed lower FRET efficiencies between hTRPC5(V94M) subunits as well as between hTRPC5(V94M) and wild-type hTRPC5 channel subunits, indicating that the assembly of hTRPC5(V94M) into homo- or heterotetrameric channel complexes may be impaired. Based on the functional analyses that demonstrate a partial loss-of-function of hTRPC5(V94M), these findings highlight p.(Val94Met) as a probable cause of the neurodevelopmental phenotype of the two affected brothers.

title: Association of Pubertal Timing and Progression with Variation in the Dual Systems Imbalance Gap: The Moderating Role of Autism Spectrum Disorder.
abstract: This study sought to examine the direct effects of puberty on dual systems imbalance for male and female youth and test for a moderating effect of autism spectrum disorder. The Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development data were analyzed. Ordinary least squares regression was used to test for direct and moderated effects of interest. Earlier pubertal development was associated only marginally significantly associated with greater dual systems imbalance characterized by greater sensation-seeking and lower impulse control for male youth. Autism spectrum disorder was significantly and negatively associated with dual systems imbalance, meaning lower sensation-seeking and greater impulse control. No significant direct effects were observed for female youth. No significant moderation effects were observed for either sex. Findings suggest the importance of autism and potentially pubertal developmental rate for understanding dual systems development for male youth, but not female youth.

title: Perspectives of parents of children with monogenic neurodevelopmental disorders on research involving patient-derived neuronal models.
abstract: Patient-derived stem cell-based neuronal models hold great promise for advancing research into monogenic neurodevelopmental disorders (mNDDs). These neuronal models are generated using induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) technologies, and are perceived as "ethically sensitive". To date, ethical discussions on the use of neuronal models have predominantly focused on three-dimensional (3D) neuronal models, such as brain organoids, while two-dimensional (2D) neuronal models - which are widely used in current research settings - remain underexplored. A better understanding of the perspectives of parents of children with mNDDs on ethical issues - including the moral status of 2D models, informed consent, autonomy, privacy and misuse - is needed. We report the results of a semi-structured interview study among parents of children with mNDDs (n = 28) investigating their perspectives on the ethically responsible use of 2D patient-derived neuronal models in research. Respondents ascribed limited intrinsic value to neuronal models, often viewing them as ethically comparable to other somatic cells. They were highly motivated to enroll their child in iPSC research, but suggested that researchers: (1) restrict the use of their child's donated material to purposes benefiting the mNDD community, (2) protect their child's privacy, (3) communicate about research findings and reuse of donated material, and (4) minimize risks and burdens of research procedures for their (vulnerable) child. Based on these findings, we provide recommendations to research groups for informed consent and engagement processes to support responsible inclusion of children with mNDDs and their families in research using iPSC-based neuronal models.

title: Lipid-induced Caveolin1 lipid droplet trafficking is associated with lipid droplet growth.
abstract: Caveolae are 50 to 100 nm sized plasma membrane invaginations involved in cellular lipid uptake and lipid accumulation. Several caveolin1 and cavin1 mutations are associated with human lipodystrophy. Previous research identified caveolae proteins at lipid droplets, although their specific cellular function at lipid droplets is not understood. Here, we show that extracellular dietary lipids like oleic acid and cholesterol shift caveolae at the plasma membrane to highly spherical invaginations and induce the internalization of caveolin1. Within 3 h of lipid treatment, caveolin1 accumulates specifically to lipid droplets. Correlative fluorescence Focused Ion Beam - Scanning Electron Microscopy and split-APEX proteomics revealed that this localization occurs in the absence of intact caveolar vesicles but caveolin1 alone. Mechanistically, caveolin1 trafficking to lipid droplets is regulated by EHD2 at the plasma membrane, is dynamin independent, and proceeds via EEA1- and Rab5-positive endosomes within 1 h of oleic acid treatment. Lipid droplet accumulation of caveolin1 is independent of lysosomal activity. Functionally, caveolin1-enriched lipid droplets exhibit a significant increase in size, demonstrating that caveolin1 is critical for lipid droplet growth. Notably, the deletion of the central caveolin1 β-barrel (Cav1-F160X), a mutation identified in lipodystrophy patients, abolished caveolin1 lipid droplet trafficking and lipid droplet growth. Taken together, our results show that dietary lipids trigger caveolin1 internalization and accumulation at lipid droplets and a caveolin1-dependent lipid droplet growth, thereby providing an initial mechanistic basis for the lipodystrophic phenotype associated with caveolin1 mutations.

title: Bone Marrow Dendritic Cells-derived Exosomes Alleviate Ovariectomy-induced Depression in Rats by Suppressing NF-κB-mediated Neuroinflammation and Restoring T-cell Homeostasis.
abstract: Depression is a prevalent neuropsychiatric disorder, particularly among post-menopausal women, and is strongly linked to neuroinflammation and immune dysregulation. Emerging evidence suggests that exosomes derived from bone marrow dendritic cells (BMDCs) possess potent immunomodulatory properties. The present study investigated their therapeutic efficacy in an ovariectomy-induced rat model of post-menopausal depression. BMDCs were prepared and identified, and then the exosomes were isolated by differential ultracentrifugation. Forty-five female rats were randomly allocated into three groups (n = 15): sham-operated rats (SO), ovariectomized rats (OVX), and ovariectomized rats treated with BMDCs-derived exosomes (EXO), administered intravenously via the tail vein at a dose of 200 µg/kg/dose in 0.2 mL PBS on days 7 and 14 post-ovariectomy. Behavioral, neurochemical, and immunological assessments were subsequently performed. Ovariectomy-induced depression was associated with increased hippocampal neuronal apoptosis, enhanced microglial activation, and elevated levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines. In addition, ovariectomy disrupted T-cell homeostasis, as evidenced by alterations in CD4, CD8, and regulatory T-cell populations, and activated NF-κB signaling, thereby promoting a shift toward the pro-inflammatory M1 microglial phenotype. Administration of BMDCs-derived exosomes significantly attenuated these alterations by suppressing M1 polarization, enhancing the M2 phenotype, restoring T-cell balance, and inhibiting NF-κB activation. BMDCs-derived exosomes can be considered as a promising candidate for the management of post-menopausal depression and similar neuropsychiatric disorders through modulation of neuroinflammation and immune responses.

title: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism in Weiss-Kruszka syndrome: a report of two cases.
abstract: Congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (CHH) and Kallmann syndrome (KS) are genetically heterogeneous disorders caused from impaired development or function of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neurons. ZNF462 variants cause Weiss-Kruszka syndrome (WKS), a neurodevelopmental disorder occasionally associated with endocrine abnormalities. We report two unrelated Japanese patients with CHH/KS who harbor de novo truncating variants in ZNF462. Case 1, harboring NM_021224.6:c.1845_1846del, p.(Arg616SerfsTer6), presented with CHH mild anosmia, and characteristic WKS features. Case 2, previously reported in a CHH cohort and harboring NM_021224.6:c.2431C>T, p.(Gln811Ter), presented with KS, anosmia, and olfactory tract abnormalities. Recent studies demonstrated that ZNF462 regulates neural lineage specification via G9A/GLP-mediated chromatin repression, and that ZNF family genes also participate in the epigenetic regulation of pubertal activation. These findings broaden the endocrine spectrum of ZNF462-related disorders and indicate that single-gene ZNF462 defects may contribute to GnRH deficiency through neurodevelopmental and epigenetic mechanisms.

title: Persistent autism-like behaviors and multilevel neurobiological abnormalities following prenatal valproic acid exposure in rats.
abstract: Prenatal valproic acid (VPA) exposure is widely used to model autism spectrum disorder (ASD), yet the persistence of its behavioral effects and the accompanying multilevel neurobiological abnormalities remain incompletely understood. Here, we integrated behavioral, histological, morphological, electrophysiological, molecular, metabolomic, and epigenomic analyses to characterize the long-term effects of prenatal VPA exposure in rats from early postnatal life through adulthood. Prenatal VPA exposure caused delayed early development and persistent ASD-like phenotypes, including repetitive behaviors, impaired social interaction, anxiety-like behavior, reduced exploration, and cognitive deficits. These behavioral abnormalities were accompanied by neuronal and glial alterations and reduced dendritic complexity and spine density in the medial prefrontal cortex and hippocampus, as well as reduced excitatory and inhibitory synaptic inputs and decreased expression of key synaptic proteins in the medial prefrontal cortex. Multi-omics profiling further identified candidate metabolic alterations involving membrane lipid remodeling, neuromodulatory metabolism, and inflammatory lipid signaling, alongside bidirectional, locus-specific DNA methylation changes enriched in neurodevelopmental and synaptic pathways. Together, these findings show that prenatal VPA exposure produces persistent ASD-like phenotypes accompanied by multilevel cellular, structural, synaptic, metabolic, and epigenetic abnormalities. This work provides an integrated framework for understanding the long-term consequences of prenatal VPA exposure and supports the VPA model as a valuable platform for investigating mechanisms underlying ASD.

title: Structural basis for the selective inhibition of the PI3KC3-C2 complex by Rubicon in endolysosome maturation and mitophagy.
abstract: Rubicon is a negative regulator of autophagy and the endolysosomal network (ELN) and an antagonist of the class III phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase complex II (PI3KC3-C2). Inhibition of Rubicon is considered a potential means to therapeutically upregulate autophagy and the ELN to treat Parkinson's disease and other conditions characterized by autophagic and ELN dysfunction. Rubicon is specific for the UV radiation resistance-associated gene protein (UVRAG)-containing PI3KC3-C2 over the purely autophagic ATG14-containing PI3KC3-C1 complex. Here, we determined the high-resolution cryoelectron microscopy structure of PI3KC3-C2 in complex with the PI3KC3-binding domain of Rubicon and compared it to cryo-EM structures of unbound PI3KC3-C2 and PI3KC3-C1. Rubicon binds directly to PI3KC3-C2 only via the BARA domain of the BECN1 subunit, which is common to both C1 and C2. The selectivity of Rubicon for the PI3KC3-C2 complex over the PI3KC3-C1 complex is attributed to a conformation of the BECN1BARA domain induced by UVRAG, rather than to direct contact with UVRAG or direct antagonism by the ATG14 subunit of PI3KC3-C1. Targeted disruption of the Rubicon:PI3K3-C2 structural interface by site-directed mutations enhances mitophagic activity in human epithelial cells to levels comparable to those observed in Rubicon knockout cells. Similarly, disruption of the interaction in Rubicon-overexpressing hippocampal neurons restored lysosomal flux to wild-type levels. These data show that suppressing the function of PI3K3-C2 can fully account for the negative regulatory effects of Rubicon in the autophagy and ELN pathways.

title: TRIM31 aggravated cerebral ischemic injury by inhibiting autophagosome-lysosome fusion through degradation of TLR9.
abstract: Recent evidence has suggested that dysfunction of the autophagy-lysosome system was a crucial factor leading to neuronal damage, yet the underlying regulatory mechanisms remain unclear. Studies have reported that Toll like receptor 9 (TLR9) is required for autophagic flux. In our investigation, we observed that TLR9 was significantly upregulated and exerted a protective role through promoting the fusion of autophagosomes and lysosomes in the stroke models. Mechanistically, we found that tripartite motif-containing protein 31 (TRIM31) interacted with TLR9 and promoted the k48-linked polyubiquitination of TLR9, consequently facilitated its degradation in a proteasome-dependent pathway. Furthermore, TRIM31 led to impaired autophagosome-lysosome fusion in cerebral ischemic injury by negatively regulating TLR9. In conclusion, we identified TRIM31 as a novel E3 ubiquitin ligase for TLR9 degradation and provided a new therapeutic strategy to alleviate ischemic brain injury by enhancing autophagosome-lysosome fusion via TLR9.

title: Cerebrospinal fluid sTREM2 and PGRN in the early diagnosis and progression monitoring of Alzheimer's disease: A longitudinal study.
abstract: BackgroundAlzheimer's disease (AD) features amyloid-β (Aβ) deposition and tau pathology, with microglial dysfunction and neuroinflammation increasingly implicated. Soluble triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells-2 (sTREM2) and progranulin (PGRN) regulate microglial function and lysosomal homeostasis, but their dynamics across the AD continuum remain unclear.ObjectiveTo investigate cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) sTREM2 and PGRN in the early diagnosis and progression monitoring of AD, and their associations with Aβ pathology and other biomarkers.MethodsData were from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). Based on CSF Aβ42 and Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) scores, subjects were categorized into Aβ-CN (n = 196), Aβ+CN (n = 101), Aβ+MCI (n = 378), and Aβ+AD (n = 96). Baseline demographics, neuropsychological assessments, imaging indices, and CSF biomarkers were compared. Spearman correlation, ROC curve analysis, and linear mixed-effects models (n = 255) were used.ResultsBaseline CSF sTREM2 was lower in Aβ+CN than Aβ-CN. PGRN was lower in Aβ+CN and Aβ+MCI than Aβ-CN. Over 2 years, sTREM2 increased most in Aβ+MCI and moderately in Aβ+CN, while PGRN declined in Aβ-CN, Aβ+MCI, and Aβ+AD. Both biomarkers correlated with CSF tau and p-tau in Aβ+ individuals.ConclusionsBaseline CSF sTREM2 and PGRN have limited cross-sectional diagnostic value for AD. However, their longitudinal trajectories raise the possibility that they may reflect the microglia-lysosome axis. Combined biomarker strategies and multi-targeted therapeutic interventions warrant further investigation.

main: Over 2 years, sTREM2 increased most in Aβ+MCI and moderately in Aβ+CN, while PGRN declined in Aβ-CN, Aβ+MCI, and Aβ+AD.

title: Dynein-dependent positioning of multiple organelles regulates adaptive gene expression during oxidative stress.
abstract: Cells respond to environmental insults through well-characterized changes to their transcriptome and proteome. The contribution that reorganization of intracellular architecture makes to the adaptive stress response is much less understood. Here, we reveal a conserved spatial response to oxidative stress in which the microtubule motor dynein enhances perinuclear clustering of multiple membrane-bound organelles. These events are triggered by reactive oxygen species and protein kinase C and occur without increased association of dynein with its activator dynactin, pointing to a noncanonical mechanism for stimulating retrograde transport. Using a chemically inducible system for dispersing individual organelles, we show that perinuclear localization of multiple compartments potentiates oxidative stress-induced gene expression, with distinct genes depending on inputs from either combinations of organelles or individual compartments. Together, these findings implicate positioning of multiple membrane-bound compartments in gene expression regulation and identify coordinated organelle trafficking by dynein as an additional regulatory layer in the cellular stress response.

title: Impaired cellular stress adaptability in Alzheimer's disease patient-derived fibroblasts: a PFKFB3-linked transcriptomic response to oxidative stress.
abstract: Aging-related impairment in cellular stress adaptability may contribute to vulnerability to Alzheimer's disease (AD), but patient-derived experimental models that preserve agingassociated molecular features remain underused. Here, we investigated transcriptomic responses to oxidative stress in ex vivo dermal fibroblasts derived from patients with AD and control participants matched for age and sex. Fibroblasts were exposed to hydrogen peroxide to induce reactive oxygen species-mediated stress, followed by RNA sequencing to identify disease-associated differences in stress-responsive gene regulation. AD-derived fibroblasts exhibited distinct oxidative stress response patterns, with altered regulation of pathways related to endoplasmic reticulum stress, immune activation, autophagy, protein synthesis, and cell cycle control. Systematic candidate gene prioritization identified PFKFB3 as a key stress-responsive gene showing reduced induction in AD fibroblasts. Lower PFKFB3 responsiveness was associated with poorer cognitive performance and higher levels of neurodegeneration-related blood biomarkers, including plasma pTau217, neurofilament light chain, and glial fibrillary acidic protein. In immortalized human astrocytes, PFKFB3 knockdown reduced cell viability under oxidative stress and altered transcriptional programs related to proteostasis, metabolic regulation, and immune activation. These findings suggest that AD is associated with impaired cellular stress adaptability in patient-derived fibroblasts and highlight PFKFB3 as a candidate node linking oxidative stress responsiveness, glial vulnerability, and AD-related pathological burden.

title: Fast-scan cyclic voltammetry for real-time serotonin dynamics in human iPSC-derived neural spheroids.
abstract: Measuring neurotransmission in the human brain could advance our understanding of disorders, including depression. Although fast-scan cyclic voltammetry (FSCV) has provided valuable insights into neurotransmission in animal models, its application to human systems remains challenging. Here, we present an FSCV-based framework for real-time serotonin measurements in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived three-dimensional (3D) neuronal cultures. We demonstrate reproducible detection of spontaneous and evoked serotonin release from 3D serotonergic spheroids and show that serotonin dynamics differ between serotonin reuptake inhibitors. We investigate how a molecular stress mediator influences serotonin signaling and antidepressant effectiveness. Finally, we extend the platform to co-cultures containing microglia-like cells to examine serotonin dynamics under inflammatory conditions. We present a translational, label-free technology to measure serotonin dynamics in real-time in human stem cell-derived models. This method studies serotonin regulation, with potential applications to drug development and the mechanistic dissection of psychiatric disorders, such as depression.

title: Galectin-3 links microglial neuroinflammation to Aβ aggregation and lysosomal processing.
abstract: Neuroinflammation is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the molecular mechanisms linking microglial dysfunction to amyloid-β (Aβ) pathology remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify galectin-3 (Gal3) as a regulator of plaque-associated microglial responses, linking Aβ aggregation, lysosomal function, and neuritic pathology. Using postmortem brain tissue from AD patients, we found that Gal3+ microglia preferentially associate with cored plaques and correlate with increased LAMP1+ dystrophic neurites. Gal3 was also detected in microglial lysosomal compartments, extramicroglial dystrophic structures, and in association with extracellular amyloid fibrils, suggesting roles in both intracellular and extracellular Aβ processing. In APP mice, Gal3 deficiency reduced plaque burden and neuritic dystrophy, increased plaque compaction, and enhanced TREM2 coverage around amyloid plaques. Mechanistically, in vitro microglial experiments showed that Gal3 modulates Aβ uptake and lysosomal processing, whereas lysosomal dysfunction promoted the accumulation of fibrillar Aβ from initially monomeric species, particularly in Gal3-deficient cells. Cell-free assays demonstrated that Gal3 preferentially binds fibrillar Aβ, inhibits secondary nucleation, and alters fibril morphology, while Gal3-modified fibrillar Aβ reduces N2a neuronal cell number. Finally, in silico structural analyses identified candidate Gal3 interactors enriched in leucine-rich-repeat and immunoglobulin-like proteins, supporting a role for this lectin in immune receptor regulation. Complementary in vivo transcriptomic profiling showed that Gal3 deletion suppresses type I interferon and microglial neurodegenerative transcriptional signatures. Together, these findings position Gal3 at the interface between Aβ remodeling, lysosomal homeostasis, and plaque-associated microglial responses in AD.

title: Metabolomics Profiling of Serum Small Extracellular Vesicle-Enriched Fractions Across Early Post-Injury Intervals Following Severe Traumatic Brain Injury.
abstract: Severe traumatic brain injury (sTBI) induces metabolic disturbances that remain difficult to assess non-invasively. This exploratory study compared metabolomics profiles of serum small extracellular vesicle-enriched fractions from healthy controls and patients with sTBI sampled at days 1, 3, and 5 post-injury. Using high-resolution liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS), we identified metabolite differences associated with each sampled post-injury interval. Principal component analysis showed group-level separation between controls and the individual post-injury interval groups, with the largest separation observed in the day 1 comparison. N-Acetyl-l-aspartic acid, a canonical marker of neuronal integrity, showed lower abundance in the day 1 group relative to controls, whereas PGF2α ethanolamide showed lower abundance relative to controls in all three interval-specific comparisons. Glu-ser and tryptophan also met the differential-abundance criteria in more than one interval vs. control comparison. Ingenuity pathway analysis (IPA) linked the day 1 metabolite alterations to literature-curated neurological functions, including demyelination and neurodegeneration; however, these associations are presented as hypothesis-generating. Collectively, these findings identify serum small extracellular vesicle-enriched fraction metabolite alterations associated with sTBI for further investigation in fully longitudinal sTBI cohorts.

title: Ribosome-associated vesicles promote activity-dependent local translation in neurons.
abstract: Local protein synthesis in axons and dendrites underpins synaptic plasticity. However, the composition of the protein synthesis machinery in distal neuronal processes and the mechanisms for its deployment to local translation sites remain unclear. Here, we employed multi-scale imaging that combines cryo-electron tomography, volume electron microscopy, and live-cell imaging to identify endoplasmic reticulum-derived KDEL-positive vesicles, a subset of which are decorated with ribosomes (Ribosome-Associated Vesicles, RAVs) in neurites. We demonstrate that neuronal stimulation triggers compartment-specific responses: dendrites accumulate stationary KDEL-positive vesicles at sites of enhanced translation, while axons accelerate vesicle transport. cLTP stimulation additionally increases the proportion of KDEL-positive vesicles that carry ribosomes, expanding the local RAV pool. Real-time imaging of translation at single mRNA resolution reveals that RAV-associated translation sites exhibit ∼30% greater nascent-peptide signal amplitude compared to periods without RAV association, indicating that RAVs boost local translation output. These findings establish RAVs as specialized platforms that integrate activity-dependent signals with local protein synthesis, providing a mechanistic framework for understanding how neurons achieve precise spatiotemporal control of translation.

title: [Building and maintaining the muscle fiber: new perspectives on the microtubule network].
abstract: The motor unit is a unique structure, formed by the association of highly specialized cells: a motor neuron transmitting information from the brain, and a muscle fiber enabling muscle contraction. This functional specialization relies on a complex cellular architecture, notably supported by the microtubule cytoskeleton, whose role is now better characterized in neurons than in muscle fibers. In this context, recent data on the links between different regulators of the microtubule network in neurons enrich our understanding of cellular homeostasis. These advances suggest the existence of similar processes in muscle fibers, opening new perspectives for neuromuscular physiology and our view of the motor unit.

title: Decoding and Rewiring Neurovascular Communication in Spinal Cord Injury via Computational Extracellular Vesicle Dynamics.
abstract: Spinal cord injury (SCI) disrupts the neurovascular unit (NVU), notably impairing the blood-spinal cord barrier (BSCB), which undergoes a biphasic transformation from acute hyperpermeability to chronic fibrotic sclerosis. This dynamic remodeling creates a heterogeneous barrier that hinders effective drug delivery and limits therapeutic success. Here we integrate pathological characterization with computational molecular dynamics to rationally engineer extracellular vesicles (EVs) capable of receptor-mediated transcytosis across the fibrotic BSCB. Coupled with computational fluid dynamics-optimized hydrogel scaffolds and neuromodulation techniques, this approach promotes NVU repair, restores synaptic homeostasis, and facilitates neural circuit rewiring. This integrated framework advances precision SCI interventions by overcoming the evolving BSCB, offering a novel paradigm for enhancing functional recovery after traumatic SCI and informing therapeutic strategies for central nervous system disorders characterized by barrier dysfunction.

title: Decolonising Autistic Phenomenology: Towards a Critical-Enactive Account of Cognitive Diversity.
abstract: Recent years have seen a turn toward phenomenological, ecological, and enactive approaches to autism and neurodiversity, within the philosophy of psychiatry and cognitive science. These approaches challenge dominant neuro-reductionist and computational biomedical paradigms, centring embodiment, relationality, affectivity, and the constitutive role of sociomaterial environments in cognition. However, both phenomenological and ecological-enactive approaches are heterogeneous; not all escape the Eurocentric neuronormative assumptions underlying colonial modernity. This paper argues that, where classical phenomenology positions autism as a deviation from implicitly Western standards of 'neurotypical' embodiment and intersubjectivity, critical phenomenology and enactivism supply promising resources to reconceive autistic traits as intrinsically meaningful forms of sense-making - whilst interrogating the universality of categories such as 'autism' and 'neurotypicality.' Critical phenomenology draws attention to how power shapes embodiment, stretching the phenomenological method to confront its own complicity in Eurocentric neuronormativity. Enactivism goes further, providing an inclusive relational ontology of cognitive diversity that can facilitate dialogue with non-Western and Indigenous ways of knowing. Yet it risks becoming politically neutralised when inattentive to coloniality and intersectional oppression. Drawing insight from South Asian autistic experiences, I sketch out a critical-enactive framework oriented toward dismantling both neuronormative and Eurocentric (including logocentric and anthropocentric) assumptions in phenomenology and cognitive science. This decolonial approach paves the way for a pluralistic, intercultural understanding of autism - and embodied cognitive diversity, more broadly - doing justice to culturally and ecologically situated styles of sense-making, without essentialising neurological or cognitive differences.

title: TFEB overexpression in excitatory neurons ameliorates amyloid-β pathology via coordinated enhancement of autophagy-lysosome and mitochondrial function.
abstract: The intraneuronal accumulation of amyloid-β (Aβ) is an early pathogenic event in Alzheimer's disease (AD), initiating a pathological cascade that includes synaptic dysfunction, metabolic deficits, and eventual neuronal loss. Transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of the autophagy-lysosomal pathway (ALP) and mitochondrial homeostasis, represents a promising therapeutic target. However, its efficacy and mechanisms when specifically activated in neurons during the prodromal stage remain unclear. Here, we used an adeno-associated virus (AAV) under the control of the CaMKIIα promoter to achieve excitatory neuron-specific TFEB overexpression in the hippocampal CA1 region of 2 months-old 5×FAD mice. This intervention significantly reduced soluble Aβ levels at 3 months and attenuated amyloid plaque burden, dystrophic neurite formation, and glial activation at 6 months, accompanied by substantial improvements in spatial learning and memory. Mechanistically, transcriptomic and functional analyses revealed that TFEB not only enhanced autophagic flux and lysosomal biogenesis but also promoted the expression of key mitochondrial genes and improved mitochondrial function. In APP695swe-N2a cells, TFEB overexpression increased levels of LC3B-II and LAMP1, enhanced mitochondrial activity and biogenesis (via PGC-1α upregulation), and effectively reduced intracellular Aβ accumulation. Our findings demonstrate that targeted TFEB overexpression in excitatory neurons during early AD pathogenesis initiates a protective cascade by co-activating autophagy-lysosomal clearance and mitochondrial pathways, thereby reducing Aβ accumulation and mitigating downstream pathology. This study highlights the potential of neuron-specific TFEB activation as a cell-type-specific therapeutic approach for early AD intervention. © 2026 The Pathological Society of Great Britain and Ireland.

title: Septin partitioning between microtubules and actin is regulated by GSK3-dependent septin 9 phosphorylation.
abstract: Septins are cytoskeletal filaments that associate with the actin and microtubule cytoskeleton but the mechanisms that govern septin crosstalk and function with these networks are largely unknown. Here, we show that glycogen synthase kinase 3 (GSK3) directly phosphorylates Septin 9 (SEPT9) and regulates bidirectionally septin distribution between actin and microtubules. We show that GSK3 inhibition redistributes endogenous SEPT9 toward microtubules in multiple cell types. Phosphomimetic mutations at serines 82 and 85 reduce microtubule binding and enhance actin association in cells and in vitro, while phosphonull mutations promote microtubule binding and growth. In primary hippocampal neurons, GSK3β inactivation promotes SEPT9-microtubule association, and phosphomimetic SEPT9 expression impairs asymmetric neurite growth during neuronal polarization. These findings reveal a phosphorylation-dependent mechanism of septin partitioning between actin and microtubules, placing the cytoskeletal functions of septins under the control of GSK3-a kinase linked to multiple signaling pathways of cell physiology and metabolism.

title: Mild perinatal hypoxia uncouples excitatory-inhibitory circuit maturation and reprograms neocortical organization.
abstract: Perinatal hypoxia is a major contributor to neurodevelopmental disorders; however, the consequences of mild-to-moderate perinatal hypoxia (MPH) remain insufficiently characterized. Here, we investigated cortical plasticity following MPH using a multimodal approach that combines behavioral assessment, histological analysis, and in vivo magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Fifty-six Wistar Han rats were exposed to hypoxia (8% O2 / 2 h) or normoxia at postnatal day 1 (P1). Neurodevelopmental assessment from P3 to P14 revealed impaired rooting and vibrissae-placing reflexes in hypoxic rats. Histological analysis of the cerebral cortex demonstrated: altered expression of microtubule-associated protein-2, apical dendrite bundling, reduced neurofilament-H expression, and decreased dendritic arbor complexity in large pyramidal neurons, indicating disrupted maturation of excitatory circuits. Increased parvalbumin expression, higher interneuron density, and its enhanced neurite elaboration indicated precocious development of inhibitory circuits, consistent with a compensatory response. MRI at P15, combined with whole-brain voxel-wise analysis, revealed a significant increase in fractional anisotropy in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC). Convergent behavioral, histological, and imaging findings identified the ACC as the most vulnerable region following MPH, followed by the somatosensory cortex. These findings reveal early cytoarchitectural and MRI detectable correlates of a single episode of MPH, which, together with previous findings from this model, support the neurodevelopmental origin of persistent alterations in cortical structure and circuit function, characterized by an excitatory-inhibitory imbalance. The study identifies and defines a framework for understanding region-specific vulnerability and plasticity in the immature brain, with implications for improving the early detection of subtle perinatal brain injury, as a prerequisite for timely therapeutic intervention.

title: Intranasal delivery of a ROS-activatable myeloperoxidase inhibitor alleviates Alzheimer's-like symptoms and pathology.
abstract: Chronic neuroinflammation and oxidative stress are important contributors to Alzheimer's disease (AD). Myeloperoxidase (MPO), a key driver of oxidative inflammation released mainly by activated microglia in the neurodegenerative brain, is a potential therapeutic target to inhibit the neuroinflammatory cascade and oxidative damage in AD, but the underlying mechanisms remain unexplored, and achieving targeted brain delivery of an MPO inhibitor and minimizing systemic effects remain significant challenges. We addressed these limitations by first establishing that genetic deletion of MPO in the 5XFAD mouse model improved memory performance and reduced amyloid deposition, validating MPO as a therapeutic target. We then developed a liposome-encapsulated reactive oxygen species (ROS)-activatable MPO inhibitor (LERAMI). LERAMI uniquely combines targeted delivery with on-demand drug release, utilizing a ROS-sensitive linker to selectively release MPO inhibitors in ROS-rich regions within the AD microenvironment, minimizing off-target effects and systemic toxicity. In the 5XFAD mouse model. By reducing MPO expression and activity, LERAMI significantly improved cognitive performance, accompanied by decreased microglial activation, attenuated oxidative DNA damage, improved synaptic and neuronal density, and reduced amyloid burden. RNA sequencing revealed a robust hippocampal transcriptomic reprogramming, with upregulation of pathways critical for synaptic plasticity, calcium signaling, axon guidance, and neuroprotection, along with downregulation of inflammatory and immune response pathways. These findings demonstrate that targeted ROS-activatable MPO inhibition with LERAMI represents a promising therapeutic strategy for AD and potentially other neuroinflammatory diseases, offering a unique approach to mitigate neuroinflammation, preserve synaptic integrity, and restore cognitive function.

title: Extracellular vesicle-mediated neuroimmune remodeling across synucleinopathies: Therapeutic implications of cell-type specificity and central-peripheral crosstalk.
abstract: Synucleinopathies, including Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, and multiple system atrophy, are characterized by convergent α-synuclein misfolding, impaired proteostasis, and chronic neuroinflammation. Despite these shared pathological features, these disorders exhibit distinct inclusion-bearing cell profiles, vulnerable neural circuits, immune phenotypes, and clinical progression rates, with neuronal inclusions dominating in Parkinson's disease/dementia with Lewy bodies and oligodendrocyte pathology predominating in multiple system atrophy. Extracellular vesicles have emerged as critical modulators integrating these multifaceted pathogenic processes. Secreted by neurons, astrocytes, microglia, oligodendrocytes, endothelial cells, and peripheral immune cells, extracellular vesicles cross biological boundaries to deliver diverse bioactive molecules and mediate intercellular communication. This review synthesizes current evidence to propose that extracellular vesicles serve as context-dependent mediators connecting intracellular proteostatic stress to local glial reactivity and systemic immune regulation. Extracellular vesicle-associated α-synuclein maintains a seeding-competent conformation, enters recipient cells, and triggers templated aggregation and inflammatory signaling, although its exact pathogenic contribution relative to free α-synuclein and non-vesicular transmission routes remains undefined. Extracellular vesicle cargo dynamically reshapes microglial and astrocytic activation, oligodendroglial homeostasis, neuronal survival, blood-brain barrier integrity, and peripheral immune recruitment. Extracellular vesicles exert bidirectional effects: pathological extracellular vesicles amplify neurotoxicity, while homeostatic or engineered extracellular vesicles restore proteostasis, optimize immune homeostasis, and facilitate neural tissue repair. Advanced techniques including immunocapture, real-time quaking-induced conversion, and single-vesicle profiling enhance the sensitivity and resolution of extracellular vesicle-based biomarkers, enabling improved discrimination among synucleinopathy subtypes. However, clinical translation is hampered by extracellular vesicle heterogeneity, inaccurate cell-origin tracing, pre-analytical variability, insufficient standardization, and limited causal in vivo and longitudinal evidence. It is concluded that extracellular vesicles function as integral components of a dynamic, multilayered communication network, with their outcomes determined by cellular origin, cargo, recipient type, disease stage, and anatomical context. Standardized protocols, longitudinal cohorts, and mechanistic models are indispensable for developing reliable extracellular vesicle biomarkers and safe extracellular vesicle-targeted therapies for synucleinopathies.

title: Chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan 4 participates in the internalization of arginine-rich dipeptide repeat proteins.
abstract: Microsatellite repeat expansion of the 5' GGGGCC 3' sequence in the C9orf72 gene is the most common monogenic form of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia. Dipeptide repeat proteins (DPRs) translated from the mutant allele can be detected in postmortem brains of afflicted individuals. The arginine containing peptides, poly proline-arginine (poly-PR) and poly glycine-arginine (poly-GR), are particularly noxious to cells. Both can undergo cell-to-cell transmission, but underlying mechanisms are not understood. We found rapid internalization and nucleolar localization of bath-applied hemagglutinin (HA) tagged poly-PR with twenty repeats (HA-PR20) in cell lines and neurons. Small molecule and RNAi approaches implicated a temperature-dependent, fluid phase endocytosis mechanism for HA-PR20. We sought to identify DPR-related cell surface uptake factors using µMap high-resolution proximity labeling. DPR-iridium conjugates identified candidate cell-surface proteins which were interrogated in a secondary RNAi screen. Focusing on our strongest candidate, chondroitin sulfate proteoglycan 4 (CSPG4), we showed cellular uptake of HA-PR20 is reduced by inhibition of glycosaminoglycan chain synthesis and knockdown or ablation of CSPG4. Knockdown of CSPG4 protected PR20-induced neuronal toxicity. Using a dual reporter system to interrogate in vitro neuron-to-neuron transmission of PR50, we found PR50 synthesized by one neuron readily spread to neighboring cells. Transmission was significantly reduced with CSPG4 knockdown. Similarly conditioned media from PR50 or GR50 expressing neurons contained transmissible protein that was internalized into neurons in a CSPG4-dependent manner. These results suggest CSPG4 participates in poly-PR/poly-GR internalization and transmission.

title: Coincidence detection in aspiny interneuron dendrites.
abstract: Recent evidence for long-term potentiation (LTP) at glutamatergic synapses on GABAergic interneurons calls for close attention to the sub-cellular phenomena that underlie the induction of plasticity in aspiny dendrites. Neurogliaform interneurons exhibit large NMDA receptor-mediated currents, Hebbian LTP and supralinear summation of glutamatergic signals converging on dendritic compartments. Dendritic supralinearity in interneurons does not require sodium channels. Here we investigate the principles governing supralinear synaptic integration and its interaction with backpropagating action potentials in the synaptic plasticity context. We developed a biophysically realistic, multi-compartmental model of a murine (Mus musculus, male and female) hippocampal neurogliaform interneuron, with dendritic architecture and ion channel densities tuned to match ex vivo recordings. The interaction between synaptic inputs and action potentials was tested with patch-clamp electrophysiology and two-photon imaging of dendritic calcium-dependent fluorescence transients. Whether simulated glutamatergic excitatory postsynaptic potentials are clustered on a dendritic fragment or dispersed across the entire arbor, they summate supralinearly as assessed from the calculated somatic voltage response. Clustered inputs induce more pronounced local depolarizations and calcium transients than dispersed inputs. Action potentials generated at the soma backpropagate throughout the dendritic arbor but are attenuated at branch points. Coincident synaptic input and backpropagating action potentials relieve this attenuation, further enhance dendritic depolarizations, and greatly potentiate calcium influx via NMDA receptors. Despite differences in dendritic anatomy and in the roles of sodium channels, the interplay of orthodromic and antidromic voltage propagation and resultant calcium signal amplification exhibits remarkable similarities between neurogliaform interneurons and principal cells.Significance Statement Neurogliaform interneurons are key regulators of brain circuit activity, yet the dendritic mechanisms that enable these inhibitory cells to undergo synaptic plasticity remain poorly understood. Combining biophysically realistic computer modeling with electrophysiology and two-photon calcium imaging, we show that coincident synaptic input and backpropagating action potentials strongly amplify dendritic depolarization and calcium influx in these interneurons. Although their dendrites lack spines and do not rely on sodium-channel-dependent dendritic spikes, neurogliaform interneurons nonetheless use computational principles remarkably similar to those of excitatory principal neurons. These findings advance the understanding of how inhibitory circuits support learning-related plasticity and may provide foundational insight into disorders such as epilepsy and schizophrenia, in which abnormal dendritic signalling and inhibitory dysfunction are implicated.

title: CosMxScope: scalable reconstruction and digital pathology integration of imaging-based CosMx spatial transcriptomics data.
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics technologies have transformed the capacity to quantify gene expression from human tissues, simultaneously capturing both the cell functional state and spatial organization at cellular and subcellular resolution. The CosMx Spatial Molecular Imager (SMI) is one of the leading platforms at single-cell spatial multi-modal omics profiling, capable of measuring thousands of RNA or protein targets at single-cell and subcellular resolution across whole slide sections. Exported data include field-of-view (FOV) image tiles, subcellular transcript coordinates, and cell segmentation polygons, outputs that are rich in spatial information but not directly compatible with widely used digital pathology tools. Here we present CosMxScope, a lightweight open-source Python framework designed for data exported from the CosMx Spatial Molecular Imager through the AtoMx platform, bridging CosMx spatial outputs with histopathology visualization environments. CosMxScope provides functions for stitching FOV image tiles into reconstructed whole-slide images, converting cell segmentation polygons and transcript coordinates into GeoJSON objects for downstream visualization and assessment within QuPath, and generating spatial visualization plots of cell types, transcript locations, and gene expression patterns. The framework is designed for practical use in translational research settings, enabling interactive exploration of spatial transcriptomic data alongside cell morphology. CosMxScope has been applied in multiple ongoing research projects involving CosMx profiling of human and mouse tissues, supporting pathology-based spatial analysis workflows. This open-source software is available at https://github.com/AivaraX-AI/CosMxScope.

title: Enhanced Endosomal Trafficking Mediated by the Proton-Activated Chloride Channel Underlies Peripheral Sensitization in Neuropathic Pain.
abstract: Endosomal trafficking is essential for protein homeostasis, yet its role in peripheral sensitization of neuropathic pain remains unclear. Here, we identify the proton-activated chloride (PAC) channel as a critical regulator of endosomal trafficking in sensory neurons. In the spared nerve injury (SNI) model, conditional deletion of the PAC channel in sensory neurons reduced neuronal excitability, Rab5/7-dependent endocytic transport pathways, P2X3R hyperfunction, and markedly alleviated mechanical and thermal hypersensitivity. Mechanistically, SNI enhances the PAC channel function, contributing to the decreased intra-endosomal Cl- and reduced endosomal membrane tension; this promotes endosomal sorting complexes required for transport-III-dependent endosomal maturation and accelerates axonal retrograde transport of P2X3R. Last, an exploratory, locus-restricted analysis identified 2 noncoding PACC1 variants associated with the study-defined chronic-pain phenotype in a cohort study. Collectively, these findings identify PAC channel as a key regulator of intra-endosomal Cl- homeostasis and membrane tension, linking dysregulated endosomal trafficking in the nociceptor to neuropathic pain.
authors: Ren Y, Chen H, Luo Y, Chen Y, Zhang Y, Jiang C, Wei Z, Rao X, Wang Y, Qin H
overview: Endosomal trafficking is essential for protein homeostasis, yet its role in peripheral sensitization of neuropathic pain remains unclear.
main: Mechanistically, SNI enhances the PAC channel function, contributing to the decreased intra-endosomal Cl- and reduced endosomal membrane tension; this promotes endosomal sorting complexes required for transport-III-dependent endosomal maturation and accelerates axonal retrograde transport of P2X3R.

title: Axon-guidance factors and their receptors could be potential targets to promote functional recovery via stimulating angiogenesis and blood-brain barrier repair after ischemic stroke.
abstract: Angiogenesis and blood-brain barrier (BBB) repair play important roles in neural functional recovery after ischemic stroke. The formation of new blood vessels improves the local blood supply, enhancing the oxygen and nutrient supply of newly formed neurons. Despite advances in the mechanistic understanding of vascular growth and repair, there are no safe and effective angiogenic treatments that currently exist because of the immature vessel-induced BBB leakage. In addition to the most studied angiogenic growth factors, the process of vascular budding and migration requires the involvement of guiding factors, many of which were initially identified as regulators of axon growth. In this review, the inhibitory and promoting effects of axon-guiding factors on the vascular system are summarized, and their roles in angiogenesis, BBB repair and neural functional recovery after ischemic stroke are discussed.

title: Establishment of polyclonal human induced pluripotent stem cell lines from peripheral blood using a semi-automated processing system.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: The generation of human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs) with homogeneous and stable quality at an affordable cost is key to industrialize hiPSC-based cell therapies and drug development; however, conventional manual production is labor-intensive and difficult to standardize. Automated closed-system approaches can improve reproducibility, reduce contamination risk, and enable scale-out manufacturing, yet concerns remain regarding the quality of hiPSCs produced using this approach specialized in hiPSC generation from peripheral blood cells. METHODS: Here we developed a prototype semi-automated hiPSC production system to generate polyclonal hiPSC lines from peripheral blood cells. The semi-automated device consists of a spiral microfluidic module for leukocyte separation, followed by modules for leukocyte expansion culture and the transduction of a Sendai virus (SeV) vector carrying reprogramming factors. Subsequently, the transduced leukocytes were manually cultured and expanded to generate polyclonal hiPSC lines. RESULTS: The generated polyclonal hiPSC populations maintained a normal karyotype and carried minimal residual SeV vector. Importantly, they exhibited self-renewing capacity and pluripotency comparable to those of established clonal hiPSC lines. Furthermore, when subjected to directed differentiation towards cartilage and kidney organoids, the polyclonal hiPSC lines efficiently differentiated into these lineages. CONCLUSIONS: The semi-automated system enabled the generation of high-quality polyclonal hiPSC lines, which will hold promise for future applications in cell therapy and drug development.

title: Neuroprotective effects of hAEC-derived exosomes against ischemic injury are associated with Foxm1 and IGF1.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Exosomes secreted by human amniotic epithelial stem cells (hAECs-Exos) have attracted considerable attention as potential therapeutic candidates for ischemic stroke. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying their neuroprotective effects remain incompletely understood. METHODS: Oxygen-glucose deprivation followed by reoxygenation (OGD/R) was applied to HT22 and BV2 cells, and a rat model of middle cerebral artery occlusion and reperfusion (MCAO) was also established. The involvement of Foxm1 in hAECs-Exos-mediated protection was investigated using Foxm1 overexpression and hAECs-Exos derived from Foxm1-knockdown donor cells. Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) was examined as a potential downstream mediator of Foxm1 through gene silencing and chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP). A rescue experiment combining Foxm1 overexpression with IGF1 silencing was performed to examine the functional relationship between these molecules. In vivo, the effects of hAECs-Exos or Foxm1-knockdown hAECs-Exos on MCAO rats were assessed via intracerebroventricular injection. RESULTS: Upregulation of Foxm1 significantly mitigated neuronal damage triggered by OGD/R, as indicated by enhanced cellular viability, alleviated oxidative stress, suppressed inflammation, and decreased apoptosis. Conversely, hAECs-Exos derived from Foxm1-knockdown donor cells exhibited attenuated protective effects in both cell types. Mechanistically, ChIP supported the association of Foxm1 with the IGF1 promoter region, while Foxm1 overexpression increased IGF1 protein expression. IGF1 silencing attenuated the protective effects of hAECs-Exos, and simultaneous IGF1 silencing weakened the protective effects associated with Foxm1 overexpression. In vivo, hAECs-Exos increased Foxm1 and IGF1 expression in MCAO rat brains, improved neurological function, decreased infarct areas, and mitigated pathological damage. These effects were attenuated following administration of hAECs-Exos derived from Foxm1-knockdown donor cells. CONCLUSIONS: hAECs-Exos protect against ischemic injury in cellular and animal models, with Foxm1 and IGF1 implicated in the observed neuroprotective effects.
