title: Echinacoside Attenuates α-synuclein Pathology and Lysosomal Dysfunction in PFF-Induced Models Relevant to Parkinson's Disease.
abstract: Abnormal aggregation of α-synuclein (α-syn) and impaired lysosomal degradation are core pathological features of Parkinson's disease (PD). Echinacoside (ECH), the major active component of Cistanche, has been shown to protect dopaminergic neurons in MPTP-induced PD models, but its effects on α-syn clearance and lysosomal function remain unclear. Here, we established a PD-relevant α-syn pathology mouse model by stereotaxic injection of α-syn pre-formed fibrils (PFFs) into the left striatum of C57BL/6 J mice. Mice were divided into four groups: Control, PFFs, PFFs + ECH20 (low-dose), and PFFs + ECH40 (high-dose). The Control group received intrastriatal injection of 0.9% saline, whereas the other groups received α-syn PFFs. ECH was administered orally at 20 or 40 mg/kg for 1 month after modeling, while the Control and PFFs groups received equal volumes of 0.9% saline by oral gavage. Motor function was assessed by rotarod and pole tests at 1, 3, and 6 months, while tyrosine hydroxylase (TH), phosphorylated α-syn (p-α-syn), and lysosome-related proteins were detected in the substantia nigra. In vitro, SH-SY5Y cells were pretreated with ECH before PFFs exposure to evaluate lysosomal morphology, acidification, and proteolytic activity. BafA1, an inhibitor of vacuolar H+-ATPase, was further used to interfere with lysosomal acidification and lysosomal degradation. Six months after PFF injection, mice exhibited significant motor deficits, decreased TH expression, and increased p-α-syn accumulation, accompanied by abnormal lysosomal aggregation, reduced expression of lysosomal proteins (GBA1, CTSD, CTSB, LAMP2, TMEM175). Oral ECH treatment, particularly at 40 mg/kg, improved motor performance, increased TH expression, reduced p-α-syn accumulation, and partially attenuated lysosome abnormalities. In SH-SY5Y cells, ECH also reduced lysosomal abnormalities and improved acidification and proteolytic readouts after PFF exposure. In addition, BafA1 treatment weakened the improvement in lysosomal functional readouts and partially reversed the reduction in p-α-syn accumulation observed after ECH treatment. These findings suggest that ECH attenuates PFF-induced PD-relevant α-syn pathology and is possibly associated with improved lysosomal function, supporting further investigation of ECH as a candidate intervention targeting α-syn pathology and lysosomal dysfunction in PD.

title: MM102 promotes axonal regeneration and synaptic remodeling through membrane lipid remodeling to restore motor function after spinal cord injury.
abstract: Spinal cord injury causes neurological deficits and dysfunction, but effective pharmacological strategies that promote neural regeneration and functional recovery are lacking. This study aimed to investigate the therapeutic potential of MM102, a small-molecule inhibitor of the MLL1-WDR5 interaction, for injured spinal cord repair. HT22 cells were treated with 10 nM MM102 for 6 days, followed by phenotypic evaluation and integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses. MM102 significantly promoted neurite outgrowth and synaptogenesis and increased the expression of the neuronal markers Nestin, synaptophysin, microtubule-associated protein-2, and βIII-tubulin. In vivo, rats with spinal cord injury received MM102 treatment (50 μM, 10 μL/100 g) for 5 weeks, and MM102 repaired spinal cord histoarchitecture, promoted axonal and myelin regeneration and synaptic remodeling, and enhanced locomotor and electrophysiological recovery. Histological staining revealed enhanced axonal and myelin regeneration following MM102 treatment, whereas immunofluorescence analysis revealed significantly increased expression of Nestin, NeuN, c-Jun, NF-200, MBP, and βIII-tubulin. Transcriptomic analysis indicated that MM102 induced gene expression programs associated with neuronal development, axon guidance and synaptic plasticity, whereas metabolomic profiling revealed prominent changes in membrane lipid abundance and neuroactive metabolism. Integrated multiomics analysis further associated these transcriptional responses with membrane phospholipid remodeling and pathways involved in neurotransmitter signaling and synaptic vesicle cycling. Collectively, these findings suggest that MM102 facilitates injured spinal cord repair by modulating responses associated with neural repair and membrane lipid remodeling, also provide novel insights into the potential mechanisms through which small-molecule inhibitors can promote neurogenic potential and elucidate potential therapeutic targets for facilitating functional recovery following spinal cord injury.

title: HDAC6 inhibition promotes peripheral nerve development and regeneration via neurofilament acetylation.
abstract: Peripheral nerve injury remains challenging due to limited neuronal regeneration. Histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6) regulates microtubule dynamics, but its role in peripheral nervous system (PNS) development and repair is incompletely understood. This study investigates the expression, function, and mechanism of HDAC6 in PNS maturation and regeneration. HDAC6 was abundantly expressed in dorsal root ganglia and sciatic nerves. During postnatal development (P1-P28), HDAC6 expression progressively declined, inversely correlating with increased α-tubulin K40 and global acetylation. Pharmacological HDAC6 inhibition with Tubastatin A (Tub A) or suberoylanilide hydroxamic acid (SAHA) accelerated nerve maturation, evidenced by enhanced conduction velocity, myelination, and cytoskeletal integrity. In a sciatic nerve crush model, HDAC6 inhibition promoted functional recovery, axonal regeneration, and remyelination. In vitro, HDAC6 inhibition or siRNA knockdown enhanced neurite outgrowth and growth cone expansion in both motor and sensory neurons. Mechanistically, acetylome identified neurofilament light chain (NEFL) as a novel HDAC6 substrate. Among several hypoacetylated lysine residues post-injury, K316 showed the greatest decrease. Direct HDAC6-NEFL interaction was confirmed by molecular docking and co-immunoprecipitation. Expression of an acetylation-mimetic NEFL (K316Q) mutant promoted neurite outgrowth and growth cone maturation compared with wild-type or acetylation-deficient (K316R) mutants. Collectively, HDAC6 acts as a key negative regulator of PNS development and regeneration, and NEFL K316 acetylation serves as a critical molecular switch for axonal growth. Targeting HDAC6 represents a promising strategy for peripheral nerve repair.

title: Stress-induced alterations in neurodevelopment in iPSC-Derived i n vitro model systems.
abstract: Psychological stress is common in women during pregnancy and after childbirth, showing a prevalence of up to 15.6% in pregnant women in developing countries. Clinical and pre-clinical studies have implicated their role in negatively affecting pregnancy outcomes and have been linked to adverse child outcomes. Yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood, specifically the signatures associated with their effect on human fetal development. Thereby, impairing our further understanding of the effects of therapeutics used to treat these disorders in expecting mothers. This study proposes the use of human iPSC-derived embryoid bodies (EBs) and forebrain-specific organoids as complementary human developmental models to investigate the effects of exposure to prenatal stress (mediated by glucocorticoids) across distinct stages, in vitro. Our findings suggested that excessive glucocorticoids altered early lineage specification in an exposure-dependent manner. This was evidenced by a brief increase in pluripotent and neural progenitor populations, with mild alterations in proliferative dynamics without a net change in proliferative capacity. Changes in lineage-associated markers were observed in ectodermal and meso-endodermal layers of EBs. Particularly, focusing on neurogenesis (forebrain-specific organoids) to understand the impact of stress on neurodevelopment, we saw concentration-dependent changes in progenitor maintenance and neuronal- glial differentiation. Furthermore, the activation of inflammatory and oxidative stress responses can be implicated as signalling mechanisms responsible for the differences observed. Together, these results suggest that glucocorticoid signalling linked to prenatal stress can alter developmental trajectories by modifying cellular states rather than directly altering proliferation or survival during early development.

title: Btbd11 regulates glutamatergic synapse organization in GABAergic inhibitory interneurons.
abstract: The mechanisms that underlie glutamatergic synapse organization and function in GABAergic inhibitory interneurons (INs) are not well described, despite evidence that impaired glutamatergic excitation of INs is implicated in psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia and anxiety. Glutamatergic synapses received by INs have unique basal transmission properties and exhibit distinct synaptic plasticity compared to those received by excitatory neurons, likely due to cell-type specific differences in postsynaptic density (PSD) composition and maintenance mechanisms. In the present study, we show that the interneuron-specific protein Btbd11 regulates excitatory synapse transmission in mixed-sex primary cultured rat and mouse hippocampal interneurons through promotion of phase separation and support of postsynaptic nanoarchitecture. Btbd11 forms a phase separated protein complex with Psd-95 and TARPγ2 and impacts the stability of TARPγ2 and GluA1 within glutamatergic IN synapses in an expression- and phase separation-dependent manner. Using super resolution imaging, we show that Btbd11 displays nanoscale clustering properties within IN synapses that correlate with Psd-95 nanostructure. Furthermore, genetic deletion of Btbd11 decreases PSD protein expression, reduces synapse size, and disrupts Psd-95 nanocluster organization. These effects manifest as a drastic reduction in glutamatergic synaptic transmission onto INs when Btbd11 is deleted. Together, these data provide insights into a novel cell type-specific synaptic regulatory mechanism in an understudied synapse population.Significance Statement Although glutamatergic excitation of GABAergic inhibitory interneurons (INs) is essential for maintenance of balanced signaling in the brain and dysregulation has been linked to neuropsychiatric disorders, the molecular mechanisms underlying IN-specific glutamatergic transmission are not well characterized. Using protein modeling, molecular biology, live-cell and super-resolution imaging, we describe a unique mechanism of glutamatergic synapse organization in INs by Btbd11, an IN-specific synaptic protein. Btbd11 promotes liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and regulates PSD protein mobility, the abundance of key synaptic proteins, and nanoscale synaptic organization. Collectively, this is critical for glutamatergic synaptic transmission within INs. Understanding Btbd11's role at the synapse highlights the importance of synaptic LLPS, providing insight into the regulatory mechanisms in an understudied synapse with psychiatric disease relevance.

title: Depth-enhanced molecular imaging with two-photon oblique plane microscopy.
abstract: High-numerical-aperture (NA) oblique plane microscopy enables noninvasive fluorescence imaging of subcellular dynamics without radical sample modification. However, performance degrades at depth in multicellular specimens as scattering and refractive-index heterogeneity raise out-of-focus background. We report a two-photon oblique plane microscope that improves resolution at depth by combining high-NA single-objective detection with multiphoton plane illumination. The microscope achieves ~ 300 nm lateral and ~ 650 nm axial resolution, with single-molecule sensitivity and < 60 nm localization precision in vivo. Compared with two-photon point scanning, the lower illumination NA delivers order-of-magnitude lower peak intensity, enabling > 5 × faster volumetric acquisition (up to 3.25 × 106 voxels s-1). In multicellular contexts, near-infrared nonlinear excitation enhances contrast throughout the illumination depth by ~ 2 × and restores volumetric resolving power by > 2 × relative to linear excitation. We demonstrate these capabilities through molecular imaging of epithelial tissue, stem-cell-derived gastruloids, and living fruit fly embryos, including multicolor transcription-factor dynamics, optogenetic subcellular control, and single-mRNA tracking, all using standard glass-based mounting.

title: Genetic Susceptibility, Neurodevelopmental Abnormalities, and Neuroimmune Interactions Across Major Psychiatric Disorders.
abstract: Major psychiatric disorders, including schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, and autism spectrum disorder, share overlapping genetic, neurodevelopmental, and neuroimmune underpinnings that challenge traditional diagnostic boundaries. This review synthesizes evidence across three interconnected domains: convergent genetic risk affecting synaptic and immune pathways, neurodevelopmental vulnerabilities shaped by early-life insults, and neuroimmune crosstalk involving blood-brain barrier dysfunction, sustained inflammation, and complement-mediated pathology. We propose a multidimensional developmental-immune framework in which genetic liability, environmental exposure timing, and peripheral immune status jointly shape transdiagnostic trajectories. This framework reframes psychiatric disorders as dynamic interactions among stable trait-like susceptibilities and fluctuating biological states, offering a roadmap for biomarker-driven stratification and early immune-targeted interventions.

title: PINK1‑regulated mitophagy dysfunction in the pathogenesis of Parkinson's disease (Review).
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disorder, characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra and the accumulation of misfolded α‑synuclein forming Lewy bodies. Emerging evidence highlights mitochondrial dysfunction as an important and early event in PD pathogenesis. Among the key regulators of mitochondrial quality control, PTEN‑induced kinase 1 (PINK1) plays a pivotal role by initiating mitophagy, the selective clearance of damaged mitochondria. Under physiological conditions, PINK1 is rapidly degraded, whereas mitochondrial depolarization stabilizes PINK1 on the outer mitochondrial membrane, where it recruits and activates Parkin, an E3 ubiquitin ligase, to promote mitophagy. Loss‑of‑function mutations in PINK1 also disrupt this process, leading to the accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria, oxidative stress, abnormal calcium homeostasis and neuronal apoptosis. Furthermore, PINK1 deficiency has been shown to exacerbate α‑synuclein aggregation, impair synaptic transmission and activate neuroinflammatory pathways, collectively accelerating dopaminergic neurodegeneration. Therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring or enhancing PINK1‑mediated mitophagy through pharmacological activation, gene delivery or modulation of parallel pathways‑represent a promising avenue for PD intervention. Continued elucidation of the molecular functions of PINK1 will provide critical insights into mitochondrial homeostasis and novel therapeutic targets for PD.

title: Spatial mTOR biology: From organelle localization to biomolecular condensates and metabolic control.
abstract: The mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) coordinates cell growth, metabolism, protein synthesis, autophagy, and survival by integrating nutrient availability, growth factors, energy status, mechanical cues, and cellular stress. Beyond classical biochemical cascades, mTOR signaling specificity is fundamentally governed by subcellular localization, temporal recruitment, and microenvironmental context. This review synthesizes current insights into the spatial architecture of mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) and mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2) across lysosomes, endosomes, plasma-membrane microdomains, organelle contact sites, neuronal processes, the nucleus, and biomolecular condensates. We examine how physical principles-including membrane composition and curvature, molecular confinement, macromolecular crowding, scaffold-mediated multivalent interactions, organelle positioning, mechanical tension, and localized translation-dictate signaling outcomes. Furthermore, we contrast membrane-anchored molecular assemblies with three-dimensional biomolecular condensates, detailing their interplay during stress adaptation. Spatial constraints in specialized cell geometries, such as neuronal compartments and developing tissues, illustrate how identical signaling machinery yields divergent functional outputs under altered diffusion environments. We also evaluate how advances in spatial multi-omics and super-resolution imaging extend these subcellular paradigms to tissue-scale heterogeneity. Finally, we highlight major translational hurdles, including the trade-off between spatial resolution and dynamic temporal tracking in current technologies, as well as the inability of conventional pharmacotherapies to selectively target discrete subcellular mTOR pools. Establishing spatial organization as a primary determinant of mTOR signaling clarifies context-dependent physiological outputs and provides a roadmap for developing next-generation spatially targeted therapeutics.

title: Astrocytes contribute to long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acid metabolism affecting microglia in fragile X syndrome.
abstract: Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) influence membrane structure and function, energy metabolism, inflammation, and the ability to regulate microglial activity. We show involvement of astrocytes in long-chain PUFA metabolism in human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived astrocytes with fragile X syndrome (FXS). FXS astrocytes secreted more n-6 docosapentaenoic acid (n-6 DPA) and displayed a higher n-3 DPA to docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) ratio in medium than controls, consistent with an altered n-6 to n-3 PUFA balance in plasma from the FXS mouse. The FXS-specific increase in n-6 DPA secretion was abolished by treatment with all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA), which affected gene expression in astrocyte subpopulations and modulated secreted triacylglycerol species. Microglial exposure to n-6 DPA stimulated expression of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), which also tended to increase in microglia with reduced inflammatory marker expression when cultured in medium from ATRA-treated astrocytes. The results indicate that astrocyte-mediated n-6 DPA regulates the trophic functions of microglia in FXS.

title: Cellular morphology emerges from polygenic, distributed transcriptional variation.
abstract: Height and disease risk are canonical polygenic traits, but whether an analogous architecture governs cellular phenotypes remains unclear. Here, we show that cellular morphology behaves as a polygenic systems phenotype by integrating cross-modal modeling, perturbation profiling, and human genetic variation. An adversarially aligned autoencoder trained on four perturbation datasets predicted morphology from gene expression and generalized without retraining to matched RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) and cell painting profiles from 100 genetically diverse induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) donors. Seventeen morphological features were strongly predicted, particularly those capturing organelle distribution and cytoskeletal architecture. Predictive signal was broadly distributed across genes, with weak individual gene-morphology correlations. Independent CRISPR perturbations supported model-prioritized genes including TIAM1, RAB31, and ABCC5, while genetic analyses identified variant-gene-morphology associations involving PDHX, SLC11A2, and MAPKAPK5. These findings extend polygenic models of complex traits to cellular architecture and provide a framework for interpreting cross-modal prediction in functional genomics.

title: A mid-throughput mitochondrial membrane potential assay in iPSC-derived RPE cells optimised for compound screening.
abstract: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is characterised by retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction and degeneration, leading to secondary photoreceptor loss and central vision impairment. Mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in AMD pathogenesis, making mitochondrial pathways attractive therapeutic targets. While induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived RPE cells are relevant to modelling this condition and for drug screening, intrinsic pigmentation complicates optical readouts and limits phenotypic screening. We optimised a mid-throughput, fluorescence-based assay to quantify mitochondrial membrane potential (ΔΨm) in iPSC-derived RPE cells, using tetramethylrhodamine ethyl ester (TMRE), with conditions adapted to minimise pigment-associated signal interference and compatible with automated 96-well screening. Using a carbonyl cyanide 4-(trifluoromethoxy) phenylhydrazone(FCCP)-challenge paradigm, we screened 160 FDA-approved compounds and prioritised a small set of reproducible TMRE-preserving hits under FCCP-induced stress. Matched viability profiling indicated compound- and line-dependent cytotoxicity at some effective doses, supporting the need for orthogonal triage when interpreting TMRE rescue. Follow-up transcriptomic profiling by Multiplex Analysis of Cells sequencing (MAC-seq) revealed inter-line variability in transcriptional responses, including cases where functional ΔΨm preservation occurred with minimal or no detectable differential expression under the tested conditions. Together, this work establishes a practical FCCP-challenge phenotypic screening platform for ΔΨm in low-pigment iPSC-derived RPE cells and supports combining functional, viability, and transcriptomic readouts to prioritise candidate modulators of mitochondrial stress resilience in genetically diverse backgrounds.

title: Serum Exosomes from Subacute Phase Post-cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Promote Microglial Pro-inflammatory Phenotype Polarization and Exacerbate Blood-Brain Barrier Disruption in Mice.
abstract: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) restores circulation but induces cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury characterized by blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption and microglial-mediated neuroinflammation. Exosomes circulate systemically following CPR, yet their temporal profiles and specific roles remain poorly understood. C57BL/6 mice (n = 5/group) underwent asphyxial cardiac arrest and CPR. BBB permeability was assessed longitudinally (3 h to 14 d) using Evans blue extravasation. Serum exosomes were isolated at 1 d and 3 d post-CPR and characterized. To determine immunomodulatory effects, exosomes were administered via intracerebroventricular injection into recipient mice, and BBB integrity and microglial polarization (CD86, CD206) were evaluated by immunofluorescence and flow cytometry. Additionally, primary cultures of microglia cells isolated from CPR mice were exposed to exosomes in vitro (n = 3/group), and pro-inflammatory phenotype/anti-inflammatory phenotype markers and inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β, TNF-α, iNOS, TGF-β, Arg1, IL-10) were quantified. CPR induced transient BBB disruption peaking at 3 d post-resuscitation. Serum exosomes isolated at both 1 d and 3 d exhibited characteristic cup-shaped morphology. Intracerebroventricular administration of post-CPR exosomes significantly exacerbated BBB leakage and skewed microglial polarization toward a pro-inflammatory phenotype (elevated CD86⁺; reduced CD206⁺), with 3-day exosomes eliciting more potent detrimental effects than 1-day exosomes. In vitro, exposure to 3-day exosomes similarly produced stronger pro-inflammatory transcriptional responses and increased nitric oxide (NO) production compared with 1-day exosomes. Serum exosomes derived from post-CPR mice exhibit pro-inflammatory activity, aggravating BBB disruption and promoting microglial pro-inflammatory phenotype polarization upon central delivery. These findings suggest that circulating exosomes may contribute to post-resuscitation neuroinflammatory injury, and highlight exosome-related pathways as candidate targets worthy of further investigation.
authors: Cai L, Lin P, Hong J, Wang Q, Liao G, Li X, Zhong M
overview: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) restores circulation but induces cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury characterized by blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption and microglial-mediated neuroinflammation.
main: CPR induced transient BBB disruption peaking at 3 d post-resuscitation.

title: Effects of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus on the Offspring's Neurodevelopment.
abstract: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is a major global health concern that affects up to 14% of pregnancies. Traditionally, it has been characterized by hyperglycemia and insulin resistance. However, GDM can also lead to long-term health consequences in offspring, particularly affecting neurodevelopment. It has been associated with an increased risk of cognitive deficits, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and emotional dysregulation in GDM-exposed offspring. Findings from human and experimental studies suggest that GDM disrupts cortical and hippocampal architecture, impairs synaptic plasticity, and induces epigenetic alterations in key neurodevelopmental genes. These mechanistic pathways include oxidative stress, inflammation, apoptosis, and altered neurotrophin expression and receptor signaling. Maternal metabolism, diet, and genetic background may negatively affect neurotrophin expression, which could impact fetal brain development. Lower levels of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and nerve growth factor (NGF) in maternal blood, placental tissue, and cord blood have been linked to poor neurodevelopmental outcomes. This suggests that neurotrophins could be considered potential biomarkers. This narrative review compiles the latest evidence on the effects of GDM on fetal brain development, emphasizing the role of neurotrophins, especially BDNF and NGF, as critical mediators in this process. Emerging data also suggest that glycemic control during pregnancy may partially restore neurotrophin levels and improve neurodevelopmental outcomes. Understanding the interaction between maternal glucose metabolism and fetal brain signaling pathways is essential for pregnancy care and the design of neuroprotective strategies.

overview: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is a major global health concern that affects up to 14% of pregnancies.
main: Lower levels of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and nerve growth factor (NGF) in maternal blood, placental tissue, and cord blood have been linked to poor neurodevelopmental outcomes.

title: Spontaneous Neuronal Activity in Autism Spectrum Disorder: Insights from Human and Animal Studies.
abstract: Developmental spontaneous neuronal activity (SNA) plays an instrumental role in the generation of precise brain circuits. Spontaneous activity patterns guide neuronal differentiation, synaptic refinement, and circuit formation; consequently, perturbations in these activity patterns can profoundly influence brain network organization. Growing evidence suggests that mutations in autism-associated genes lead to alterations of the SNA pattern during early brain development, thereby giving rise to the behavioral features of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). This review integrates findings from neuroimaging studies, which reveal widespread alterations in neuronal excitability in individuals with ASD. Regional homogeneity and functional connectivity analyses consistently demonstrate region-specific abnormalities, including hyperactivity in higher-order cortical regions, hypoactivity in sensorimotor areas, and disrupted long-range connectivity. These functional alterations are closely linked to the underlying molecular and cellular mechanisms such as excitation-inhibition (E/I) imbalance, impaired GABAergic signaling, glutamatergic dysregulation, and abnormalities in calcium-dependent signaling pathways. Identification of activity-based biomarkers, together with advanced neuroimaging techniques and computational and machine learning (ML) approaches, may facilitate early diagnosis of ASD. Understanding the origin and consequences of alterations in SNA provides a unifying framework for identifying novel targets for designing pharmacological intervention strategies.
journal: The Neuroscientist : a review journal bringing neurobiology, neurology and psychiatry
authors: Dey S, Singh A, Bandyopadhyay S, Das A
overview: Developmental spontaneous neuronal activity (SNA) plays an instrumental role in the generation of precise brain circuits.

title: The Cxcl14 chemokine defines pioneer axon guidance and early circuit assembly in the inner ear.
abstract: The nervous system wiring requires the precise coordination of axon guidance, neuronal migration, and target cell recognition. Here, we show that inner ear circuit formation relies on pioneer cells extending an axonal scaffold that selectively targets early-born hair cells. High spatiotemporal imaging of pioneer axons reveals how they navigate through the cranial environment, establishing dynamic cell-cell contacts with other axons to finally stabilize in target cells. These pioneer axons are required not only for follower axon growth but also for coordinated migration of follower neurons, revealing a cellular hierarchy underlying circuit assembly. We identify the chemokine Cxcl14 as a novel instructive guidance cue regulating pioneer axon extension, turning, and fasciculation at discrete cellular decision points. Loss of Cxcl14 disrupts axonal navigation, compromises synaptic organization in hair cells, and impairs mechanosensory-based behavior. Together, our findings establish a new chemokine-based mechanism linking pioneer axon guidance to early sensory circuit assembly necessary for building mechanosensory networks.

title: Endosomal signalling of protease-activated receptor-2 amplifies histamine-induced pain of irritable bowel syndrome.
abstract: BACKGROUND.: Proteases and histamine, co-secreted by mast cells and bacteria, sensitize colonic nociceptors and contribute to irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) pain. OBJECTIVE.: To determine whether irreversible proteolytic cleavage of protease-activated receptor-2 (PAR2) and its continued activity in endosomes amplify and sustain otherwise transient pronociceptive actions of histamine receptors (HRs) to cause recurrent pain, the defining symptom of IBS. DESIGN.: We investigated PAR2 and H1R coexpression in nociceptors using RNAscope and assessed the consequences of coactivation using electrophysiological assays of nociceptor sensitization and biophysical measurements of receptor and effector activity. RESULTS.: PAR2 and H1R were coexpressed by human and mouse dorsal root ganglion nociceptors. Intracolonic infusion of fecal supernatants from IBS patients with elevated histamine and proteolytic activity enhanced mechanosensitivity of colonic nociceptors in mice. Antagonists of PAR2 or H1R abolished this response. Combined administration of subthreshold concentrations of trypsin and histamine replicated the effects of fecal supernatant and caused hyperexcitability of isolated nociceptors. Pre-activation with trypsin sensitized histamine-induced hyperexcitability in nociceptors from wild-type but not Par2−/− mice. Endocytosis inhibitors prevented this hypersensitivity, consistent with sustained endosomal signaling of PAR2 and persistent nociceptor hyperexcitability. Trypsin amplified histamine-induced activation of H1R and β-arrestin2 and Gαq effectors at the plasmalemma and in endosomes. Conversely, histamine did not sensitize trypsin-induced hyperexcitability of neurons, in line with the inability of histamine to induce sustained nociceptor hypersensitivity. CONCLUSIONS.: By amplifying and maintaining the otherwise transient actions of H1R and possibly other pain receptors, persistent PAR2 endosomal signaling makes a dominant contribution to IBS-related colonic pain.

title: APC regulates NSLIT2-induced internalization and signaling of the chemorepellent receptor, ROBO1.
abstract: The SLIT-Roundabout signaling pathway regulates axon guidance and cell migration, and ROBO1 is a receptor for SLIT ligands. ROBO1 undergoes constitutive endocytosis, which is enhanced upon NSLIT2 binding, but the molecular mechanisms and functional consequences of this process are not well understood. Using pharmacologic inhibitors and molecular techniques, we found that clathrin-mediated endocytosis is necessary for NSLIT2-induced inhibition of cell spreading. To explore the underlying mechanisms, we performed proximity-dependent biotin identification to identify ROBO1-interacting proteins whose association with the cytoplasmic domain of ROBO1 is differentially regulated by NSLIT2. We discovered that adenomatous polyposis coli, a multifunctional tumor suppressor, is in close proximity to ROBO1 but dissociates upon binding of NSLIT2 and that this dissociation is necessary for clathrin-mediated endocytosis of ROBO1 and subsequent effects on cell morphology. These findings provide new insights into the functional mechanisms by which NSLIT2 binding to ROBO1 affects changes in actin cytoskeletal architecture.

title: Cell adhesion molecule-related proteins signal to promote cytoneme elongation from Sonic Hedgehog-producing cells.
abstract: Tissue morphogenesis and postdevelopmental homeostasis rely on efficient information exchange between communicating cells. Cytonemes are actin-based protrusions that contribute to precise information flow by facilitating contact-mediated directional transport of diverse signaling cargoes. How pathway-specific cytonemes are formed is poorly understood, as are the molecular mechanisms promoting actin organization for elongation and stability of the dynamic cellular extensions. We investigated biogenesis of Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) cytonemes, revealing functional repurposing of cell adhesion molecule-related proteins Brother of CDON (BOC) and Cell adhesion molecule-related, Down-regulated by Oncogenes (CDON) into recruiters of actin regulators FARP1 and Cdc42 for cytoneme elongation. Loss of BOC and CDON function blunts protrusion-localized Cdc42 activity, reducing cytoneme lengths and occurrence in SHH-expressing cells. Live imaging of developing murine spinal cords reveals that CDON loss in SHH-expressing cells reduces the frequency of neuroepithelial cytonemes and alters neuronal cell fate specification. These results inform a model whereby SHH-binding proteins promote ligand transport through stimulating formation of long cytonemes.

main: These results inform a model whereby SHH-binding proteins promote ligand transport through stimulating formation of long cytonemes.

title: Incomplete synaptic vesicle priming functionally disconnects CA1 pyramidal cells.
abstract: The hippocampal CA1 area is perceived as a nonrecurrent neuronal network, i.e., CA1 pyramidal cells (CA1PCs) within the CA1 area innervate mainly γ-aminobutyric acid-releasing interneurons but not each other. Here, we performed an unbiased examination of the functional properties of local CA1PC output synapses using in vitro two-photon glutamate imaging. Fluorescent transients measured with iGluSnFR3 in individual boutons displayed extraordinary heterogeneity in their amplitudes and short-term plasticity patterns upon a complex train of presynaptic action potential firing. Post hoc electron microscopy of the imaged boutons demonstrated that distinct postsynaptic structure-innervating boutons display different functional properties. Approximately 25% of the boutons innervate CA1PC spines, which either release glutamate with very low release probability or completely fail to release. Phorbol 12,13-dibutyrate and elevated calcium (2+) concentration, manipulations that enhance synaptic vesicle priming and fusion, convert these silent into properly functioning synapses. Our results provide evidence that CA1PCs are interconnected with structurally and molecularly intact glutamatergic synapses, but incomplete synaptic vesicle (SV) priming precludes SV release.

title: A Correlative Light and Electron Microscopy Workflow for Nanoscale Three-Dimensional Reconstruction of Synaptic Projections From the Thalamic Reticular Nucleus.
abstract: Correlative light and electron microscopy (CLEM) combines molecular specificity with nanoscale ultrastructural resolution and has become an important approach for investigating neural circuit organization. However, ultrastructural reconstruction of long-range projection terminals remains technically challenging. This study aimed to develop a CLEM workflow for the identification, localization, three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction, and ultrastructural characterization of thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN)-derived presynaptic terminals in the mouse thalamus. TRN presynaptic terminals were selectively labeled by stereotaxic injection of rAAV-hSyn-Synaptophysin-mCherry. Confocal microscopy was combined with serial section scanning electron microscopy (ssSEM) to achieve fluorescence-guided ultrastructural imaging and 3D reconstruction of labeled axonal boutons and synaptic contacts. The CLEM workflow enabled fluorescence-guided identification of presynaptic terminals within serial EM datasets. 3D reconstruction of a representative TRN axon segment revealed multiple en passant boutons along continuous axonal shafts. Ultrastructural analysis demonstrated synaptic contacts with multiple postsynaptic dendritic profiles, together with distinct vesicle distributions and mitochondrial organization within presynaptic boutons. This study presents a practical CLEM-based workflow for nanoscale reconstruction of long-range synaptic projections. Application of this method to the TRN-to-thalamus pathway illustrates the spatial organization of presynaptic boutons and their postsynaptic contacts in the thalamic neuropil. The workflow provides a methodological framework for ultrastructural studies of defined neural projections in the mammalian brain.

title: The people behind the papers - Pavel Tomancak and Jean-Yves Tinevez.
abstract: Segmenting cells and tracking their internal structures remains a complex image-analysis challenge in cell and developmental biology. In their work, Johannes Girstmair, Tobias Pietzsch, Pavel Tomancak, Jean-Yves Tinevez and colleagues demonstrate how Mastodon, an existing Fiji/ImageJ plugin, can visualise and analyse cell lineages and track cells in 3D within large microscopy datasets. To learn more about their work, we talked to the two corresponding authors, Pavel Tomancak, Principal Investigator at the Max Planck Institute of Molecular Cell Biology and Genetics, Germany, and director of the Central European Institute of Technology, Czech Republic, as well as Jean-Yves Tinevez, founder and leader of the Image Analysis Facility, Institute Pasteur, France.
overview: Segmenting cells and tracking their internal structures remains a complex image-analysis challenge in cell and developmental biology.

title: Integrating Cytoskeletal Systems in Neurons and Glia: Dynamic Orchestration of Structure and Function.
abstract: Neurons and glia form the circuitry of our nervous system, allowing nerve cells to communicate with each other and other cell types throughout the body in a highly specific manner to integrate sensory, motor, and cognitive functions. The ability of these cells to do this is profoundly dependent on an elaborate and dynamic cytoskeleton which allows these cells to adopt complex shapes and specialized structures such as myelin sheaths, the blood-brain barrier, axonal growth cones, dendritic spines, nodes of Ranvier, synapses, and elaborate sensory organs. The cytoskeleton is also critical for morphogenetic movements, the migration of neuronal precursors, and axon growth, which together establish the organization and wiring pattern of the central and peripheral nervous system during development. This review provides a primer on our current understanding of the cytoskeleton of neurons and glia, with an emphasis on how the protein polymers of the cytoskeleton-microtubules, actin filaments, intermediate filaments, and septins-work together to orchestrate the remarkable shapes and functions of these cells. We also highlight key questions and challenges for the field and technological advances that may help address them.
journal: The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
authors: Jahan N, York HM, Bailey HM, Swann IC, Leterrier C, Spiliotis ET, Aiken J, Tymanskyj SR, Brown A, Winckler B

title: Brain organoids: Experimental access to human-specific brain development.
abstract: Human cerebral cortical development includes species-divergent cellular programs and unusually prolonged trajectories that remain difficult to investigate experimentally. These processes support human-specific cognitive abilities and are thought to be associated with vulnerability to neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders. Human brain organoids provide a tractable system for studying these processes across developmental time and under controlled perturbation. Here, we review how cortical organoids model human-specific features of progenitor biology and cell diversification, as well as progressive cellular maturation and circuit formation. We consider the limitations that constrain later-stage maturation and how approaches including the addition of missing cell types, the use of assembloids, and transplantation can extend the developmental processes accessible to study. Finally, we examine how patient-derived, isogenic, chimeric, and perturbation-based organoid systems are being used to investigate neurodevelopmental disorders and, in turn, reveal mechanisms of typical human development.

title: ER-mitochondria contacts orchestrate mitochondrial transport via C19orf12.
abstract: Endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-mitochondria contact sites facilitate lipid transfer, calcium signaling, and mitochondrial division; however, their role in mitochondrial transport remains unclear. Here, we identify hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP)-associated protein C19orf12 as an ER-anchored regulator of mitochondrial trafficking. The loss of C19orf12 leads to perinuclear mitochondrial clustering in cells, impaired anterograde transport in neurons, and progressive locomotor dysfunction in mice that recapitulates key features of HSP in humans. Mechanistically, C19orf12 forms a discrete complex with the mitochondrial Rho GTPase Miro1 and the Kinesin-1 motor Kif5b, thereby providing a molecular link between ER-mitochondria contacts and microtubule-based anterograde transport. Ca2+ also modulated C19orf12-Miro1 behavior in vitro and showed a biphasic association with mitochondrial motility in live cells. Therefore, our findings establish ER‒mitochondria contact sites as logistical hubs for Kinesin-1 motor loading and highlight the importance of the Ca2+-tunable C19orf12 scaffold in sustaining directional mitochondrial transport, providing a mechanistic framework for how C19orf12 loss may contribute to neurodegeneration.

title: J-Aggregation-Reshaped pKa in a Spirocyclic BODIPY Enables Ratiometric Lysosomal pH Sensing and Super-Resolution Imaging.
abstract: Ratiometric fluorescent pH probes typically rely on complex intramolecular energy/charge transfer, rendering the design strategies increasingly rigid. We report a conceptually distinct ratiometric probe based on pH-driven J-aggregate disassembly utilizing a spirocyclic BODIPY platform. Strategic installation of β-Cl and α-3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)phenylvinyl substituents on BODIPY synergistically drives J-aggregate formation via directional X···π, F···H, and π···π interactions. The resulting J-aggregates and the corresponding monomer displayed markedly different pKa values (4.69 vs. 7.54, ΔpKa = 2.85). As pH increases, spirocyclization is triggered, driving the cooperative disassembly of the J-aggregates, while monomer emission remains constant, thereby enabling a robust ratiometric readout (I714/I654) with excellent reversibility. This supramolecular J-aggregate enables quantitative lysosomal pH detection in cells, diagnosis of acute gastritis in mice, and self-blinking super-resolution lysosomal imaging without exogenous additives. This work establishes a new paradigm for ratiometric probe design via aggregation control and stimulus-responsive supramolecular disassembly.

title: International Multicenter Retrospective Study on UBTF-Related Neurodevelopmental Disorder.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: UBTF encodes the upstream binding transcription factor (UBTF), a protein essential for rRNA synthesis. Dominantly acting pathogenic variants, either de novo or inherited, have been associated with a broad clinical childhood-onset neurodegenerative/neurodevelopmental spectrum whose genotype-phenotype correlation has not been accurately defined yet. This multicenter study aims to conduct a retrospective analysis of a large cohort of patients with pathogenic variants in the UBTF gene to refine diagnostic criteria and identify clinically relevant outcome measures for future trials. METHODS: Clinical centers provided clinical, molecular, and neuroimaging data on patients carrying pathogenic or predicted pathogenic UBTF variants, consistent with the clinical phenotype. Data were collected using an human phenotype ontology-based standardized electronic case report form and included unreported cases or updated information on patients reported in the literature from January 2017 to December 2024. RESULTS: A cohort of 49 patients (23 previously unreported) was included in the study. The disease typically presented at ≤3 years (89.6%) with neuroregression in 71.4% of cases, either in a child with preexisting neurodevelopmental delay (42.9%) or after previously normal psychomotor development (28.6%). Less frequently, neurodevelopmental delay occurred in isolation (26.5%). During disease progression, patients developed behavioral abnormalities (81.6%), movement disorders (78.3%), autonomic manifestations (50.0%), and epilepsy (34.7%). At the last follow-up (mean age 13 years and 6 months), only 2 patients were deceased (4.1%). The main neuroimaging findings included white matter hyperintensity (68.1%), cerebral (66.0%) and cerebellar (51.1%) atrophy, and thinning of the corpus callosum (38.3%). However, brain MRI findings were reported as normal in 21.3% of cases. We identified 7 novel UBTF variants (c.271G>C; c.349A>T; c.495C>A; c.517G>A; c.761A>G; c.1048-2A>G; and c.1625_1626+15del). Genotype-phenotype analysis led to the distinction of 2 allelic, clinically distinct disorders: a childhood-onset neurodegenerative disease due to gain-of-function variants, characterized by the triad of neuroregression, movement, and behavioral disorders, and a neurodevelopmental disorder with a milder clinical course associated with loss-of-function/hypomorphic variants. DISCUSSION: The results from our deep-phenotyping analysis suggest the classification of UBTF-related disease into 2 main clinical syndromes impacting the natural history of the disease with a different degree of severity and complexity. This novel observation should be considered in the management and prognosis of patients and will be fundamental in the design of targeted therapies.
authors: Balletto G, Carli S, Coppola A, Torella A, Lee HF, Korenke C, Lebon S, Sedlackova L, Nagy A, Eichler FS

title: Reduced hypoxanthine Ameliorates LPS-triggered autism-like stereotyped behaviors in intestinal Tlr4 knockout mice via the DRN ROS-5-HT axis.
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) involves social deficits and severe stereotyped behavior. While central serotonin (5-HT) systems and Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) activation are known to be implicated in ASD, how gut TLR4 affects central 5-HT and stereotyped behavior remains unknown. This study demonstrated that prenatal lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced social deficits in offspring of both intestinal Tlr4 knockout (Tlr4△IEC) and Tlr4fl/fl mice. However, the stereotyped behaviors and the inhibition of dorsal raphe nuclei (DRN) 5-HT were reduced in Tlr4△IEC-LPS mice compared with those in Tlr4fl/fl-LPS mice. By intersecting metabolites present in both colonic and cerebrospinal fluid, and selecting those exclusively changing in the colon of Tlr4fl/floffspring, hypoxanthine was identified as a metabolite that can cross the blood-brain barrier and mediate the effects of intestinal Tlr4 knockout on DRN 5-HT signaling. Remarkably, hypoxanthine and xanthine oxidase were increased in the serum of ASD children compared to typical development (TD) children. In vivo and in vitro experiments confirmed that hypoxanthine increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) and reduced 5-HT production, thereby promoting 5-HT neuron apoptosis. The inhibition of both the PI3K/AKT and 5-HT pathways in H2O2-treated PC12 cells was rescued by glutathione pretreatment in vitro. Meanwhile, the above LPS-induced DRN changes were significantly different in the Tlr4fl/fl offspring, and were reversed in the Tlr4△IEC mice after LPS exposure. Collectively, intestinal Tlr4 knockout reduces LPS-induced stereotyped behaviors, and the mechanism involves reduced hypoxanthine production and ROS-mediated inhibition of PI3K/AKT signaling, thereby decreasing 5-HT neuronal apoptosis by elevating the 5-HT level in DRN.
authors: Luo R, Liu Y, Yan J, Hu R, Lin F, Yuan B, Xiang X, Yang T, Sun Z, Xiao L
overview: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) involves social deficits and severe stereotyped behavior.
main: Remarkably, hypoxanthine and xanthine oxidase were increased in the serum of ASD children compared to typical development (TD) children.

title: Microglial Cofilin-1 Regulates Neuroinflammatory Responses and Behavioral Outcomes Following Intracerebral Hemorrhage.
abstract: Cofilin-1, an actin-binding protein, modulates cytoskeletal dynamics and cellular motility. Although its role in conditional neuron knockout (KO) and neuronal injury has been well studied, the specific deletion of cofilin-1 in microglia and its role in neuroinflammation after intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) remains unknown. This study aimed to characterize the effects of microglia-specific cofilin-1 deficiency on microglial morphology, homeostasis, behavioral phenotypes, and neurobehavioral and neuroinflammatory outcomes following ICH in male and female mice. A conditional KO mouse model was generated by crossing cofilinfl/fl (Flx) mice with CX3CR1-Cre drivers to achieve microglia-specific deletion. Baseline behavioral performance, microglial morphology, and homeostatic markers were evaluated in both sexes. ICH was then induced by intra-striatal collagenase injection, and neurobehavioral function, brain edema, hematoma volume, microglial activation, and peripheral immune responses were evaluated three days post-injury. Microglial deletion of cofilin-1 was associated with reduced TMEM119 expression, increased IBA1 immunoreactivity, and morphological transformation toward an activated phenotype. Female KO mice showed pronounced hyperlocomotion and decreased anxiety-like behavior, whereas both sexes exhibited impaired neuromuscular performance in the wire hang test. After ICH, KO mice had significantly larger hematoma volumes, enhanced microglial activation, and increased peripheral leukocyte counts compared with Flx controls. Notably, these changes were more severe in female KO mice, indicating a sex-dependent vulnerability. Our findings establish cofilin-1 as a key regulator of microglial homeostasis and immune balance within the brain. Deficiency of microglial cofilin-1 predisposes to worse secondary brain injury after ICH in a sex-dependent manner.
authors: Almarghalani DA, Ali M, Rust MB, Hall FS, Shah ZA
overview: Cofilin-1, an actin-binding protein, modulates cytoskeletal dynamics and cellular motility.
main: Microglial deletion of cofilin-1 was associated with reduced TMEM119 expression, increased IBA1 immunoreactivity, and morphological transformation toward an activated phenotype.

title: CellScore: an open-source image-based pipeline for automated cell quantification in microalgae.
abstract: Accurate quantification of microalgal cell density is essential for both basic research and industrial applications, as it directly reflects culture growth, productivity, and physiological status. There are existing methods routinely used to measure cell counts, although many are limited by high cost, labor-intensive workflows, or steep technical barriers. To address these limitations, we developed CellScore, a rapid and accessible image-based pipeline for microalgal cell counting implemented in ImageJ, a widely adopted open-source platform in the biological sciences ( https://github.com/shijieh/imageJ-annotate ). By leveraging the broad user base and ease of installation of the software, CellScore enables researchers to obtain reliable cell counts from standard microscopy images with minimal specialized equipment. Although the workflow has only been tested with three microalgae species of similar morphologies, the pipeline balances automation with user control and includes practical troubleshooting strategies to facilitate adoption by new users. Thus, CellScore has the potential to be used broadly across other species, however, broader validation across diverse morphologies is required. Overall, CellScore provides a cost-effective, user-friendly, and reproducible solution for routine microalgal cell quantification in both laboratory and applied settings.

title: Exosome-associated cargo is linked to familial Alzheimer's disease-associated phenotypes in vitro.
abstract: The propagation of pathological proteins such as tau and amyloid-beta (Aβ) in Alzheimer's disease (AD) is poorly understood. Here, we developed a human-relevant in vitro conditioned medium (CM)-based model using human neural progenitor ReN cells carrying Familial AD (FAD) mutations in amyloid precursor protein (APP Sw/Lo) and presenilin 1 (PSEN1ΔE9). Healthy ReN-derived neurons and astrocytes treated with FAD-CM for nine weeks exhibited AD features, including cellular toxicity, neuro-glial alterations, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Exogenous Aβ42 further induced neuroglial and mitochondrial damage. Exosomes released by FAD cells and -to a lesser extent- by CM-treated healthy cells showed elevated Aβ42/40 ratios. Proteomic analysis also revealed that exosomes from FAD-cells carried a distinct content, including overrepresentation of proteins linked to inflammation, extracellular matrix remodelling, synaptic dysfunction, and Aβ processing, as well as Calmodulin-like protein 3. Moreover, exosomes were actively internalized by healthy cells through an actin-dependent mechanism. In summary, these findings support a model based on FAD-associated APP/PSEN1 mutations in which exosome-associated cargo alongside soluble and non-vesicular factors contribute to the transfer of AD-associated cellular phenotypes.

title: Rab GTPases and the Rabopathy framework: from synaptic trafficking to neurodegeneration via LRRK2-driven pathology.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and Huntington's disease (HD) show significant differences in their clinical manifestations, but they all seem to share a common upstream problem: malfunction in the membrane transport controlled by Rab GTPases. This review introduces the concept of Rabopathy, a framework that connects developmental synaptic maturation defects with late-onset protein aggregation. The LRRK2-Rab phosphorylation axis is emerging as a potential common amplifying mechanism across these disorders, with the strongest mechanistic support in PD and growing implications in AD and HD. When Rab substrates are excessively phosphorylated at specific sites, vesicular transport is impaired or arrested, leading to progressive depletion of the reserve pool of synaptic vesicles and the surface pool of receptors, and severe compromise of the autophagy-lysosome flux. The failure of distinct Rab sub-networks also produces disease-specific signatures, including Rab5-driven endosomal congestion in AD, Rab35-mediated α-synuclein secretion in PD, and Rab11/Rab7 trafficking collapse in HD. Restoration of Rab flux may be a therapeutic strategy for neurodegenerative diseases, which can be achieved through calibration of LRRK2 activity, modulation of selective Rab subtypes, and rescue of the trafficking network at the systems level.
authors: Zha L, Xu J, Zhu X, Tu Q, Zhong C, Zhan L, Zhang M, Zhou D, Wang X, Wu J
overview: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and Huntington's disease (HD) show significant differences in their clinical manifestations, but they all seem to share a common upstream problem: malfunction in the membrane transport controlled by Rab GTPases.
main: Restoration of Rab flux may be a therapeutic strategy for neurodegenerative diseases, which can be achieved through calibration of LRRK2 activity, modulation of selective Rab subtypes, and rescue of the trafficking network at the systems level.

title: An Optimized Stem Cell Secretome Proteomics Platform: Application to Progranulin-Deficient iPSCs.
abstract: Stem cells secrete diverse extracellular proteins that regulate pluripotency, differentiation, and cell-cell communication, making them powerful model systems for studying development, disease mechanisms, and regenerative medicine. However, robust stem cell secretome analysis remains technically challenging. Unlike many other cell types, pluripotent stem cells cannot tolerate serum starvation or growth factor deprivation, while low-abundance secreted proteins are often masked by media-derived proteins and intracellular contamination. Here, we systematically optimized the secretome proteomics workflow in induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) by evaluating culture medium composition, conditioned-media collection time, cell plating density, media harvest and preparation methods, LC-MS acquisition methods, and data analysis strategies. Full-strength Essential 8 medium, 48 h media collection, 80% cell confluency, two-step centrifugation, and data-independent acquisition (DIA)LC-MS/MS provided the optimal secretome proteomics data quality. We then applied the optimized platform to an isogenic iPSC disease model to investigate how progranulin deficiency reshapes the extracellular and intracellular proteomes. Progranulin-deficient iPSCs showed a coordinated reduction of extracellular lysosomal hydrolases despite relatively modest intracellular proteome changes, suggesting altered lysosome trafficking and possible impairment of lysosomal exocytosis. Together, this work establishes a robust and standardized workflow for stem cell secretome proteomics and demonstrates its utility for investigating extracellular proteome remodeling in human disease models.

title: PRKN-independent mitophagy regulators in dopaminergic neurons identified by genome-wide CRISPR screening.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta. Genetic and epidemiological studies have suggested that mitochondrial dysfunction is implicated in the development of PD. PRKN/Parkin is known to play an essential role in mitochondrial quality control and mitophagy. Indeed, mutations and inactivation of this gene are associated with hereditary and idiopathic forms of PD. Despite extensive studies on PRKN-dependent mitophagy, the molecular regulators of PRKN-independent mitophagy in dopaminergic neurons remain incompletely understood. We generated a PRKN knockout iPSC-derived dopaminergic neuronal line expressing the fluorescent mitophagy biosensor mito-SRAI, which reports the delivery of mitochondria to lysosomes as an increase in the TOLLES/YPet fluorescence ratio. We used this cell line to conduct a genome-wide CRISPR knockout screen to reveal genetic regulators involved in PRKN-independent mitophagy. Dozens of genes were identified whose knockout increased the TOLLES/YPet ratio in an uncoupler-dependent manner. Of these, several genes emerged as candidates with potential therapeutic implications, one of which was Cathepsin F (CTSF). CCCP treatment increased the TOLLES/YPet ratio in neurons with siRNA-mediated CTSF knockdown, and CTSF knockdown partially preserved the proportion of tyrosine hydroxylase-positive dopaminergic neurons after paraquat exposure. These results suggest that CTSF is a candidate regulator of PRKN-independent mitophagy and that this lysosomal enzyme may represent a potentially druggable candidate target for PD.

overview: Parkinson's disease (PD) is characterized by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta.

title: Live-cell imaging of inter-organelle contacts using an integrated dimerization-dependent fluorescent protein reporter.
abstract: Organelles communicate with each other by building membrane contact sites (MCSs) via specialized protein-protein and/or protein-membrane interactions. Conventional light microscopy cannot distinguish organelles connected by MCSs from those merely juxtaposed. In addition, organelle contacts are dynamic, yet only a limited number of tools are available to monitor MCSs in living cells. In this study, we developed a series of reporters based on dimerization-dependent fluorescent proteins (ddFP) to visualize, quantify and follow inter-organelle contacts. We first generated an integrated system specifically designed to study contacts between late endocytic compartments (late endosomes and lysosomes) and the endoplasmic reticulum (ER). This system utilizes a single plasmid coding for the two complementary ddFP components: green A (GA) and green B (GB) targeted to the ER and late endosomes and lysosomes (LE/Lys), respectively. This construct enabled the generation of a stable reporter cell line suitable for semi-quantitative imaging. The ddFP reporter, which we called ddFP LELYS-ER, did not perturb endogenous LE/Lys-ER contacts in stable cells, and detected changes in the number of LE/Lys-ER contacts, for example, upon downregulation of the ER-resident VAP tether protein family, or under conditions of lysosomal damage. Moreover, live-cell imaging revealed that LE/Lys-ER contacts have distinct shapes, mobilities and lifetimes. Finally, using the same vector design, we generated two additional integrated reporter systems adapted to the study of contacts between the ER and the plasma membrane, and between the ER and mitochondria.

title: CelFDrive - multimodal deep learning-assisted microscopy for automated detection of rare events.
abstract: The emergence of automated microscopy has enabled the collection of large datasets of rare biological events, accelerating discovery in biology. However, most existing methods cannot be readily integrated into microscopy setups or are limited to a single microscope type. We present CelFDrive, a software package that automatically detects rare events of interest and automates high-resolution three-dimensional imaging of target cells by integrating deep learning-assisted cell classification of auxiliary low-magnification fluorescence images. We show that CelFDrive reduced the mean time required to nominate a mitotic prophase candidate for high-resolution light-sheet imaging by over 30-fold relative to manual expert selection. This approach can be used to define the order of kinetochore assembly upon nuclear envelope breakdown. The trained CelFDrive detector demonstrated transferability by retaining mitotic cell detection capability in an independently generated dataset using a different cell line, DNA marker and imaging setup. As datasets grow and models improve, CelFDrive offers a clear path toward intelligent imaging systems that not only accelerate data collection, but also fundamentally enhance how biological questions are explored.

title: Evaluation of the effect of p38γ gene delivery using exosomes derived from mesenchymal stem cells on Alzheimer's rat model.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by dementia, memory loss, and cognitive decline. This study investigated the therapeutic potential of delivering the p38γ gene via exosomes derived from adipose-derived stem cells (ADSC-Exos) in a rat model of streptozotocin (STZ)-induced AD. METHODS AND RESULTS: After the AD model was established, the rats were administered via intraperitoneal injections of p38γ, Exo, or p38γ-loaded ADSC-Exo (Exo+p38γ). Cognitive and memory assessments were performed via novel object recognition (NOR), passive avoidance, elevated plus-maze (EPM), and the Barnes maze (BM). Histological techniques were used to evaluate cell density and beta-amyloid (Aβ) plaque accumulation, while quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT‒PCR) was used to measure the transcription levels of neuronal nuclei (NeuN), glial cell line-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF), nerve growth factor (NGF), and sex-determining region Y-box 2 (SOX2). Additionally, the expression of GDNF, brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), SOX2, and malondialdehyde (MDA) was analyzed via an ELISA kit. The Exo and Exo+p38γ groups demonstrated significant improvements in STZ-induced memory deficits across various assessments. However, no significant differences in the protein expression levels of GDNF, BDNF, SOX2, and MDA or the gene expression levels of SOX2, NeuN, GDNF, and NGF were detected between STZ-treated rats that received Exos+p38γ and those that received Exos alone. CONCLUSIONS: Taken together, this study demonstrates that ADSC-derived exosomes effectively improve cognitive deficits in an AD rat model; Although Exo+p38γ was associated with a significant increase in SOX2 gene expression compared with the AD group, the direct comparison between Exo+p38γ and ADSC-Exos did not demonstrate a statistically significant additional effect.
authors: Sheykhhasan M, Kalhor N, Sheikholeslami A, Fazaeli H, Movahed TK, Dolati M, Naserpour L, Sahraei SS, Asl FD, Seyedebrahimi R

title: Apolipoprotein E4 (ApoE4) causes disruption of glypican-1 recycling and processing in ApoE4/4 fibroblasts and induced neurons.
abstract: The apolipoprotein E4 (ApoE4) isoform confers increased risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. ApoE2 and ApoE3 can be S-nitrosylated (Cys-SNO), but not ApoE4. The recycling heparan sulfate (HS) proteoglycan glypican-1 (GPC1) can also carry SNO and release HS by a Cu/NO dependent cleavage. ApoE3/3 and ApoE4/4 fibroblasts and the respective induced neurons (-iN) were exposed to inhibitors of NO-synthases (NOS), to NO donor or ascorbate and examined by immunofluorescence microscopy. Exposure to NO donor increased co-localization between ApoE3-SNO and GPC1 in ApoE3/3 fibroblasts. Co-localization between ApoE3 and GPC1 diminished when cNOS/NOS3 was inhibited in ApoE3/3 fibroblasts. Exposure to NO donor or ascorbate indicated almost fully utilized capacity to release HS from GPC1. When nNOS/NOS1 and iNOS/NOS2 were inhibited in ApoE3/3-iN, release of HS decreased, and exposure to ascorbate again showed that the capacity to release HS was almost fully utilized. In ApoE4/4 fibroblasts endosome transport was retarded and HS and GPC1-SNO accumulated in late endosomes. Inhibition of cNOS/NOS3 in ApoE4/4 fibroblasts had no effect on HS release but inhibition of iNOS/NOS2 had a substantial effect. Exposure to NO donor or ascorbate revealed unutilized capacity to release HS from GPC1. In ApoE4/4-iN, nNOS/NOS1 and iNOS/NOS2 were major producers of NO. Inhibition of nNOS/NOS1 and iNOS/NOS2 in ApoE4/4-iN again showed unutilized capacity to release HS. We propose that expression of ApoE4, which retards endosome trafficking, but also activates iNOS/NOS2, results in accumulation of GPC1-SNO and slow exit of HS from endosomes which can be restored by ascorbate.

overview: The apolipoprotein E4 (ApoE4) isoform confers increased risk of developing Alzheimer's disease.

title: Analysis of motor-based transport in primary cilia by dynamic mode decomposition of live-cell imaging data.
abstract: Kinesin-3 motor proteins are increasingly recognized for their important roles in cilia. The mammalian kinesin-3 motor KIF13B moves bidirectionally in primary cilia and regulates ciliary content, but its relationship to the intraflagellar transport (IFT) machinery is unclear. Here, we combine quantitative live-cell imaging with a new kymograph analysis based on dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) to separate mobile from immobile protein populations in primary cilia. This approach simplifies extraction of molecular velocities from kymographs and improves directional analysis of molecular tracks using the Fourier and Radon transforms. Our novel analysis reveals that a KIF13B deletion mutant only retaining the motor domain and part of the forkhead-associated domain does not alter steady-state IFT velocity or frequency. However, when retrograde dynein-2 function is inhibited by ciliobrevin D or tanespimycin, both anterograde and retrograde IFT velocities decrease in parental cells, as expected, but remain unchanged in KIF13B mutant cells. Structured illumination, confocal and stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy further show that KIF13B localizes to the ciliary membrane and concentrates at the periciliary membrane region and the centriolar subdistal appendages, below the distal appendage marker FBF1. Our improved kymograph approach provides new insight into KIF13B ciliary function and simplifies the quantitative analysis of ciliary protein transport.

overview: Kinesin-3 motor proteins are increasingly recognized for their important roles in cilia.

title: Making smart microscopy deployable in imaging core facilities.
abstract: Smart microscopy, in which real-time image analysis enables microscopes to adapt their acquisition dynamically, is becoming central to biological imaging. However, deploying such workflows in imaging facilities remains challenging. The computers that control microscopes in a facility are shared, governed by institutional policies, often offline and run vendor-specific software. As a result, installing custom software environments for the workflow of each user is both unsafe and unsustainable. We argue that smart microscopy requires a practical deployment strategy that links open-source bioimage analysis with commercial acquisition software without turning acquisition computers into development platforms. Using our recently developed tools, NucleiSky and LabConstrictor, as examples, we demonstrate how microscope control and external image analysis can be integrated while keeping the custom Python environment separate from the vendor-managed environment. The deployment strategy might vary - for instance, a USB drive, a facility workstation, a server or a network share - but the underlying principle remains the same: smart-microscopy workflows must be straightforward to approve, launch, reuse, audit and remove. Smart microscopy will become routine only when it is both powerful and deployable.

title: Lipid homeostasis and cellular metabolism in neurodegenerative diseases: A maturing framework to guide therapeutic development.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and dementia with Lewy bodies have long been viewed through the lens of protein aggregation. Emerging evidence, however, highlights lipid transfer, load, metabolism, and cellular homeostasis as upstream drivers of pathology. This perspective integrates established neurobiological, genetic, and mechanistic evidence of lipid dysfunction and outlines how these pathways can guide patient stratification, biomarker discovery, and therapeutic development. Of critical importance, lipid transport and lysosomal and trafficking networks are at the center of cholesterol regulation, glycosphingolipid clearance, endolysosomal function, and neuron-glia lipid exchange across genetic and sporadic neurodegenerative diseases. We present an integrated framework where correcting lipid imbalances and metabolic dysregulation may complement or obviate protein-targeted approaches, creating more precise clinical trials and combination strategies. By re-centering the therapeutic focus on lipid and cellular metabolism, we aim to catalyze translational advances in neurodegenerative disease treatment.

title: Alcohol use disorder - progress in mechanism discovery and new pharmacotherapy design.
abstract: The systematic use of alcohol is a frequent behaviour on a world-wide scale. Some of the users develop an abuse pattern of consumption and an alcohol use disorder (AUD). This is considered as a major psychiatric disorder causing significant suffering for the individual and society. As yet, there are no satisfactory and broadly working treatment options for AUD available, which has sparked research in a better understanding of neurobiological mechanism of alcohol and AUD and the search for an evidence-based treatment rational. Here we review the development of neuropharmacological insights focusing on selected brain mechanisms that have recently experienced significant progress and which give rise to new pharmaco-development ideas for AUD. Those include alcohol action and AUD mechanisms in the actin cytoskeleton system, in the nociceptin/orphanin system, and in the endocannabinoid system. Besides progress in pharmacotherapeutic targets, there are developments in how this therapy may be better applied in a personalized and addiction phase-sensitive way. This embraces new technologies like Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) for near real-time AUD symptom diagnosis, treatment allocation, and success monitoring. Emergence and future potential of this combination are discussed here. Altogether, current research in alcohol and AUD shows significant progress in our understanding of disease mechanisms and may spark the implementation of a new generation of technology supplemented pharmacotherapies of AUD.

title: αvβ3 integrin recycling is associated with the intracellular trafficking and efflux of cRGDfK-modified PLGA nanoparticles.
abstract: Understanding the cellular transport mechanisms of active-targeting nanocarriers is essential for improving their therapeutic performance. In this study, cRGDfK-modified poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) nanoparticles (cRGDfK-PLGA-NPs) were developed as an αvβ3 integrin-targeted delivery system, and their cellular uptake, intracellular trafficking, and efflux behaviors were systematically investigated in HeLa cells. Confocal laser scanning microscopy and HPLC analyses demonstrated enhanced cellular uptake of cRGDfK-PLGA-NPs compared with non-modified nanoparticles in HeLa cells. The uptake advantage was associated with αvβ3 integrin targeting, while pathway-inhibition studies suggested contributions from clathrin-mediated endocytosis and macropinocytosis. Following internalization, cRGDfK-PLGA-NPs were rapidly transported to early endosomes (EE), followed by redistribution to the endocytic recycling compartment (ERC) and gradual accumulation in late endosomes (LE). Real-time and fixed-cell colocalization analyses suggested three intracellular trafficking routes: the EE-LE pathway, a proposed EE-ERC-slow efflux pathway, and an EE-fast efflux pathway. Efflux studies indicated a two-stage kinetic process, with an initial rapid efflux phase (∼5 min) and a subsequent slower phase (∼10 min). To further elucidate the underlying mechanism, the intracellular trafficking behavior of the αvβ3 integrin receptor was investigated using an ELISA-based method, revealing a cyclical pattern of endocytosis and recycling with a periodicity of approximately 5 min. Comparative analysis using a cRGDfK fluorescent probe demonstrated that its rapid efflux behavior closely paralleled receptor recycling dynamics, suggesting that the fast efflux pathway of cRGDfK-PLGA-NPs is associated with αvβ3 integrin-mediated recycling, whereas the slower efflux pathway may involve ERC-mediated transport. Overall, this study provides insights into the potential relationship between target-receptor trafficking dynamics and the intracellular fate of active-targeting nanoparticles. These findings offer a theoretical basis for the rational design and optimization of active-targeting nanocarriers and contribute to improving their therapeutic efficacy.

title: Lysosome-targeted near-infrared fluorescent probe ROCL enables dynamic hypochlorous acid imaging in living cells and a mouse model of Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Hypochlorous acid (HClO) plays critical roles in oxidative stress and is strongly implicated in the progression of Parkinson's disease (PD). Here, we report ROCL, a new lysosome-targeted near-infrared fluorescent probe for sensitive and selective detection of HClO in living systems. ROCL displays rapid response, excellent selectivity, and a low detection limit of 49 nM, based on an HClO-induced spirolactam ring-opening mechanism. The probe enables real-time imaging of exogenous and endogenous HClO in SH-SY5Y and PC12 cells, exhibits low cytotoxicity, and effectively visualizes elevated HClO levels in MPTP- and rotenone-induced PD models. ROCL also shows favorable blood-brain barrier permeability and allows noninvasive in vivo HClO imaging in PD model mice. These results establish ROCL as a valuable tool for probing HClO-associated oxidative stress in neurodegenerative diseases.
journal: Spectrochimica acta. Part A, Molecular and biomolecular spectroscopy

title: Corpora amylacea and synaptic organization in the human brain analyzed by volume electron microscopy.
abstract: The presence of corpora amylacea in the brain is a frequent finding in normal aging and in a broad spectrum of neurological disorders, yet the significance of these deposits for the organization of human cortical circuits remains unclear. Here, we combined complementary light and electron microscopy approaches to analyze temporal lobe epilepsy biopsy specimens with and without corpora amylacea. Samples containing corpora amylacea showed marked alterations in synaptic circuit microorganization, which were not restricted to areas of corpora amylacea accumulation but extended throughout the cortical tissue. These changes were characterized by neuronal loss, gliosis, reduced synaptic density, an increased proportion of inhibitory synapses, and larger synapses. Integration of these structural findings with clinical data from the same patients further supports the view that corpora amylacea are associated with disease-related pathological processes. Together, these findings provide a basis for understanding the potential significance of corpora amylacea in human brain circuit dysfunction and may help to inform future research studies focusing on disease mechanisms.
