title: Human amniotic mesenchymal stem cell-derived exosomes alleviate cerebral Palsy-Associated neuronal damage via TSC1/mTOR/ULK1 autophagy suppression and PINK1/Parkin mitophagy restoration.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Cerebral palsy (CP) from perinatal hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury lacks effective therapies. Human amniotic mesenchymal stem cell-derived exosomes (hAMSC-exos) show neuroprotective potential, but their mechanisms remain unclear. This study investigated the effects and molecular pathways of hAMSC-exos in a neonatal rat CP model and an oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R) neuronal model. METHODS: hAMSC-exos were isolated and characterised. Severe CP was induced in postnatal day 21 rats by carotid ligation and hypoxia; hAMSC-exos or vehicle were given via tail vein 24 h later. Brain histology, ultrastructure, TSC1/mTOR/ULK1 pathway proteins, and apoptosis were assessed. In vitro, cortical neurons underwent OGD/R with or without exosomes; mitochondrial function (ATP, ROS, membrane potential), morphology, dynamics proteins (DRP1, FIS1, MFN1, MFN2), and PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy were evaluated. RESULTS: hAMSC-exos significantly ameliorated cortical neuronal degeneration, Nissl loss, and mitochondrial ultrastructural damage, and reduced autophagosome accumulation. They reversed CP-induced TSC1 upregulation, restored mTOR phosphorylation, and decreased ULK1 phosphorylation, correlating with fewer apoptotic neurons. In vitro, exosomes restored ATP content, reduced mitochondrial ROS, and normalised membrane potential. OGD/R caused excessive mitochondrial elongation via MFN1 upregulation; exosomes selectively downregulated MFN1 without affecting fission proteins (DRP1, FIS1). Moreover, exosomes restored impaired PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy, increasing co-localisation of phospho-PINK1, phospho-Parkin, and LAMP1 with mitochondria, and rescued their phosphorylated protein levels. CONCLUSION: hAMSC-exos protect against hypoxic-ischaemic injury through coordinated regulation of mitochondrial quality control, involving suppression of excessive TSC1/mTOR/ULK1-mediated autophagy (in vivo) and restoration of PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy (in vitro), collectively preserving mitochondrial integrity and reducing neuronal apoptosis. These findings support hAMSC-exos as a promising cell-free therapeutic strategy for CP.

title: P2RX7 drives inflammatory microglia and pathogenic extracellular vesicle secretion in tauopathy.
abstract: P2X purinoreceptor 7 (P2RX7), an ATP-gated ion channel, contributes to Alzheimer's disease (AD) progression, but its molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that genetic disruption of P2rx7 mitigates brain atrophy, tau accumulation, and cognitive impairment in PS19 mice. Microglia-specific, but not astrocyte-specific, deletion of P2rx7 suppresses tau propagation. Single-cell RNA sequencing identifies a previously unrecognized first-responding microglial state (FRM) with prominent P2rx7 expression. P2RX7 promotes the transition from FRM to an inflammatory microglial state enriched in extracellular vesicle (EV) biogenesis. P2RX7 increases EV loading of tau and of mitochondrial proteins and DNA, which activate cytosolic DNA sensing and interferon signaling in recipient microglia. Tau-containing microglial EVs disrupt neuronal endolysosomal integrity and facilitate endosomal tau escape and phosphorylation. Thus, P2RX7 regulates the FRM branch point, driving inflammatory microglial transition and EV-mediated spread of tau and toxic mitochondrial molecules and highlighting the P2RX7-EV axis as a therapeutic target in AD.

title: Tubulin autoregulation mediator TTC5 regulates neuronal morphology and migration.
abstract: Microtubule dynamics are essential for neuronal development, yet how neurons regulate tubulin levels remains poorly understood. Tetratricopeptide repeat domain 5 (TTC5) mediates tubulin autoregulation, the co-translational degradation of tubulin transcripts in response to excess soluble tubulin, and TTC5 mutations cause cerebral atrophy with speech and motor impairment. Here, we show that tubulin autoregulation is active in induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cortical neurons and depends on TTC5. TTC5 loss, or structure-guided mutations that disable autoregulation suppress microtubule polymerization, axonal outgrowth, and arborization, while enhancing cellular motility. Motility changes extend to non-neuronal cells, where they alter focal adhesion dynamics and can be rescued by manipulating soluble tubulin levels. Furthermore, downregulation of TTC5 interactor and autoregulation mediator S-phase cyclin A-associated protein in the endoplasmic reticulum (SCAPER) also suppresses neurite outgrowth and enhances motility. In vivo, TTC5 loss in mouse cortical projection neurons disrupts axon and dendrite arborization and causes hypermigration, recapitulating the cellular phenotypes observed in vitro. Patient-derived TTC5 disease mutants phenocopy this motility dysregulation, directly linking loss of TTC5 function to neurological deficits seen in patients. Together, these findings establish TTC5 as an essential regulator of neuronal morphogenesis and connectivity, with direct implications for TTC5-associated neurodevelopmental disease.
authors: Sarbanes SL, Ziak J, Sacks DC, Qi YA, Kolodkin AL, Roll-Mecak A
overview: Microtubule dynamics are essential for neuronal development, yet how neurons regulate tubulin levels remains poorly understood.
main: Here, we show that tubulin autoregulation is active in induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cortical neurons and depends on TTC5.

title: Tubulin autoregulation factors recruit γ-tubulin to non-centrosomal MTOCs for neuronal microtubule nucleation.
abstract: Neuronal function and survival depend on stereotyped non-centrosomal microtubule (MT) arrays. How these arrays form remains poorly understood. Here, we found that two factors previously implicated in tubulin mRNA turnover control neuronal MT content through γ-tubulin-dependent nucleation. In C. elegans neurons, loss of scaper, ttc5, or both reduced MT numbers to a similar degree as depletion of γ-tubulin, the main MT nucleator. Using conditional single-cell degradation alleles and endogenous tagging, we find that scaper and ttc5 are required to recruit γ-tubulin to non-centrosomal MT organizing centers (MTOCs). SCAPER is also instructive, as its overexpression raises γ-tubulin levels at nucleation sites and increases MT density. SCAPER, TTC5, and γ-tubulin are dispensable for developmental axon growth but play essential roles during regeneration, where SCAPER recruits γ-tubulin to a growth-cone-localized MTOC to orient MT nucleation. Last, SCAPER is required for activity-dependent MT nucleation in rat hippocampal neurons, suggesting a conserved role. These findings reveal mechanisms governing neuronal cytoskeleton assembly and function and suggest potential crosstalk between tubulin autoregulation and MT nucleation.
authors: Xie Y, Comincini A, Feng C, Davison CA, Hammarlund M, Bartolini F, Yogev S
overview: Neuronal function and survival depend on stereotyped non-centrosomal microtubule (MT) arrays.
main: Here, we found that two factors previously implicated in tubulin mRNA turnover control neuronal MT content through γ-tubulin-dependent nucleation.

title: Restoration of BDNF/TrkB signaling rescues presynaptic dysfunction in GM1 gangliosidosis iPSC-derived neurons.
abstract: GM1 gangliosidosis is a lysosomal storage disease characterized by progressive neurodegeneration and severe central nervous system (CNS) dysfunction. Although the abnormal intracellular accumulation of GM1 ganglioside is recognized as a major pathological feature, the molecular mechanisms underlying neuronal dysfunction remain unclear. Brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) plays essential roles in CNS development and the maintenance of synaptic function and plasticity; however, its contribution to the pathology of lysosomal storage diseases remains unclear. We previously identified a marked impairment of neurotransmitter release in GM1 gangliosidosis neurons, accompanied by reduced expression of synapse-related molecules. In this study, we investigated the potential involvement of endogenous BDNF signaling in synaptic dysfunction using human iPSC-derived neurons. We found that endogenous BDNF expression was significantly reduced in GM1 gangliosidosis neurons, accompanied by a marked decrease in full-length tropomyosin receptor kinase B (TrkB), a key mediator of BDNF signaling. Further, the gene expression of synapse-related molecules involved in neurotransmitter release, including SNAP25 and VAMP2, was reduced. Importantly, exogenous BDNF supplementation ameliorated presynaptic dysfunction and substantially restored the expression of synapse-related molecules, which were reduced in disease neurons. Furthermore, 7,8-dihydroxyflavone (7,8-DHF), a selective TrkB agonist, markedly reversed presynaptic dysfunction. These findings suggest that impaired BDNF/TrkB signaling contributes to presynaptic dysfunction in GM1 gangliosidosis and identify the enhancement of this pathway as a potential therapeutic strategy.

title: Multi-omics profiling suggests deep brain stimulation-associated expansion of CLIC3+ NK cells attenuates neuroinflammation in Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) alleviates Parkinson's disease (PD) symptoms, but its immunomodulatory mechanisms remain elusive. Through integrating microarray (GSE23676), single cell/nucleus RNA-seq (GSE184950, GSE202210, GSE223138, GSE243639; after quality control (mitochondrial gene content <25%, gene number >200) 616,076 high-quality cells were included), and GWAS data, we identified CLIC3 as a DBS-associated, potential protective implications in PD. CLIC3 was selectively up-regulated in a distinct natural killer cell subset (NK_CLIC3), which secreted TGFB1 to restrain neuroinflammation. CellChat and immunohistochemistry revealed that NK_CLIC3 cells communicated with PD-relevant neuronal populations: excitatory (SLC18A2+), inhibitory (SLC18A2+), oligodendrocyte (SLC18A2+), and astrocytic (SLC18A2+) cells via THY1-ADGRE5 and GZMA-PARD3 axes. Immune infiltration analysis (GSE114517; n = 75) suggested NK infiltration and deficient M2 macrophage recruitment in PD brains, underscoring an inadequate anti-inflammatory response. We further isolated CLIC3-positive NK cells (from a healthy donor) by fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) and confirmed their ability to degrade α-synuclein, the pathological protein in Parkinson's disease, supporting the potential NK(CLIC3+) cells' protective function in PD. Our findings suggest DBS may expand NK_CLIC3 cells to suppress neuroinflammation through TGFB1 mediated immune-neuronal crosstalk, positioning CLIC3 as a prospective therapeutic target for PD.

title: Redox-dependent remodeling of mitochondrial nucleoids contributes to bioenergetic decline during neuronal aging.
abstract: Why mitochondria progressively fail in aging neurons remains a fundamental question in neurobiology. Although bioenergetic decline and oxidative stress are hallmarks of aging, whether redox signaling remodels mitochondrial nucleoids (mt-nucleoids) to impair neuronal bioenergetics remains unclear. Using aged mouse neurons and human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived neurons, we demonstrate that redox-driven mt-nucleoid remodeling underlies reduced mtDNA transcript abundance and bioenergetic decline. Combining minimal photon fluxes (MINFLUX) nanoscopy with single-molecule transcription mapping, we identify distinct mt-nucleoid architectures governed by mitochondrial transcription factor A (TFAM)-mediated mtDNA compaction. Aging-associated oxidative stress drives mt-nucleoid remodeling from compact, transcriptionally active structures toward decompacted forms with reduced mtDNA transcript abundance and impaired mitochondrial ATP production. This remodeling involves species-specific TFAM redox mechanisms: cysteine oxidation promotes human TFAM polymerization, whereas methionine oxidation weakens mouse TFAM-mtDNA interactions. Notably, expressing an oxidation-resistant TFAM variant restores mt-nucleoid organization, mtDNA transcript abundance, and ATP production in aged neurons, identifying mt-nucleoid architecture as a potential target for preserving neuronal bioenergetics during aging.

title: Disulfidptosis in neurological disorders: from disulfide stress to actin cytoskeletal collapse.
abstract: The mechanisms driving irreversible neural cell loss in neurodegenerative diseases remain elusive. The collapse of cellular redox balance has unveiled a complex network of emerging metabolic cell death modalities that extend far beyond classical apoptosis. Disulfidptosis, a newly identified form of regulated cell death driven by disulfide stress and uniquely marked by actin cytoskeletal collapse, adds a critical dimension to this network. This review establishes an integrative framework-from sulfur metabolic imbalance to cytoskeletal collapse-for understanding this lethal pathway specifically within the nervous system. we focus on three features that are distinctive to neural tissue: the neuron-glia metabolic coupling that dictates which cell type is most vulnerable; the contrast between chronic disulfide stress dynamics in neurodegeneration and acute stress dynamics in ischemic stroke; and the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and cellular heterogeneity constraints that shape translational strategies. We first establish the cystine/cysteine cycle as the central hub of sulfur metabolism, revealing how it transforms from an antioxidant defense into a lethal driver of disulfide stress upon crossing a critical threshold. We then systematically dissect the molecular machinery of disulfidptosis, centered on NADPH depletion, the SLC7A11 bidirectional paradox, and aberrant cytoskeletal crosslinking. By systematically comparing disulfidptosis with ferroptosis and cuproptosis, we identify the SLC7A11-cystine-NADPH axis as a shared regulatory node. We further discuss how this mechanism may converge to contribute to neural cell injury across chronic neurodegenerative and acute neurological conditions, including Alzheimer's disease and Parkinson's disease, and may also extend to acute neurological conditions such as ischemic stroke. Finally, we propose a dual neuroprotective strategy targeting disulfidptosis and highlight its biomarker potential. Collectively, this review offers a new paradigm for understanding metabolic cell death in neurodegenerative diseases and lays a theoretical foundation for neuroprotective strategies targeting disulfide homeostasis.

title: A rare TMEM175 mutation drives Parkinson's disease pathology by disrupting proton gating and lysosomal acidification.
abstract: Transmembrane protein 175 (TMEM175), implicated in Parkinson's disease (PD) risk, has been variably proposed to function as a background K+ "leak" channel or a proton-activated proton channel in lysosomes. Here, we identified the rare TMEM175 variant p.L275R in a patient with early onset PD. Electrophysiological analyses revealed that TMEM175-L275R mutant proteins retain normal lysosomal expression and K+ "leak" activity, but specifically lose proton- and agonist-dependent activation gating. In skin fibroblasts isolated from the patient with PD harboring the monoallelic p.L275R mutation (TMEM175+/L275R), and in derived induced pluripotent stem cells and induced dopaminergic neurons, lysosomal H+ flux, acidification, and degradation were impaired. These lysosomal defects were corrected upon genome editing to produce the isogenic WT allele (+/+Cor), but appeared when the mutant allele was introduced onto a WT background (+/L275RMut). Pathological α-synuclein aggregation was facilitated in patient-derived (+/L275R) and mutation-introduced (+/L275RMut) neurons. Consistent with these genetic findings, pharmacological activation of TMEM175 with small-molecule agonists restored lysosomal functions and reduced α-synuclein aggregation in TMEM175+/L275R neurons. In in-vivo studies, equivalent-site-mutation knock-in mice demonstrated synucleinopathy and PD-like motor phenotypes. Collectively, our work provides genetic and pharmacological evidence that severe loss-of-function mutations may contribute causally to the onset age and pathogenesis of PD and identifies lysosomal proton channels and transporters as potential therapeutic targets for PD intervention.

title: SSH1 knockdown increases autophagosome formation through ATG9A recruitment and promotes MAPT/tau protein degradation.
abstract: Pathological accumulation of MAPT/tau protein is a defining feature of Alzheimer disease (AD) and related tauopathies, highlighting the need to identify druggable regulators of MAPT/tau clearance. Using Drosophila behavioral assays focused on cytoskeletal remodeling pathways dysregulated in AD, we identified genes whose genetic modulation mitigates MAPT/tau-induced behavioral deficits. These modifiers were validated by histopathology and mechanistically examined in human tauopathy cell models to determine their impact on autophagy-dependent MAPT/tau degradation. Autophagic flux, ATG9A trafficking, and autophagosome biogenesis were further analyzed. Across models, reduction of the phosphatase SSH1 consistently lowered steady-state MAPT/tau levels by enhancing autophagic flux through a mechanism distinct from its canonical regulation of CFL1. Mechanistically, SSH1 functions as a negative regulator of early autophagosome formation: SSH1 depletion promotes ATG9A mobilization to the endoplasmic reticulum-phagophore assembly site (ER-PAS), thereby accelerating autophagic vesicle biogenesis. Importantly, the MAPT/tau-lowering effect of Dmssh attenuation was abolished in flies haploinsufficient for DmAtg9, demonstrating that SSH1-mediated MAPT/tau clearance requires ATG9 function. Consistent with a direct regulatory interaction, in vitro phosphatase assays revealed that recombinant SSH1 decreases ATG9A phosphorylation in the presence of actin, identifying an SSH1-ATG9A regulatory axis controlling autophagosome initiation. These findings position SSH1 as a nodal inhibitor of autophagy initiation whose inhibition enhances MAPT/tau proteolysis. Notably, SSH1 haploinsufficiency also reduces SNCA/α-synuclein accumulation in vivo, indicating broader relevance to neurodegenerative proteopathies. By integrating in vivo functional screening with mechanistic studies in human cells, this work identifies SSH1 as a druggable phosphatase that constrains autophagy at the level of ATG9A-dependent vesicle formation.Abbreviations: Aβ: amyloid-beta; AD: Alzheimer disease;AMP-AD: Accelerating Medicines Partnership-Alzheimer's Disease; ANOVA: analysis of variance;ATG9A: autophagy related 9A; BDSC: Bloomington Drosophila stock center; BSA: bovine serum albumin; CFL1: cofilin 1; DIOPT: DRSC Integrative Ortholog Prediction Tool; DmAtg9: Drosophila ortholog of ATG9; DMEM: Dulbecco's modified Eagle medium; DMSO: dimethyl sulfoxide; Dmssh: Drosophila ortholog of SSH1; Dmtsr: Drosophila ortholog of CFL1 and CFL2; ER-PAS: endoplasmic reticulum-phagophore assembly site; ESCRT: endosomal sorting complexes required for transport FC: fold change; FTD: frontotemporal dementia; HeLa: Henrietta Lacks; LIMK: lim domain kinase; MTOR: mechanistic target of rapamycin kinase; ND: neurodegenerative disease; NFE2L2/Nrf2: nuclear factor, erythroid derived 2, like 2; PBS: phosphate-buffered saline PD: Parkinson disease; PFA: paraformaldehyde; PHF-1: paired helical filament 1; RNAi: RNA interference; ROSMAP: The Religious Orders Study and Memory and Aging Project; SDS-PAGE: sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis; snRNA-seq: single nucleus RNA-sequencing; SQSTM1/p62: sequestosome 1; SS inhibitor: SAR405 + SBI-0206965 inhibitors; SSH1: slingshot protein phosphatase 1; ULK1: unc-51 like kinase 1; WT: wild type.

title: RBM42 couples alternative splicing to cytoskeletal organization to direct cortical development.
abstract: Alternative splicing coordinates gene expression programs that shape the developing cerebral cortex. Here, we used nervous system-specific Rbm42 conditional knockout mice, RBM42-depleted human SH-SY5Y cells, RNA sequencing, RIP-seq, proteomics, and splice-switching rescue to define how the spliceosomal RNA-binding protein RBM42 supports cortical development. Rbm42 loss caused perinatal lethality, cortical thinning, defective lamination, reduced progenitor proliferation, increased apoptosis, and disrupted neuronal cytoskeletal organization. RBM42 bound and regulated cytoskeleton-associated transcripts, including NIN/Nin and NUMA1/Numa1, and its loss altered their splicing in human cells and mouse cortex. Restoring RBM42 corrected these splicing defects and improved proliferation and neurite growth. Selective correction of NIN exon 18 mis-splicing partially restored βIII-tubulin organization and proliferation but did not rescue apoptosis. These findings connect spliceosome-dependent isoform control with cytoskeletal remodeling during cortical development and provide a mechanistic framework for RBM42-associated neurodevelopmental disease.

title: Plasma P-Tau217 and NfL Longitudinal Changes Across Neurodegenerative Diseases: Impact of α-Synuclein in Alzheimer Disease.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Plasma phospho-tau217 (p-tau 217) is a validated biomarker of Alzheimer disease (AD), and its longitudinal dynamics may reflect AD progression. Plasma neurofilament light chain (NfL) reflects axonal injury and neurodegeneration. Their trajectories may be modulated by concomitant proteinopathies such as α-synuclein (aSyn). We aimed to characterize longitudinal changes (36 months) in plasma p-tau217 and NfL across neurodegenerative and non-neurodegenerative cognitive disorders and to examine biomarker trajectories according to aSyn pathology status within AD. METHODS: In this prospective single-center cohort, participants were recruited from a memory clinic in Barcelona, Spain. Participants were eligible if they had cognitive impairment because of neurodegenerative or non-neurodegenerative conditions between 2019 and 2022 and if baseline and 3-year follow-up blood samples were available. CSF AD biomarkers measured with Lumipulse and aSyn pathology assessed using real-time quaking-induced conversion assay were determined at baseline and used for patient diagnosis. Plasma p-tau217 and NfL were measured with Lumipulse at baseline and 36 months and analyzed as study outcomes. Between-group differences at longitudinal level were assessed using linear mixed-effects models. RESULTS: A total of 223 participants were included: 92 AD-aSyn- (69.6 [5.6] years, 57.8% female), 15 AD-aSyn+ (69.1 [5.8] years, 53.3% female), 17 dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB)-AD- (70.9 [6.8] years, 23.5% female), 13 DLB-AD+ (age 72.3 [5.0] years, 30.8% female), 48 frontotemporal lobar dementia (FTD) (65.5 [8.8] years, 45.8% female), and 38 non-neurodegenerative cognitive impairment (NNCI) (65.3 [7.7] years, 35.9% female). At baseline, AD-aSyn+ and AD-aSyn- groups showed the highest plasma p-tau217, whereas DLB-AD+ showed intermediate levels and DLB-AD-, FTD, and NNCI the lowest. Over 36 months, AD-aSyn+ exhibited the steepest increase in p-tau217 (2.19 pg/mL; p < 0.001), whereas AD-aSyn- and DLB-AD+ showed smaller increases; DLB-AD-, FTD, and NNCI remained stable. For NfL, FTD and AD-aSyn+ had the highest levels at baseline and follow-up (both p < 0.001), with similar increases. AD-aSyn-, DLB-AD+, and DLB-AD- showed intermediate values with moderate increases, whereas NNCI displayed limited changes. DISCUSSION: Plasma p-tau217 changes longitudinally in AD, and its trajectory is modulated by α-synuclein pathology. Patients with AD-aSyn+ show higher levels of NfL, similar to FTD, highlighting greater neuroaxonal injury. α-synuclein positivity identifies an AD-aSyn+ subgroup with steeper increases in p-tau217 and NfL, supporting biomarker-based stratification for prognosis and trial enrichment.

title: miR-132-3p-Enriched Exosomes Modulate Axonal and Mitochondrial Markers in Middle Cerebral Artery Occlusion Rats.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Ischemic stroke causes substantial neurological disability, but effective neural repair strategies remain limited. Mesenchymal stem/stromal cell (MSC)-derived exosomes may offer therapeutic potential because of their low toxicity, limited immunogenicity, and ability to cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB). Among their bioactive cargo, miR-132-3p is implicated in axonal growth and neuronal survival. This study aimed to investigate whether miR-132- 3p-enriched exosomes improve early outcomes and modulate axonal and mitochondrial markers after experimental ischemic stroke. MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this randomized experimental animal study, 115 adult male Wistar rats were assigned to the sham, middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO), exosome-treated (Exo), or miR-132-3p-enriched exosometreated (Exo-miR-132) groups (n=5 per group). Focal ischemia was induced by 90 minutes of intraluminal MCAO. Human umbilical cord MSC-derived exosomes were isolated by differential ultracentrifugation and characterized using transmission electron microscopy, nanoparticle tracking analysis, Western blotting, and flow cytometry. miR-132-3p was loaded into exosomes by electroporation, with the optimal concentration selected based on brain Nefh expression. Animals received Exo or Exo-miR-132 intravenously at 0 and 24 hours after MCAO. At 48 hours, six behavioral assessments were performed. Infarct volume, BBB permeability, brain water content, and neuronal cell death were assessed, whereas axonal and mitochondrial markers were evaluated by immunofluorescence. RESULTS: Exosomes showed characteristic morphology and expressed CD9, CD63, and CD81. The 5-nmol loading concentration produced the greatest increase in brain Nefh expression. Compared with Exo, Exo-miR-132 was associated with higher NF-H and mitofusin-2 expression and lower peptidyl-prolyl cis-trans isomerase D, cytochrome c, dynamin-1-like protein, and p21 expression. Exo-miR-132 also reduced infarct volume, BBB permeability, cerebral edema, neuronal cell death, and neurological deficits, with greater effects than Exo for several outcomes. CONCLUSION: miR-132-3p-enriched exosomes modulated axonal regeneration-associated markers and mitochondrial fission/fusion balance, alongside reduced injury and improved early neurological outcomes. Direct evidence of axonal regrowth and long-term functional recovery requires further investigation.

title: Isozyme-Specific Inhibition of GSK-3 Reveals Distinct Cellular Responses in Huntington's Disease Fibroblasts.
abstract: Inhibition of glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK-3) has been implicated in alleviating Huntington's disease (HD)-associated phenotypes. However, the mechanisms linking GSK-3 to HD pathogenesis, and particularly the distinct roles of GSK-3 isozymes in regulating HD-associated cellular dysfunction, remain poorly understood. Here, we investigated the cellular responses of patient-derived HD fibroblasts to selective inhibition of GSK-3α or GSK-3β using isozyme-specific inhibitors, focusing on metabolic and bioenergetic pathways. Although inhibition of either isozyme suppressed mTORC1 signaling, selective GSK-3β inhibition elicited broader cellular responses, including altered oxidative stress signaling, increased expression of proteins associated with mitochondrial fission, enhanced lysosomal activity, and mitophagy, together with lysosomal redistribution and increased α-tubulin acetylation, suggesting improved microtubule-dependent intracellular trafficking. Quantitative proteomic analysis of four independent patient-derived HD fibroblasts corroborated these findings: GSK-3β inhibition elicited a broad set of proteins involved in cytoskeletal organization, adhesion signaling, and metabolic adaptation, whereas GSK-3α inhibition produced a more restricted and heterogeneous response. Collectively, these findings identify distinct cellular responses to selective GSK-3 isozyme inhibition and reveal GSK-3β as a predominant regulator of intracellular trafficking and mitochondrial and cytoskeletal dynamics in HD fibroblasts. Thus, inhibition of GSK-3β may represent a potential therapeutic approach for modulating HD-associated cellular dysfunction.

title: A Cilia-Centered Nicotinamide Adenine Dinucleotide (NAD+) Signaling Network Regulates Hypothalamic Lysosomal Homeostasis and Metabolic Aging.
abstract: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) is an essential metabolite that regulates diverse cellular metabolic processes. Primary cilia, hair-like organelles on the cell surface, function as critical signaling hubs. Here, we demonstrate that cellular NAD+ levels are key regulators of both primary cilia growth and lysosomal function in hypothalamic neurons. NAD+ depletion induces ciliary shortening and diminishes lysosomal activity in a cilia-dependent manner. Mechanistically, the lysosomal repair complex protein CHMP4B translocates from periciliary satellites to lysosomes during lysosomal stress, a process impaired by ciliary dysgenesis. Disrupted lysosomal recruitment of CHMP4B leads to abnormal lysosomal Ca2+ signaling and lysosomal dysfunction. Aged mice with hypothalamic NAD+ deficiency exhibit shortened cilia and lysosomal stress phenotypes, both of which are restored by calorie restriction (CR). Moreover, CR improves aging-associated metabolic dysfunction, at least in part, through hypothalamic cilia-dependent mechanisms. These findings identify a primary cilium-mediated-NAD+ signaling axis that maintains lysosomal homeostasis in hypothalamic neurons, the disruption of which drives metabolic aging.

title: Novel NaV1.6-Mitochondrial Complexes in Retinal Astrocyte Pockets Sequester GABA.
abstract: Voltage-gated sodium channels are best known for their capacity to generate and propagate electrical currents in neurons and muscle. Their expression in glial cells may also be of great importance given these cells' involvement in various disease processes. Here we identify a previously unrecognized voltage-gated sodium channel NaV1.6-enriched microdomain in mouse retinal astrocytes. Using super-resolution confocal microscopy, electrophysiology, and transcriptomic analyses, we show that NaV1.6 forms high-density clusters within intracellular compartments devoid of the calcium-binding protein, S100β, typically understood to distribute throughout the entire astrocyte. These NaV1.6 pockets are polarized, clustering only on the bilayer facing retinal ganglion cell neurons, and are packed with unusually large, anaplerotic, and relatively depolarized mitochondria that closely appose NaV1.6 puncta. These metabolic compartments also accumulate high levels of GABA. Together, our findings reveal a specialized NaV1.6-mitochondrial complex in retinal astrocytes that expands the functional repertoire of voltage-gated sodium channels beyond direct neuronal electrical excitability.

title: STMN2: Membrane-Binding Microtubule Regulator or Tubulin Effector?
abstract: STMN2, a protein implicated in motor neuron degeneration, is widely viewed as a membrane-associated microtubule inhibitor, but emerging evidence challenges whether this activity defined its cellular function. Three alternative models integrates available evidence to offer perspectives beyond microtubule regulation. The vesicle cargo adaptor model proposes that STMN2 recruits diverse cargos to transport vesicles for axonal delivery. The membrane-bound signaling messenger model links STMN2 turnover to local signaling, effector, degradation, or effector release. The traffic director model proposes that STMN2 regulates cargo routing between delivery and degradative pathways. These models are not mutually exclusive and position tubulin binding as a regulator of STMN2 function rather than its defining activity.

title: Reduced BNIP1 impairs autophagosome-lysosome fusion in hippocampal neurons and contributes to Alzheimer's disease pathology.
abstract: BNIP1 (BCL2‑interacting protein 1) belongs to the soluble N‑ethylmaleimide‑sensitive factor attachment protein receptor (SNARE) family. Statistical screening based on the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) dataset GSE48350 reveals reduced BNIP1 expression in patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD), suggesting that BNIP1 is a potentially key regulatory protein for investigating AD pathogenesis. In this study, we detected BNIP1 protein levels in APP/PS1 transgenic mice and APP‑overexpressing HT22 hippocampal neuronal cells, screened key interacting proteins of BNIP1 via mass spectrometry, and further performed gain‑ and loss‑of‑function assays using overexpression plasmids and small interfering RNA (siRNA) to verify the protein function of BNIP1. Our findings indicate that, in these experimental models, reduced BNIP1 expression contributes to AD‑related pathological alterations by impairing autophagosome‑lysosome fusion. Restoration of BNIP1 expression enhances Rab5b‑mediated Rab7 recruitment and consequently ameliorates autophagosome‑lysosome fusion. This study suggests that reduced BNIP1 expression is involved in AD‑related pathological alterations.NIP1 (BCL2-interacting protein 1) belongs to the soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor (SNARE) family. Statistical screening based on the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) dataset GSE48350 reveals reduced BNIP1 expression in Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients, which renders BNIP1 a potentially key regulatory protein for investigating AD pathogenesis. In this study, we detected BNIP1 protein levels in APP/PS1 transgenic mice and APP-overexpressing HT22 hippocampal neuronal cells. Mass-spectrometry analysis was performed to screen key interacting proteins of BNIP1. Gain- and loss-of-function experiments were further conducted using overexpression plasmids and small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) to verify the protein function of BNIP1. Our findings indicate that decreased BNIP1 may act as an important contributing factor mediating AD-associated autophagosome-lysosome fusion defects in these experimental models. Restoration of BNIP1 expression enhances Rab5b-mediated Rab7 recruitment and consequently ameliorates aberrant autophagosome-lysosome fusion. This study suggests that BNIP1 serves as a potentially key regulatory protein for mechanistic research into Alzheimer's disease.

title: Lipid Droplet-Associated Hsp70 Palmitoylation Drives Lysosomal Dysfunction in Ischemic Stroke.
abstract: Lipid droplet (LDs) accumulate in glial cells across neurodegenerative and ischemic brain pathologies. LDs modulate cellular stress via organelle crosstalk, particularly with lysosomes, whose dysfunction and cathepsin leakage drive glial activation after cerebral ischemia. However, the molecular link between accumulated LDs and lysosomes in pathological glial activation remains incompletely understood. Using a mouse middle cerebral artery occlusion ischemia/reperfusion (I/R) model and oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/Re) cell models, we found that both LD signal intensity and lysosomal cathepsin B leakage progressively increased from day 1 to day 14 after I/R. Etomoxir, an inhibitor of carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 A (CPT1A), the rate-limiting enzyme for fatty acid β-oxidation, aggravated I/R-induced LD accumulation and lysosomal damage in glial cells. Exogenous LDs derived from OGD/Re-treated glial cells aggravated lysosomal damage and promoted the proliferation of astrocytes and microglia. LD accumulation was associated with Hsp70 palmitoylation and redistribution of Hsp70 from lysosomes to the extracellular space, leading to lysosomal damage and reactive glial activation. Mechanistically, using multiple genetic and pharmacological approaches, including Plin3 knockdown, an Hsp70 palmitoylation‑site mutant, recombinant human Hsp70 (rhHsp70), as well as a pan-palmitoylation inhibitor and TLR2/4 antagonist, we consistently validated that Plin3, an LD surface protein, interacts with lysosomal Hsp70, causing Hsp70 palmitoylation and redistribution, and lysosomal damage. Extracellular Hsp70 activates TLR2/4 on glial cells, promoting cell proliferation and pro-inflammatory cytokine release. Collectively, these findings indicate that pathological LDs interacting with lysosomes drive Hsp70 palmitoylation and redistribution, causing lysosomal impairment and astrogliosis in ischemic stroke. We uncover Hsp70 palmitoylation as a potential drug target for ischemic stroke therapy.

title: Glial handling of alpha-synuclein seeds: uptake, degradation and redistribution in pathological propagation.
abstract: α-synuclein (αS) aggregation and propagation are central features of Parkinson's disease pathology. Preformed fibril (PFF) models have shown that extracellular αS aggregates can enter neurons and seed aggregation of endogenous αS. Within the brain, these seeds also encounter microglia and astrocytes, which efficiently internalise fibrillar αS and can influence its subsequent fate. This review examines the mechanisms through which glial cells take up, process, degrade and redistribute extracellular αS seeds. When lysosomal trafficking and degradation are effective, glia can act as a sink for seed-competent αS and restrict neuronal seeding and propagation. In contrast, lysosomal dysfunction, incomplete proteolysis or excessive aggregate burden can promote persistence, modification and redistribution of seed-competent αS, including through extracellular vesicles and intercellular transfer. Evidence from microglial and astrocytic models therefore indicates that the outcome of glial uptake depends on the balance between internalisation, intracellular processing and subsequent release. Differences in αS conformation, fibril preparation, inflammatory state, genetic background and experimental model may further explain the apparently protective and pathogenic effects of glia reported across different studies. Understanding the factors that determine whether glial uptake results in productive clearance or continued propagation may identify therapeutic strategies that enhance the removal of pathogenic αS without broadly suppressing glial function.

title: ALS-linked FUS mutation impairs GEMIN5-dependent mRNA recruitment to neuronal late endosomes.
abstract: Neurons depend on tightly regulated positioning of cellular components to maintain long-distance signaling, but the mechanisms guiding specific mRNAs to distant regions remain unclear. Here, we show that late endosomes function as selective RNA carriers in human motor neurons and uncover the molecular logic guiding their loading. Using APEX2-mediated proximity labeling, we identify the external transcriptome of RAB7A-positive endosomes and find a specific population of mRNAs enriched for endosomal, axonal, and synaptic functions. We find that mRNAs enriched in RAB7A endosomes contain evolutionarily conserved 5'UTRs that act as localization signals, and that the RNA-binding protein GEMIN5 interacts with these regions to promote endosomal RNA recruitment. Finally, we show that there is a conspicuous loss of endosome-associated transcripts in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis-associated conditions, accompanied by the mislocalization of GEMIN5 from endosomes. These findings uncover fundamental principles of RNA compartmentalization and highlight endosomal mRNA loading as a vulnerable axis in neuronal homeostasis.

title: Extracellular neuroligin-ICAM5 coupling drives dendritic growth via actin remodeling.
abstract: Neuroligins (NLGNs) organize neuronal connectivity by engaging a diverse set of interaction partners, yet how extracellular recognition couples to intracellular growth programs remains unclear. Using affinity proteomics, we identify intercellular adhesion molecule-5 (ICAM5), a cell-surface protein localized to dendritic filopodia, as a NLGN interactor. Surface plasmon resonance and cell-based assays demonstrate direct binding between the ICAM5 and NLGN3 extracellular domains and reveal that ICAM5 engages all NLGN isoforms. In neurons, NLGN3 and ICAM5 preferentially colocalize at extrasynaptic, F-actin-positive dendritic sites, linking this interaction to regions of active cytoskeletal reorganization and growth. Accordingly, ICAM5 strongly enhances NLGN-induced dendritic outgrowth, but the NLGN3-ICAM5 complex does not detectably contribute to synaptogenesis. Mechanistically, ICAM5 sustains PAK-cofilin signaling and F-actin organization in growth cones, positioning it as a modulator linking NLGN engagement to actin remodeling. Together, these findings define a NLGN-ICAM5 axis that couples extracellular recognition to intracellular cytoskeletal remodeling to control neuronal structural development.

title: iPSC-derived RPE and retinal organoids from two phenotypically different Stargardt disease patients show differences in ABCA4 function.
abstract: Stargardt disease is a phenotypically heterogeneous disease caused by bi-allelic mutations in the ABCA4 gene. We generated retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, photoreceptor precursors (PhRPs), and retinal organoids (ROs) from two induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cell lines derived from two phenotypically different Stargardt disease patients. We observed that RPE cells from the patient with peripheral affectation showed reduced ABCA4 expression, reduced phagocytosis and digestion of photoreceptor outer segments (POSs), and accumulation of lipid byproducts. ROs from both patients show stunted segments, more rods, caspase-3 activation, and lipofuscin accumulation at week 45 of maturation. Phenotypical differences seen in Stargardt disease patients are caused by their specific ABCA4 variants, but cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying the process of photoreceptor degeneration are still poorly understood. Here, we suggest that peripheral phenotypes associated with these macular dystrophies can be linked to poor clearance of POSs by RPE cells, giving these cells a higher role in the pathogenesis of the disease.

title: Evaluation of deep learning-based super-resolution reconstruction in fetal brain T2-weighted single-shot fast spin-echo imaging.
abstract: PURPOSE: The study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of a deep learning-based Precise IQ Engine (PIQE) in enhancing image sharpness and quality during MRI reconstruction to enhance the image quality of fetal brain single-shot fast spin-echo (SSFSE) imaging. METHODS: Fetal brain MRI scans of 14 patients, including an SSFSE sequence, acquired between January 2024 and February 2025, were analyzed. Images were reconstructed with and without PIQE (zoom ratio of 3 from low-resolution matrices). We quantified the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and image sharpness using the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the fetal brain. Two board-certified radiologists assessed the image noise, contrast, sharpness, artifacts, and overall image quality of the two image types on a 4-point scale. We compared the quantitative and qualitative scores between the images with and without PIQE using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. RESULTS: SNRs, CNRs, and FWHM were significantly enhanced with PIQE compared to those without PIQE (SNR, CNR: p < 0.001, FWHM : p < 0.01). Qualitative scores for noise (p < 0.001), contrast (p < 0.001), sharpness (p < 0.001), artifacts (p < 0.001), and overall image quality (p < 0.001) were superior in images obtained with PIQE compared to those without it. Kappa analysis revealed moderate-to- excellent agreement for different image quality aspects: noise (κ = 0.52), contrast (κ = 0.74), sharpness (κ = 0.82), artifacts (κ = 0.61), and overall image quality (κ = 0.80). CONCLUSION: PIQE potentially enhances the image quality of fetal brain MRI using an SSFSE sequence.

title: Deep brain stimulation of the nucleus basalis magnocellularis ameliorates autistic behavior in a rat model of autism via cholinergic modulation in the prefrontal cortex.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: In the present study, we investigated whether deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the nucleus basalis magnocellularis (NBM) improves autism spectrum disorder (ASD)-related behavioral abnormalities in a valproic acid (VPA)-induced rat model of autism, consistent with changes in cholinergic markers in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). METHODS: On the 12.5th day of gestation, pregnant rats ( n  = 16) received a single intraperitoneal injection of 500 mg/kg sodium valproate dissolved in 0.9% saline, while others ( n  = 5) received saline alone. Male offspring were allowed to reach 3 months of age and then were randomly assigned to one of four experimental groups: Contr - prenatally saline injected, VPA - prenatally VPA-injected, VPA/I - VPA-injected with electrode implantation in the NBM, and VPA/S - VPA-injected with electrical stimulation. DBS was initiated in rats of the VPA/S group 10 days after surgery (two consecutive hours per day, every day for 2 weeks; DBS parameters: 60 Hz, 120 µs, and 50 µA). RESULTS: The prenatally VPA-exposed rats demonstrate deficits in social behavior, increased locomotor activity, and reduced anxiety levels. Immunohistochemical evaluation shows a decrease in the number of acetylcholinesterase-immunoreactive neurons in the mPFC and choline acetyltransferase-immunoreactive neurons in the NBM. NBM-DBS improves VPA-induced autistic behavior and increases the number of acetylcholinesterase-immunoreactive neurons in the PFC. CONCLUSION: The correlation between ASD-like behavior and cholinergic markers in the mPFC supports our hypothesis that NBM-DBS improves behavioral deficits by modulating cholinergic neurotransmission in the PFC in a rat model of autism.

title: Paclitaxel-induced disruption of lysosome motility and function in DRG neurons.
abstract: Lysosomal trafficking and homeostasis are biological functions that are pivotal for DRG neurons, given their metabolic demands and extremely long axons. Previous studies indicate that lysosomal signaling is altered in a mouse model of chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) and that blocking mitogen activated protein kinase-associated kinase (MNK1/2) signaling can alleviate pain behaviors in CIPN. Here, we investigated lysosome dynamics and lysosome-associated signaling in a mouse model of CIPN induced by paclitaxel (PTX), a chemotherapeutic agent used for various types of cancer. Using spinning disk super-resolution microscope (SPINSR), we demonstrate that PTX treatment in vivo causes reduced lysosome motility observed in vitro. PTX likewise drives the accumulation of Sequestosome 1 (SQSTM1), also known as P62, in cultured mouse DRG neurons, indicating lysosomal dysfunction in DRG neurons. The transcription factor EB (TFEB), a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis, was also upregulated in the nucleus of cultured mouse DRG neurons treated with PTX. In line with this, increased lysosomal-associated membrane protein 1 (LAMP1) expression was observed in PTX-treated mice. Given that our previous work demonstrated PTX treatment increases MNK1/2-eIF4E signaling in DRG neurons, we examined whether MNK1/2 inhibition could rescue lysosomal dysfunction. Treatment with Tomivosertib (eFT508), a potent MNK1/2 inhibitor, restored P62 levels in DRG neurons of PTX-treated mice and reduced TFEB in DRG treated in vitro. To establish translation relevance, we further show that PTX elevates phosphorylated eiF4E (p-eIF4E) in human DRG neurons, and concurrent eFT508 administration attenuates this effect. Collectively, these findings indicated that PTX disrupts lysosome trafficking and biogenesis, and that MNK inhibition with eFT508 restores lysosomal signaling and can serve as a neuroprotective strategy for CIPN.

title: Exosomes derived from N2 neutrophils reprogram the immune microenvironment to promote spinal cord injury repair.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Spinal cord injury induces irreversible neurological impairments via secondary pathological cascades dominated by excessive inflammation, oxidative stress, and neuronal apoptosis. As the first-responder immune cells following spinal cord trauma, neutrophils can acquire an N2-like reparative phenotype, yet direct neutrophil transplantation is hampered by poor cellular survival. Exosomes, nanoscale cell-secreted vesicles with low immunogenicity and favourable biostability, constitute promising cell-free candidates for regenerative therapy. Nevertheless, the therapeutic potential of exosomes derived from N2-polarized neutrophils remains poorly defined for spinal cord injury repair. METHODS: Murine bone-marrow-derived neutrophils were polarized toward the N2 phenotype using interleukin-6 (IL-6) and granulocyte-colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF), with non-polarized neutrophils set as the control group. Exosomes were purified by ultracentrifugation and comprehensively characterized by transmission electron microscopy, nanoparticle tracking analysis, and western blotting. In vitro functional assays were performed to evaluate macrophage phenotypic reprogramming, neuronal axonal regeneration, and neuronal apoptosis. A modified Allen's weight-drop mouse spinal cord injury model was adopted for in vivo intervention. Motor functional recovery was evaluated using the Basso Mouse Scale and gait analysis, while neural tissue repair was assessed via immunofluorescence staining. RESULTS: Exosomes derived from N2-polarized neutrophils (N2-exos) exhibited canonical exosomal hallmarks. In vitro, these exosomes drove lipopolysaccharide-primed macrophages to switch to an anti-inflammatory reparative phenotype, alleviated oxidative-stress-mediated axonal injury, and suppressed neuronal apoptosis. In vivo administration of N2-exos markedly enhanced hind-limb motor performance and gait coordination, and facilitated axonal regeneration across the injury epicenter. CONCLUSIONS: N2-exos remodel the post-traumatic immune microenvironment and confer combined neuroprotective and axon regenerative effects. This cell-free modality represents a promising therapeutic candidate for regenerative interventions against spinal cord injury.

title: Cellular-resolution three-photon ultra-deep imaging (TrUDI) of neuronal population activity at 2-mm depth in the mammalian brain.
abstract: Extending the depth reach of multiphoton microscopy for imaging neuronal population activity in the scattering mammalian brain is an 'exponentially hard' problem. Three-photon (3p) microscopy has enabled imaging of neuroactivity at depths up to ~1.2 mm in the mouse brain; however, the fundamental depth limit of 3p imaging, as set by the depth at which out-of-focus background fluorescence exceeds the in-focus fluorescence signal, is well beyond 2 mm. Reaching this fundamental depth limit in 3p imaging has been hampered by insufficient in-focus fluorescence signal. Here we demonstrate a three-photon ultra-deep imaging (TrUDI) system that approaches this fundamental depth limit via systematic and principled optimization of the in-focus fluorescence signal. TrUDI matches the parameters of the excitation laser, the optical system, and the acquisition to linear and nonlinear limits for safe laser exposure while satisfying the spatiotemporal requirements of single-cell resolution calcium (Ca2+) imaging. TrUDI achieves a ~250-fold increase in detected fluorescence photon yield at the same laser power as in previous approaches thereby enabling in vivo cellular-resolution recordings of neuronal population activity within fields of view of ~230 × 230 µm2 at 8.6 Hz at tissue depths of up to ~2 mm in mouse cortex and hippocampus.

title: DINOSim: Training-Free Semantic Segmentation on Microscopy Images.
abstract: We present DINOSim, a training-free method for segmenting objects in microscopy images without the need for large annotated datasets or additional model training. DINOSim builds on the pretrained DINOv2 image encoder, which captures semantic information from images. By comparing the encoder's features of image patches to those of a user-selected reference, DINOSim generates pseudo-labels that guide semantic segmentation. Subsequently, a k-nearest neighbors framework is used to refine predictions across new images. Our experiments show that DINOSim can effectively segment previously unseen objects in diverse microscopy datasets, offering performance comparable to supervised approaches while avoiding the need for costly manual labeling. We also investigate how different choices of user prompt selection and model size affect accuracy and generalization. To make the method widely accessible, we provide an open-source napari plugin (github.com/AAitorG/napari-DINOSim), enabling researchers to apply DINOSim to their own data easily. Overall, DINOSim offers a fast, flexible and practical solution for bioimage analysis, particularly valuable in resource-constrained settings.

title: The pathological roles of intrinsically disordered proteins in lysosomal acidification dysfunction in neurodegenerative diseases.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), frontotemporal dementia (FTD), and Parkinson's disease (PD) are characterized by the accumulation of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), including amyloid-β (Aβ), tau, and α-synuclein (αSyn). These proteins disrupt neuronal homeostasis through toxic aggregation, impaired proteostasis, and progressive neurodegeneration, in part via dysfunction of the autophagy-lysosomal pathway (ALP). A central feature of this impairment is defective vacuolar-type (H+)-ATPase (V-ATPase) function, leading to lysosomal deacidification and reduced degradative capacity. Pathological IDP species converge on V-ATPase through direct interactions with its subunits or by perturbing its assembly, while also exerting protein-specific effects, including lysosomal membrane destabilization, impaired hydrolase activity, and disrupted endolysosomal trafficking. These combined mechanisms create a reciprocal relationship between lysosomal dysfunction and IDP accumulation, in which impaired lysosomal degradation further promotes the persistence and aggregation of pathological IDP species. This review synthesizes current insights into the molecular interplay between IDPs and lysosomal acidification across AD, FTD, and PD, and highlights how these processes contribute to disease progression. We further discuss emerging therapeutic strategies aimed at restoring lysosomal function. These findings underscore lysosomal dysfunction as a common feature of IDP-driven neurodegeneration and a potential therapeutic target across these disorders.

title: Immunometabolic dysregulation of reactive microglia and astrocytes in neurodegenerative diseases: Mechanistic insights and therapeutic implications.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs) are increasingly understood as multifactorial disorders characterized by intertwined pathological processes, in which metabolic dysfunction may act as a critical and potentially disease-amplifying contributor to the proteinopathy-driven pathological cascade. Despite growing recognition that microglial and astrocytic metabolism governs central nervous system tissue damage-repair homeostasis, intercellular metabolic crosstalk between glia and neurons remains insufficiently synthesized across major NDDs. This review delineates how core metabolic pathways, including glycolysis, mitochondrial respiration, lipid processing, and amino acid transport, shape glial reactivity in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. We highlight glial metabolic reprogramming, a proposed theoretical framework arising from severe glial metabolic dysregulation. Within this framework, persistent pathological stress may drive reactive glia to sequester local energy substrates in excess, which is hypothesized to trigger bioenergetic failure in neighboring neurons. Broad-spectrum anti-inflammatory agents show poor clinical performance because they only block cytokine outputs rather than reverse glial metabolic exhaustion. Therapeutic efforts should therefore shift toward restoring glial metabolic flexibility. Cell-type-specific metabolic reprogramming, instead of pan-metabolic suppression, may circumvent systemic adverse effects. Precision strategies targeting such intercellular metabolic imbalance could provide promising cell-resolved metabolic avenues to retard NDD progression.

title: Comprehensive Clinical, Neuroradiologic, and Oral Health of 23 Individuals With MOPDII: Molecular Spectrum and Phenotypic Features.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Microcephalic osteodysplastic primordial dwarfism type II (MOPDII; MIM #210720) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by severe growth failure and microcephaly, frequently complicated by central nervous system (CNS) anomalies and early-onset cerebrovascular disease. This study aimed to define the neurologic, radiologic, molecular, and oral-dental features of a MOPDII cohort, with particular emphasis on cerebrovascular involvement, and to assess genotype-phenotype correlations. METHODS: Molecular diagnosis was established using next-generation sequencing, including targeted gene panel sequencing (n = 11) and exome sequencing (n = 1), or Sanger sequencing (n = 11). Clinical data, neuroimaging and vascular findings, systematic oral-dental examinations, and molecular results were retrospectively reviewed. RESULTS: Twenty-three patients from 18 unrelated consanguineous families were included. Seventeen distinct homozygous PCNT variants were identified, including 5 splice-site, 5 frameshift, and 7 nonsense variants; of these, 12 were novel. Structural CNS anomalies were common, with the thin corpus callosum being the most frequent finding, observed in 14 of 17 patients (82%) who underwent cranial imaging. Moyamoya disease was identified in 12 patients (70.5%), of whom 7 experienced chronic or acute cerebral infarctions and/or intracranial hemorrhage. Three patients with moyamoya disease died of complications related to vascular involvement. The 2 oldest patients developed severe peripheral arterial and coronary artery occlusions, leading to spontaneous limb amputation and acute myocardial infarction. Oral-dental evaluation, performed in 14 patients (61%), revealed microdontia, malformed teeth, and root shortening. No consistent genotype-phenotype correlation was identified for cerebrovascular or orodental manifestations. DISCUSSION: MOPDII is strongly associated with moyamoya disease and represents a major cause of neurologic morbidity and mortality. Early and longitudinal neuroimaging, including brain MRI and angiographic assessment, should be integral to patient management. Oral-dental abnormalities are common and merit routine evaluation.

title: Progranulin haploinsufficiency disrupts cathepsin D function, resulting in lysosomal abnormalities and elevated TDP-43 levels in the mouse brain.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is a leading cause of early-onset neurodegeneration, frequently linked to mutations in the GRN gene, which encodes the protein progranulin (PGRN). PGRN is known to play a crucial role in lysosomal function, and its deficiency contributes to FTD pathogenesis. Here, we examined the consequences of PGRN loss on lysosomal homeostasis, focusing on the lysosomal protease cathepsin D (CTSD) and TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) aggregation, hallmarks of FTD and related neurodegenerative diseases. METHODS: Using mouse models with homozygous and heterozygous GRN deletions and double knockouts for GRN and CTSD, we assessed lysosomal function, CTSD expression and activity, lysosomal-associated membrane protein (LAMP) levels and localization, TDP-43 aggregation, and survival. RESULTS: PGRN deficiency resulted in significant alterations in lysosomal function. Despite significantly elevated levels of mature and immature CTSD in PGRN-deficient mice, enzymatic activity was significantly reduced. PGRN deficiency also caused accumulation of lysosomal-associated membrane protein (LAMP) and perinuclear clustering of LAMP1-positive lysosomes, suggestive of disrupted lysosomal trafficking. Correspondingly, insoluble TDP-43 levels significantly increased, implicating lysosomal impairment in defective protein degradation and aggregation. Remarkably, double-knockout mice lacking both PGRN and CTSD exhibited significantly shortened lifespans, highlighting a potential functional interaction between these proteins in maintaining neuronal health and longevity. DISCUSSION: These findings underscore the importance of PGRN as a central regulator of lysosomal function and protein homeostasis. Together, the data provide mechanistic insight into PGRN-dependent lysosomal biology and identify pathways that may contribute to GRN-associated FTD and other neurodegenerative disorders.
authors: Fazal R, Tharkeshwar AK, Beel S, Storm A, Schevenels B, Tomé SO, Thal DR, Van Den Bosch L, Beckers J, Van Damme P
overview: INTRODUCTION: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is a leading cause of early-onset neurodegeneration, frequently linked to mutations in the GRN gene, which encodes the protein progranulin (PGRN).

title: Allele-selective and pan-allelic huntingtin lowering differentially affect neuronal homeostasis and BDNF transport.
abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is a devastating genetic neurodegenerative disorder caused by the abnormal expansion of CAG-repeats, which encode a poly-glutamine stretch in the huntingtin (HTT) protein. HD patients typically carry one wild-type and one mutant allele. We compared pan-allelic (PAN) and allele-selective antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) targeting a single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) in the sequence encoding the mutant isoform in human iPSC-derived cortical neurons carrying 69Q or 109Q alleles. SNP ASO selectively reduced mut-HTT mRNA and protein, while PAN ASO lowered both alleles. Proteomic profiling revealed that allele-selective mutant HTT lowering preserved pathways for neuronal morphogenesis, synaptic function, and mitochondrial metabolism. In human HD neuronal networks reconstituted in microfluidic devices, SNP ASO maintained synaptic connectivity, network synchronization, and BDNF vesicle trafficking. By contrast, PAN ASO impaired axonal transport, energy metabolism, activity-dependent survival signaling, and network oscillations. These findings support the rationale for allele-selective HTT silencing to preserve neuronal functions during HTT lowering while limiting extensive depletion of total HTT.

title: A novel fluorescent probe for smartphone-assisted dual-mode detection of glyphosate in food and environmental samples and live-cell imaging.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Glyphosate residues in crops and the aquatic environment threaten human health, and rapid, sensitive detection methods are urgently needed. Conventional instrumental methods are sensitive but unsuitable for on-site analysis, while many fluorescent probes lack portability or cellular imaging capability. This work addresses the need for a simple, rapid, quantitative glyphosate sensing platform that also enables subcellular visualization. RESULTS: We developed a Cu2+-mediated fluorescent probe, BiDPA, by conjugating di-(2-picolyl)amine with N-methylated benzoindole. BiDPA coordinates with Cu2+ to form non-fluorescent BiDPA-Cu2+; glyphosate competitively displaces Cu2+ and restores fluorescence, enabling rapid detection with a limit of detection of 21.3 nM and good selectivity. The method was applied to food and water samples, showing no statistically significant difference from HPLC (P > 0.05). The BiDPA-Cu2+ solution showed a visible color change from pale yellow to pink in the presence of glyphosate, enabling smartphone RGB-based quantification. BiDPA-Cu2+-loaded test strips and a hydrogel enabled on-site quantitative analysis. In PC12 cells, the probe showed mitochondrial targeting (Pearson correlation coefficient = 0.957) and visualized glyphosate within mitochondria. SIGNIFICANCE: This work provides an integrated fluorescent and smartphone-assisted colorimetric platform for rapid on-site glyphosate quantification in food and environmental samples, and extends the probe to mitochondrial imaging of glyphosate. The combined solution, test strip, hydrogel, and cellular imaging formats offer a practical tool for glyphosate monitoring and future studies on its subcellular effects.

title: Non-electrophilic TRPA1 modulator MNP-021 protects neuronal and glial function from diabetes-associated glucotoxicity and neuroinflammation.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Diabetes-associated neurodegeneration is amplified by methylglyoxal (MGO)-driven dicarbonyl stress linking hyperglycemia to neuronal insulin resistance and maladaptive neuroinflammation. We tested the neuroprotective activity of MNP-021, a non-electrophilic transient receptor potential ankyrin 1 (TRPA1) modulator, in neurons and glial cells in vitro. METHODS: SH-SY5Y neurons were pretreated with MNP-021 and challenged with MGO, then profiled by high-content imaging, RNA-seq, Seahorse Oxygen Consumption Rate (OCR) and Extracellular Acidification Rate (ECAR), glycolytic stress assays, and immunoblotting for AKT, ERK, and cAMP response element-binding protein (CREB). In an additional sustained glucotoxicity paradigm, differentiated SH-SY5Y cells were exposed to high glucose for 7 days and viability was assessed by LIVE/DEAD™ high-content imaging. HMC3 glial cells were treated with MNP-021, exposed to Lipopolysaccharide (LPS), Tumor Necrosis Factor-α (TNF-α) or Aβ(25-35), and tested for viability and inflammatory markers by Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) and RT-qPCR. RESULTS: MGO increased nucleus-to-cytoplasm area ratio by 49% and dysregulated glucose handling, increasing 2-(N-(7-Nitrobenz-2-oxa-1,3-diazol-4-yl)Amino)-2-Deoxyglucose (2-NBDG) uptake by ~ 25%, with GLUT1/GLUT4 membrane redistribution; MNP-021 normalized morphology, glucose uptake, and transporter localization without cytotoxicity up to 10 µM. RNA-seq identified 754 MGO-deregulated genes, including ISR/metabolic nodes such as glucokinase (GCK), Sestrin-2 (SESN2), phosphoglycerate dehydrogenase (PHGDH), Phosphoserine Aminotransferase 1 (PSAT1), phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase 2 (PCK2); MNP-021 buffered stress-induced transcription with limited baseline effects, modulated mitochondrial morphology and redox-associated fluorescence while preserving overall respiratory flux and blunting stress-evoked compensatory glycolysis. MNP-021 restored pro-survival signaling (pAKT/pERK and nuclear pCREB), including insulin responsiveness during MGO exposure. In a sustained high-glucose model, MNP-021 reduced the high-glucose-associated increase in cell death, extending its protective effects beyond the acute MGO paradigm. MNP-021 reduced Interleukine-6 (IL-6)/TNF-α release while increasing Interleukine-10 (IL-10) and Arginase 1 (ARG1) (~ 1.9-fold vs. LPS/TNF-α) in HMC3 glial cells, shifting them toward a pro-resolving IL-10/ARG1 program with reduced amyloid β-peptide 25-35 (Aβ(25-35))-evoked cytokine release and Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 (GLP-1) remaining very low (≤ 10 pg/mL) and not significantly increased in this system. CONCLUSIONS: MNP-021 coordinates transcriptomic restraint, transporter-level glucose handling, mitochondrial resilience, and pro-survival/pro-resolving signaling in neuron-microglia cell models. These findings support further preclinical evaluation of MNP-021 in dicarbonyl-linked neuro-metabolic stress and provide pharmacological evidence consistent with a TRPA1-linked component of its activity.

title: Mitochondrial quality-control states in cadmium neurotoxicity: Adaptive clearance, disproportionate elimination and stalled flux.
abstract: Cadmium (Cd) is a persistent environmental toxicant associated with neurological injury, but the role of mitophagy remains unresolved because increased pathway markers may indicate protective clearance, broad mitochondrial selection or incomplete downstream degradation. This review evaluates mitochondrial quality-control checkpoints in Cd-exposed neural systems, focusing on PINK1-Parkin, BNIP3L/NIX and autophagy-lysosome completion, and examines intervention evidence from puerarin, daidzein and ginsenoside Rg1. Three states are proposed as a conceptual synthesis: adaptive clearance, candidate disproportionate mitochondrial elimination and initiated but stalled flux. Protective PINK1- and BNIP3L-dependent activity has loss-of-function support, whereas selection-pathway engagement accompanied by mitochondrial loss is consistent with, but does not establish, disproportionate elimination because degradation and replacement have not been measured together. Cd also disrupts trafficking, autophagosome-lysosome fusion, lysosomal integrity and proteolysis, providing stronger evidence for incomplete bulk autophagic processing than for mitochondria-specific stalled flux. Among the compounds examined, puerarin has the broadest checkpoint coverage, largely from related cortical studies, linking reduced Cd burden and mitochondrial stress with pool preservation and improved bulk autophagic processing. Evidence for daidzein remains marker-limited, whereas Rg1 protects neuronal and glial endpoints without an established Cd-specific mitochondrial quality-control mechanism. This narrative, non-systematic synthesis is limited by potential selection bias, reliance on static markers, dominance of acute or high-dose exposure models, limited measurement of mitochondria-specific degradation and replacement, inadequate cell-type resolution and scarce independent replication. Resolving these states requires mitochondria-specific flux reporters, direct degradation and replacement indices, causal pathway perturbation and matched Cd and compound exposure. Therapeutic benefit is more likely to arise from restoring selective, proportionate and completed mitochondrial turnover balanced by replacement than from uniformly activating or suppressing mitophagy.

title: Label-free, real-time optical biopsy with a handheld quantitative phase microscope.
abstract: We present a compact, handheld quantitative phase imaging microscope that enables label-free, real-time optical imaging of bulk tissues with clear cellular and subcellular histological detail, effectively providing an "optical biopsy." The approach uses quantitative oblique back-illumination microscopy (qOBM) to obtain quantitative phase information of opaque samples using epi-illumination. The probe has a wide-field, non-scanning architecture that achieves 0.8 µm lateral and 5 µm axial resolution across a 300 µm × 300 µm field of view at 25 frames per second. The probe is also low-cost, contains no moving components, is easy to use and can operate through a sterile sheath, addressing key barriers to clinical implementation. To demonstrate its utility, we image (1) human skin in vivo, (2) murine and human brain tumors ex vivo, and (3) swine brain in vivo under typical neurosurgical conditions. By providing real-time, label-free histological information in a robust and accessible handheld format, this technology creates broad opportunities for future clinical translation, including intraoperative and point-of-care histological tissue assessment.

title: 53BP1 as a cofactor in the activation of the p53-family transcriptional program: A correlative multimodal microscopy approach.
abstract: Understanding how molecular mechanisms regulate cell function in tissues requires approaches that link phenotypes to mechanisms across different spatial scales. Here, we present automated multimodal multiplexed microscopy for image cytometry (A.M3.I.CO), a correlative imaging platform that combines multiscale resolution, from millimeters to nanometers, with automated workflows for high-throughput phenotypic profiling and targeted single-molecule analysis in situ. Applying A.M3.I.CO, we observed that 53BP1 is recruited at transcribed p53 target genes independently of the activating stimulus, providing evidence for the formation of a putative complex between 53BP1, p53, and the basal transcription machinery in single cells, as also supported by in vivo observations in tumor models. Extending our measurements to p63 and p73, we found that 53BP1 localized at p63- and p73-targeted transcription sites, suggesting a broader role in participating in p53 family-dependent transcription. These findings indicate an additional genome-surveillance pathway in transcriptional control regulating diverse cellular functions while establishing A.M3.I.CO as a platform for spatially resolved functional analysis.

title: Chronic thoracic aortitis versus primary medial degeneration in ascending aorta: a digital morphometric analysis of aortic layers remodelling.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Chronic aortitis (CA) represents a diverse group of inflammatory conditions often diagnosed incidentally in ascending aorta biopsies. While the 2015 and 2016 Consensus Statements on the surgical pathology of the aorta provide standardised histological classifications, data quantifying structural remodelling within individual aortic layers remain limited. Furthermore, distinguishing CA from primary non-inflammatory medial degeneration (MD) can be challenging, particularly when inflammation is sparse or burnt out, and secondary degenerative changes predominate. We aimed to compare morphological changes in CA and MD aneurysms and apply digital image analysis to quantify aortic wall layers. METHODS: Retrospective histological analysis was performed on 63 ascending aortic specimens: CA (n=21), MD (n=21), and autopsy controls (n=21). Digitised elastic-stained sections were analysed using QuPath software to measure the thickness and cross-sectional area of the intima (I), media (M), and adventitia (A). Overall MD scores (i.e., summaries of each MD grade component) were evaluated. Diagnostic performance was assessed using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis based on binary logistic regression models. RESULTS: CA demonstrated a profound architectural shift, characterised by medial thinning alongside marked intimal and adventitial expansion, resulting in significantly lower M/(I+A) thickness and area ratios compared with MD and controls (p <0.001). CA specimens also exhibited the most severe secondary degenerative changes, with significantly higher overall MD scores (median: 15 vs. 8; p < 0.001). ROC curve analysis revealed diagnostic utility of both the M/(I+A) thickness ratio (AUC = 0.964) and the M/(I+A) area ratio (AUC = 0.955) for identifying CA. A multivariable model combining the overall MD score with the M/(I+A) thickness ratio achieved an AUC of 0.971 (accuracy 88.1%), whereas combining it with the M/(I+A) area ratio yielded an AUC of 0.968 (accuracy 90.5%). CONCLUSION: Digital morphometric analysis provides a reproducible and feasible method for quantifying structural remodelling in chronic aortitis. Changes in the proportions of the aortic layers, specifically intimal and adventitial expansion combined with medial thinning and severe secondary medial degeneration, can facilitate accurate differentiation of aortic wall pathologies, particularly in cases with sparse inflammation.

title: The spectrum within the spectrum: Neural heterogeneity in autism.
abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) encompasses diverse behavioral, cognitive, and neural profiles that vary widely across individuals. Because diagnosis remains predominantly behavior-based, clinically meaningful within-spectrum differences are often missed. Recent advances in neuroimaging analysis have created opportunities for the identification of distinct neural profiles within ASD. These new avenues provide ways to examine intra-ASD heterogeneity directly, identifying person-specific brain-behavior patterns that group-level comparisons fail to capture. The present systematic review focused on neuroimaging methods (i.e., resting-state fMRI; rs-fMRI, cortical morphology) that emphasized heterogeneity-informed outcomes based on normative modeling, data-driven subtyping, clustering analysis and similar analytic choices. For rs-fMRI, findings showed that differences in connectivity within the default mode and salience networks were linked to social-communication and language impairments, with subtype-specific patterns emerging across samples. In cortical thickness and surface area, studies identified distinct developmental trajectories and individual deviation profiles, with prefrontal and temporal regions often tied to repetitive behaviors and social-communication difficulties. Voxel-based analyses revealed subgroup-specific gray matter alterations, including cerebellar and cortical differences, that aligned with variation in repetitive behaviors and social difficulties. Collectively, this emerging evidence supports the notion that neural heterogeneity in autism is a core feature rather than a limitation. Embracing individual variability can provide crucial insight into the inconsistencies and contradictions of earlier case-control and group-level findings. Moving forward, autism research must prioritize heterogeneity-based methods to establish reproducible subtypes and individualized brain-behavior links.
