title: Attention load modulates functional brain connectivity reorganization in children with high autistic traits: Evidence from phase and amplitude coupling metrics.
abstract: Whether emotional processing difficulties in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) stem from deficits in recognizing emotional stimuli or from limitations in flexibly reorganizing brain networks under increasing cognitive demands remains an open question. To our knowledge, this study is among the first to investigate the effects of graded attentional load (low/moderate/high) on EEG-based functional connectivity and brain network organization during task-irrelevant emotional prosody processing in children with high autistic traits (n = 31), by integrating phase-based (iPLV, wPLI) and amplitude-based (AEC) metrics together with graph-theoretic indices within a unified analytic framework. Connectivity matrices from a sliding-window approach were decomposed into edge-level, distributional, and graph-theoretic features and load-dependent changes in connectivity were assessed with statistical analyzes and classification models. The results suggested that attentional load did not uniformly increase or decrease connectivity but rather produced a multi-layered pattern of reorganization that varied as a function of frequency band, connectivity metric, and network topology. Phase-based connectivity in the beta band was decreased with increasing load, while amplitude envelope coupling (AEC) in the theta and alpha bands was increased under high load. This dual-mechanism pattern was most pronounced under the high-load condition, which yielded the greatest number of nominally significant features (uncorrected p < 0.05; none survived FDR correction), the largest theta-AEC effect size (Kendall's W up to 0.22), and the best-performing classification model among those tested (accuracy = 72.6%, F1 = 0.725, AUC = 0.764). In conclusion, this exploratory study suggests that, in children with high autistic traits, increasing cognitive demands may be associated with band-specific network reorganization characterized by attenuated phase-based coordination alongside enhanced amplitude-based coupling; these patterns did not survive correction for multiple comparisons, have not been compared with those of typically developed children, and should be treated as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory. If replicated, such findings could eventually inform how environmental stimulation and cognitive load are structured in special education settings.

title: Pathogenesis and therapeutic targets of neuroinflammation in Alzheimer's disease mediated by microglia lysosomal dysfunction.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a multifactorial neurodegenerative disorder characterized by two core pathological features: senile plaques formed by amyloid-β protein (Aβ) deposits and neurofibrillary tangles formed by hyperphosphorylated tau protein. In recent years, neuroinflammation has been recognized as a key driver in the pathogenesis of AD, and microglia, as innate immune cells of the central nervous system, play a central role in regulating the onset and progression of neuroinflammation. Lysosomes are key organelles within microglia responsible for degrading pathological proteins and regulating inflammatory signaling; dysfunction of lysosomes in microglia severely impairs their ability to clear Aβ, damaged proteins, and cellular debris, thereby promoting inflammatory responses. This manuscript summarizes upstream mechanisms that may influence microglial lysosomal dysfunction from four perspectives: pathological proteins, genetic factors, lipid metabolism disorders, and proinflammatory cytokines. Pathological proteins can impair lysosomal acidification and biogenesis by interfering with key pathways such as the TFEB-v-ATPase axis; various genetic factors exacerbate functional dysregulation by influencing the expression of lysosome-related genes and lipid metabolism; lipid metabolism disorders promote lysosomal membrane permeabilization, block the autophagy cascade and activate the inflammasome; proinflammatory cytokines can exert varying effects on the clearance of pathological substrates and by regulating lysosomal function. The aforementioned factors can influence microglial lysosomal function through various mechanisms, thereby contributing to impaired clearance of pathological substrates and the onset and progression of neuroinflammation. Intervention strategies targeting microglial lysosomal dysfunction, including enhancing lysosomal degradation capacity, regulating autophagy related pathways, correcting cellular metabolic dysregulation and suppressing excessive neuroinflammation, may offer new avenues for AD treatment.

title: A fibril-selective single-domain antibody targets pathogenic amyloid-β assemblies and protects human neurons.
abstract: Alzheimer disease is characterized by extracellular amyloid-β deposition that contributes to neuronal dysfunction and degeneration. Although anti-amyloid-β antibodies reduce plaque burden, their use requires monitoring for amyloid-related imaging abnormalities. Here, phage display against immobilized Aβ40 fibrils representing a patient-relevant polymorph identified J8, a fibril-selective, Fc-free single-domain antibody. J8 bound fibrils with high apparent affinity, showed no detectable binding to monomeric Aβ40, decorated fibril surfaces, and recognized plaque-associated amyloid in Alzheimer disease brain tissue. During concurrent fibril exposure, J8 reduced apoptotic signaling in human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived cortical neurons and forebrain organoids. Single-nucleus profiling of pooled organoids identified fibril-associated stress programs and opposite-direction expression patterns in the FibJ8 condition; fibril-associated changes showed the strongest directional concordance with advanced disease pathology. These findings identify J8 as a fibril-selective candidate and support organoid-based evaluation of anti-amyloid reagents as a fit-for-purpose preclinical tool.

title: Evaluating the NLRP3 inflammasome in chemotherapy-induced cognitive impairment: A multi-timepoint study of methotrexate and 5-fluorouracil in female rats.
abstract: Chemotherapy-induced cognitive impairment (CICI) affects many cancer survivors, who often report cognitive difficulties during and/or after treatment that reduce quality of life. While the exact mechanisms that underlie CICI are unclear, neuroinflammation is widely proposed to contribute. One candidate mediator is the nucleotide-binding domain leucine-rich repeat and pyrin domain containing receptor protein 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome, which drives microglial inflammation and is implicated in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease. This study therefore investigated whether NLRP3 inflammasome components are altered in a rat model of CICI. Female Sprague Dawley rats were randomly allocated to receive methotrexate (MTX), 5-fluorouracil (5-FU) or saline (n = 18/treatment) and were euthanised at 96-hours, 31-days or 93-days post-treatment (n = 6/treatment/timepoint). This cohort was previously shown to develop cognitive deficits. In the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus, NLRP3 and pro-caspase-1 were measured by western blot, and interleukin-1β (IL-1β) by ELISA. Microglial number and activation were assessed by ionized calcium-binding adaptor molecule 1 (IBA1) immunohistochemistry (n = 4/treatment/timepoint). Compared with saline controls, neither chemotherapy altered NLRP3 or pro-caspase-1 in either brain region at any timepoint, and treatment effect sizes were small (ηp² ≤ 0.06). IL-1β, detectable only at 96-hours, was also unchanged. Similarly, there were no differences in either total microglial number or the percentage of activated microglia. These findings provide no evidence that NLRP3 inflammasome components are altered in this female rat model of CICI at the timepoints examined. However, as inflammasome assembly and activation were not directly assessed, future work should measure ASC speck formation, cleaved caspase-1 and mature IL-1β, and include earlier timepoints, particularly within the first two weeks after chemotherapy.

title: Protocol for imaging and analyzing the synaptic coverage of astrocytes with super-resolution STED microscopy in mouse brain slices.
abstract: Super-resolution has allowed us to image areas previously inaccessible due to the limits of standard microscopy techniques. Here, we present a protocol to determine the astroglial coverage of synapses. We detail the steps to obtain and label mouse brain slices followed by imaging using 3D stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy and analysis using a custom-made Fiji plug-in, with imaging at a lateral resolution of 80 nm. This technique ascertains the interaction between astrocytes and the glial cell's role in signaling and brain region function.

title: Research Progress of Low-Intensity Pulsed Ultrasound in Parkinson's Disease.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder where current pharmacological and surgical interventions, including Deep Brain Stimulation, often fail to reverse neuronal degeneration or halt disease progression. Low-intensity pulsed ultrasound (LIPUS) has emerged as a novel, non-invasive neuromodulation technology with significant therapeutic potential. This review synthesizes current research on the key acoustic parameters, biological mechanisms, and clinical applications of LIPUS in PD. Unlike High-Intensity Focused Ultrasound (HIFU), which relies on thermal ablation to destroy target nuclei (e.g., Vim, STN), LIPUS utilizes low-energy mechanical waves (typically <3 W/cm²) to exert non-thermal regulatory effects without damaging tissue. Mechanisms of action include the modulation of mechanosensitive ion channels (e.g., Piezo1), enhancement of neuroplasticity via brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), promotion of autophagy, and regulation of microglial phenotypes to reduce neuroinflammation. We further compare LIPUS with HIFU, highlighting the superiority of LIPUS regarding safety, reversibility, and the absence of requirement for MRI-based thermal monitoring. While preliminary clinical studies using wearable LIPUS devices indicate improvements in motor and cognitive functions, a unified consensus on optimal stimulation parameters and targeting strategies is lacking. Future research should focus on large-scale, standardized clinical trials to establish precise protocols for LIPUS as a disease-modifying therapy for PD.

title: Preoperative sleep deprivation prolongs postoperative hyperalgesia by downregulating spinal cord D2R expression via the PP2A/AKT-dependent NMDA receptor phosphorylation.
abstract: Preoperative sleep deprivation (SD) is known to exacerbate postoperative pain, but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Using a male mouse model of 48-h continuous SD followed by incisional surgery, we found that SD alone induced transient mechanical hyperalgesia, and when combined with surgery (SI group) it significantly aggravated and prolonged postoperative pain recovery until day 10. On postoperative day 7, SI mice showed marked downregulation of spinal dopamine D2 receptor (D2R) expression and decreased spinal dopamine concentration. D2R was predominantly expressed on spinal glutamatergic neurons. Overexpression of D2R on these neurons via intrathecal AAV injection effectively alleviated the prolonged hyperalgesia, normalizing pain sensitivity by day 7. Mechanistically, D2R downregulation led to increased phosphorylation of NMDA receptor subunits (p-NR1 and p-NR2B) without altering total NMDA receptor levels. Co-immunoprecipitation revealed an interaction between D2R and protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A). SI mice exhibited decreased PP2A expression but increased p-AKT, p-GSK3β, and β-catenin, indicating activation of the PP2A/AKT signaling pathway, which were reversed by D2R overexpression. Furthermore, pharmacological activation of PP2A with DT-061 not only downregulated p-AKT, p-GSK3β, β-catenin, p-NR1 and p-NR2B, but also produced significant analgesia in SI mice. Collectively, these results demonstrate that preoperative sleep deprivation prolongs postoperative hyperalgesia by downregulating spinal D2R on glutamatergic neurons, which disinhibits the PP2A/AKT pathway and enhances NMDA receptor phosphorylation. Targeting D2R or its downstream PP2A/AKT signaling may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for managing persistent postoperative pain caused by preoperative sleep deprivation in male mice.

title: Cucurbituril-modulated NIR emission and two-photon mitochondrial imaging of an acridine derivative.
abstract: Host-guest assemblies of an acridine dye with cucurbit[7]uril and cucurbit[8]uril give distinct NIR emissions at 674 and 708 nm, respectively. Both exhibit efficient two-photon absorption near 925 nm and successfully enable single- and two-photon mitochondrial imaging in live A549 cells.

title: Three-photon population imaging of subcortical brain regions.
abstract: Monitoring large-scale neuronal activity in deep brain circuits is crucial for understanding the principles of brain function. However, existing large-scale cellular-resolution imaging techniques are limited in imaging depth and cannot monitor activity in areas deeper than the cortex in the intact brain. To address this challenge, we developed a Large Imaging Field of view Three-photon (LIFT) microscope with a FOV of  > 3 mm2. LIFT combines high-numerical-aperture optimized sampling, using a custom scanning module, with deep learning-based denoising, to enable population imaging in subcortical brain regions of mice and deep cortical regions of rats. We demonstrate calcium imaging in the intact mouse brain from more than 1500 cells across CA1, the surrounding white matter, and adjacent deep layers of the cortex, and show population imaging with high SNR at a depth of 1.2 mm in the rat cortex. The LIFT microscope offers versatility in imaging scale and rate and was built entirely from off-the-shelf components.

title: QuRad: Radiomics Feature Extraction for QuPath.
abstract: Radiomic features provide a quantitative description of tissue organization in histopathology images. QuPath, a widely used open-source platform for whole-slide image analysis, offers morphology, intensity, and Haralick texture measurements but no standardized radiomic feature set such as that of PyRadiomics. Researchers must therefore export data to external Python pipelines, interrupting their QuPath workflow. QuRad extracts radiomic features from cell detections and annotation regions directly inside QuPath. The extension and equivalent Groovy script implement 119 features: 103 two-dimensional features enabled by default and 16 optional legacy shape descriptors. We compared QuRad 0.4 with PyRadiomics 3.0.1 on identical grayscale images and pixel masks. All 103 default features met a 10-9 absolute-or-relative agreement tolerance on a breast-cancer benchmark tile (410 cells). On 20 melanoma tiles (8,644 nuclei), 97 of 103 features met this tolerance and 6 polygon-derived shape features differed from PyRadiomics' raster-derived mesh (minimum concordance correlation coefficient 0.942). The 22 synthetic regions accepted by PyRadiomics reproduced the expected intensity and texture values. A single-threaded server benchmark reached about 1,900 nuclei per second, and processing the 184,242 cells of a whole-slide image took 2.7 min on a laptop. A random forest distinguished tumor cells from lymphocytes in melanoma (pooled macro-F1 0.853) and classified 197 tissue regions of 6 breast-cancer slides into 3 compartments (0.696). QuRad exports the features with object coordinates and extraction settings for use in QuPath or downstream analyses.

title: A seamless workflow for STXM-NEXAFS data analysis using napari: implementation of an ROI spectrum extraction function.
abstract: Scanning transmission soft X-ray microscopy (STXM), combined with near-edge X-ray absorption fine structure (NEXAFS), enables the mapping of elemental distributions and chemical properties at a spatial resolution of tens of nanometers. A common approach for analyzing STXM data is to compare NEXAFS spectra obtained from regions of interest (ROIs). However, ROI-based spectral comparison typically requires frequent switching among multiple software applications. ROI spectrum extraction, spectrum normalization, and figure creation are often performed using separate applications, which increase analytical time and the likelihood of errors.•We developed a Python-based workflow for STXM-NEXAFS data analysis that implements functions for extracting mean ROI spectra in napari, an open-source multidimensional image viewer.•These napari-based functions provide a seamless workflow from ROI selection to figure preparation within Python, without switching between multiple software applications.•The seamless workflow improves analytical efficiency and facilitates broader use of STXM-NEXAFS analysis.

title: Extended field-of-view two-photon imaging in the deep brain of freely behaving mice using lightweight microfabricated corrective optics.
abstract: Investigating neural circuits underlying complex behavior requires high-resolution imaging of large neuronal populations during naturalistic conditions. Miniaturized two-photon microscopes (MINI2Ps) enable deep brain imaging in freely moving animals when coupled with gradient index (GRIN)-based microendoscopes. However, intrinsic optical aberrations in GRIN-based microendoscopes degrade spatial resolution and limit the effective field-of-view (FOV). Here, we address these limitations using lightweight microfabricated optics to correct GRIN aberrations during deep brain MINI2P imaging. The aberration corrected system demonstrated improved and more homogeneous axial resolution across the FOV, resulting in more than fourfold increase in effective FOV. We applied the corrected system to the ventral posteromedial thalamus in freely moving mice and performed optical mapping of head direction (HD) tuned cells. These measurements revealed the absence of spatial clustering of HD preference, suggesting spatially sparse HD coding in sensory thalamus. Combining the MINI2P with aberration corrected GRIN-based microendoscopes is a powerful approach for large-scale and high-resolution functional imaging of deep brain circuits during naturalistic behavior.

title: Unraveling the Genotype-Phenotype Landscape of Kleefstra Syndrome Through EHMT1 Variant Analysis.
abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Kleefstra syndrome type 1 (KLEFS1) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder caused by pathogenic variants in EHMT1, which play a key role in epigenetic regulation. Core features include global developmental delay (GDD), intellectual disability (ID), facial dysmorphism, congenital heart defects (CHDs), and neuropsychiatric manifestations. METHODS: This retrospective study included patients with KLEFS1 evaluated at Seoul National University Hospital between January 2022 and April 2025. Genetic diagnoses were made using chromosomal microarray or whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing, and clinical data were extracted from medical records. To enhance statistical power, we conducted a joint analysis with established cohorts of at least 30 clinically characterized patients. RESULTS: Among the 15 patients with KLEFS1, 14 (93.3%) exhibited GDD or ID, with frequent comorbidities such as CHDs (8/12, 66.7%), orthopaedic manifestations (6/12, 50.0%), epilepsy (6/15, 40.0%), and sleep problems (4/11, 36.4%). Brain MRI revealed abnormalities in 10 of the 12 patients (83.3%), including pituitary anomalies in 2 (16.7%). By combining our data with recently published multicenter international cohorts, we assessed genotype-phenotype correlations by comparing the clinical features of 202 patients with different variant subtypes. Patients with multigene deletions had a significantly higher prevalence of CHDs (53.5% vs 25.8%, p value = 2 × 10-4), cortical visual impairment (12.5% vs 1.7%, p value = 0.004), microcephaly (37.1% vs 17.8%, p value = 0.009), corpus callosum abnormalities (17.9% vs 5.9%, p value = 0.02), and hearing impairment (39.7% vs 25.6%, p value = 0.04) than those with single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) or short insertions/deletions (indels), in addition to the previously identified features including epilepsy, constipation, and short stature. We also observed that a recurrent EHMT1 variant (p.Arg948Trp), identified in multiple unrelated patients, was linked to significant phenotypic heterogeneity, including late-onset neurocognitive regression. DISCUSSION: Our study showed that patients with multigene deletions are significantly more likely to exhibit multiorgan involvement, including CHDs, cortical visual impairments, microcephaly, corpus callosum abnormalities, and hearing impairments, compared with those with SNVs or indels, emphasizing the importance of genotype-informed management. We report pituitary gland abnormalities in KLEFS1, expanding the phenotypic and neuroimaging spectrum of KLEFS1. The patient showing regression in their 30s necessitates long-term, comprehensive studies to support care.

title: Advancing Pregnancy and Pediatric Science through the NIH Transporter Elucidation Network.
abstract: Human gestation is characterized by dynamic changes in maternal physiology and maturation of tissue functions before and after birth. The fetus and neonate are highly dependent upon transfer of maternal nutrients via the placenta and lactating mammary gland, which frequently involve selective membrane transporter proteins. At the same time, developmental changes in fetal and infant transport mechanisms critical for regulating absorption at the intestinal and blood-brain barriers are occurring. Coordinate regulation of cellular entry and efflux of nutrients, supplements, and xenobiotics, including drugs and environmental chemicals, must occur during this critical developmental period. In 2023, the National Institutes of Health launched the Transporter Elucidation Network (TEN) across four centers. This initiative applies experimental, computational, and translational approaches to (1) identify SoLute Carrier (SLC) superfamily and ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters in the human placenta, mammary gland, as well as the pediatric brain and intestinal barriers and, (2) characterize their localization, expression, function, and regulation. The Network seeks to identify functional determinants of transporters as gatekeepers of entry to placenta, mammary gland and brain, and applies structural biology, proteomics, metabolomics, organoids, liquid biopsies, and microphysiological systems to this end. Computational strategies, such as machine learning, virtual screening, physiologically based pharmacokinetics, and perinatal epidemiology complement our experimental approaches. This paper highlights the TEN's multidisciplinary strategies to address current challenges in perinatal and pediatric transporter research and its commitment to advancing state-of-the-art tools and new approach methodologies to fill critical gaps in our understanding of nutrient and xenobiotic exposure during early human development.

title: Overexpression of endoplasmic reticulum acetyl-CoA transporter AT-1 alters neuronal metabolism, growth, and synaptic activity.
abstract: Acetyl-CoA is a molecule central to cellular metabolic homeostasis. As part of the secretory pathway, acetyl-CoA is imported into the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) by a membrane-bound transporter AT-1 (SLC33A1). AT-1 mutations have been linked to peripheral neuropathy, developmental delay with premature death, and intellectual disability with progeria. Here, we show that AT-1 overexpression impacts diverse phenotypes related to neuronal function and plasticity. Differences in ribosomal, synaptic processing, and metabolic pathways were identified at transcriptomic and proteomic levels. Metabolic adaptations included changes in mitochondrial membrane potential, architecture, and respiration, and tracing experiments revealed changes in the fate of glucose favoring glycogen storage over the pentose phosphate pathway. Altered redox was linked to NAD-dependent proteins SIRT1 and CtBP2. Depletion of lipid stores was associated with greater plasticity in fuel substrate utilization. Metabolic adaptation was coincident with decreased synaptic activity, indicating that neuronal communication is coordinated, in part, through acetyl-CoA metabolism.

title: Targeting cryptic splicing variants in SDCCAG8, CEP290, and ABCA4: A translational workflow from diagnosis to ASO-based therapy.
abstract: A definitive molecular diagnosis is essential for the clinical management of rare genetic diseases (RGDs), guiding prognosis, genetic counseling, and therapeutic development. RNA-based therapeutics have emerged as promising strategies for RGDs owing to their ability to modulate gene expression and splicing. Here, we establish an integrated and scalable pipeline from variant discovery to RNA-based therapy in inherited retinal diseases (IRDs). Genome sequencing identified three cryptic variants in known IRD genes. Two novel deep intronic variants in SDCCAG8 were characterized by RT-PCR to induce pseudoexon inclusion. In addition, a previously described deep intronic variant in CEP290 was detected and reproduced on patient-derived fibroblasts, confirming aberrant splicing. A third family carrying the recurrent ABCA4 c.768G>T silent variant was included to corroborate the translational strength of our pipeline and to provide an additional model for RNA-based therapeutic correction. We designed and tested 16 splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides (ssASOs) in patient-derived fibroblasts, HeLa cells transfected with mutant minigenes, and, when available, human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived retinal organoids. For each variant, at least one ssASO successfully improved normal splicing and increased gene expression in patient-derived models. Overall, this study validates an innovative end-to-end translational workflow and highlights how molecular diagnosis can directly drive the development of personalized RNA-based therapies.

title: Levetiracetam restores GABAergic function and network homeostasis following Vps35 deficiency in excitatory neurons.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Alzheimer's disease (AD) and related dementias (ADRDs) remain incurable, partly due to their complex and poorly understood pathogenic mechanisms. Loss of vacuolar protein sorting-associated protein 35 (VPS35), a core component of the retromer complex, has been implicated in AD and ADRDs. While Vps35 deficiency is known to increase amyloidogenesis by regulating its cargo proteins, such as APP and BACE1, the precise mechanism by which VPS35 dysfunction leads to cognitive impairment remains elusive. While neuronal VPS35 regulates trafficking and functions of multiple synaptic membrane proteins, such as postsynaptic glutamatergic and GABAnergic receptors and pre-synaptic vesicle protein SV2A, and Levetiracetam (LEV), an antiepileptic drug that improves cognition, interacts with the SV2A, exactly how LEV enhances cognition is still a matter of debate. METHODS: Given the abundant expression of VPS35 in pyramidal excitatory neurons, we generated a conditional knockout mouse model with Vps35 deletion from postnatal glutamatergic excitatory neurons (Vps35CaMKIIα) and characterized its phenotypes using a combination of behavioral assessments, and electrophysiological, biochemical, and immunohiotological analyses in the hippocampal CA1 region. A targeted pharmacological screen was conducted to evaluate the therapeutic potential of LEV. RESULTS: Vps35 deletion did not disrupt the gross brain development but led to progressive cognitive decline beginning at three months of age. Electrophysiological analyses revealed earlier-onset hippocampal CA1 hyperexcitability, marked by depolarized resting membrane potentials and reduced Kir2.1 expression. However, restoring Kir2.1 to suppress hyperexcitability failed to rescue cognitive deficits. Instead, cognitive impairment was associated with weakened GABAergic transmission and disruption of the excitatory/inhibitory balance in the Schaffer collateral-CA1 circuit. Notably, LEV treatment diminished these deficits in mutant mice. Intriguingly, LEV increased the levels of retromer component, VPS26A, and multiple pre- and postsynaptic GABAergic proteins, in addition to SV2A, all of which were reduced in Vps35-deficient CA1 neurons. CONCLUSIONS: These findings identify VPS35 in excitatory neurons as a critical factor for inhibitory synapse maintenance and network homeostasis. This study also highlights LEV as a potential therapeutic strategy for ADRDs through the preservation of GABAergic synapses.

title: Glucosamine and selenium differentially regulate glutathione, lipid peroxidation, and mitochondrial function during glutamate stress in retinal neural cells.
abstract: Glutamate can disrupt cystine-dependent glutathione metabolism and promote oxidative and mitochondrial dysfunction in neural cells. We integrated human multiple-sclerosis optic-chiasm transcriptomics (GSE100297), glutamate-treated primary-neuron RNA sequencing (GSE255041), R28 differential-expression summaries, a normal human optic-nerve single-nucleus atlas (GSE236566), and R28 retinal precursor-cell experiments to characterize glucosamine (GlcN) and selenium responses. Human tissue showed enriched unfolded-protein-response, oxidative-stress, apoptosis, and ferroptosis programs, whereas glutamate-treated neurons predominantly exhibited amino-acid stress, unfolded-protein response, oxidative stress, and apoptosis, with weaker concordant ferroptosis enrichment. Glutamate reduced R28 metabolic activity, GSH/GSSG, and mitochondrial respiration and increased DCFH-DA and BODIPY-C11 oxidation. GlcN (2.5 mM) shifted the glutamate dose-response curve rightward and preserved GSH/GSSG and respiration, but lowered basal metabolic activity, mitochondrial membrane potential, and ATP-based viability. GlcN increased the LC3B-II/LC3B-I ratio, while changes in PCNA-normalized NRF2-related protein signals were modest. Ferrostatin-1 (Fer-1) partially restored respiration during glutamate exposure and was associated with higher ATP-based viability. RSL3 and erastin markedly reduced viability without glutamate; Fer-1 substantially restored viability, whereas GlcN did not. Selenium (1 μM) partially reduced RSL3-associated loss of viability without glutamate; the selenium-associated viability gain diminished during glutamate co-exposure (adjusted interaction P = 0.0342). Selenium showed dose-dependent effects: 1 and 5 μM preserved metabolic activity, 5 μM reduced lipid oxidation, and 20 μM increased basal lipid oxidation. GlcN increased global O-GlcNAc modification approximately 3.6-fold and altered gp130 migration. In normal human optic nerve, redox/lipid-peroxidation programs were highest in myeloid cells, whereas hexosamine/O-GlcNAc capacity and SLC7A11 expression were prominent in astrocytic-stromal compartments. These findings identify distinct functional responses to GlcN and selenium within a mixed glutamate-stress phenotype that includes a ferrostatin-sensitive component. The GPX4 dependence of GlcN-mediated protection against glutamate remains unresolved.

title: Isolated Axoplasm from Squid and Pathogenic Mechanisms in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
abstract: The squid giant axon is an experimental model that has been instrumental in providing answers to many fundamental questions in cell biology, including the discovery of the motor protein kinesin and probing molecular mechanisms of neurodegenerative diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). The giant axon offers scale and ease of access that is not possible in mammalian models. The power of this model stems from the fact that one can introduce reagents and proteins that would not cross a plasma membrane at defined concentrations in a buffer environment that is closely modeled on normal components of the axoplasm. By leveraging the unique biology of the squid axon, early studies were able to define the channels and ion specificities of the action potential. Subsequent studies using video-enhanced contrast- differential Interference contrast microscopy (VEC-DIC) and the isolated axoplasm led to the identification of kinesins, a class of motor proteins responsible for intracellular vesicle trafficking toward the plus end of microtubules. This combination of isolated axoplasm and advanced imaging continues to provide insights into pathogenic mechanisms for adult-onset neurodegeneration, including ALS, and regulation of fast axonal transport, a process disrupted in motor neuron disease. Here, procedures for dissecting the giant axon, isolating axoplasm, and perfusing defined amounts of proteins and/or reagents into the axoplasm are detailed, as well as methods for visualizing and interactively analyzing vesicle traffic in real time. This model represents a singular avenue to understand the critical function of neurons, shedding light on the mechanisms driving ALS pathology and other neurodegenerative diseases. This system also offers a tractable platform for drug testing, where candidate therapeutic compounds can be introduced directly into the axoplasm, and their effects on vesicle trafficking can be assessed in real time, providing a rapid and physiologically relevant means of identifying potential ALS therapeutic targets.

title: Beyond cell replacement: restoring organelle homeostasis as the next frontier of regenerative medicine.
abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases (NDs) have traditionally been viewed as disorders driven by individual pathological processes, including protein aggregation, mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, impaired autophagy, and neuroinflammation. However, growing evidence demonstrates that these mechanisms are not isolated events but interconnected manifestations of disrupted intracellular organelle communication. Dynamic interactions among mitochondria, the ER, lysosomes, peroxisomes, and other organelles coordinate calcium signaling, bioenergetics, proteostasis, lipid metabolism, and cellular stress adaptation, thereby preserving neuronal homeostasis. Progressive disruption of this communication network represents a fundamental driver of neuronal dysfunction and degeneration, suggesting that restoration of organelle homeostasis may constitute a more effective therapeutic strategy than targeting individual molecular pathways. In parallel, regenerative medicine has evolved beyond the concept of cell replacement toward approaches that enhance the resilience and repair capacity of surviving cells. Among these, mesenchymal stem cell (MSC)-derived secretomes and extracellular vesicles (EVs) have emerged as promising cell-free therapeutics owing to their diverse repertoire of proteins, lipids, metabolites, cytokines, growth factors, and regulatory RNAs capable of simultaneously modulating multiple cellular pathways. Accumulating evidence indicates that these bioactive cargos modulate mitochondrial function, alleviate ER stress, improve autophagy-lysosomal activity, reduce oxidative stress and neuroinflammation, and reinforce proteostasis, collectively promoting intracellular homeostasis. Here, we propose organelle homeostasis as a promising focus for regenerative medicine and discuss how cell-free therapies may redefine therapeutic strategies for NDs by restoring the intracellular communication networks that sustain cellular resilience. Finally, we highlight current translational challenges and future opportunities for engineering next-generation cell-free therapeutics targeting complex diseases.

title: Early-life exposure to environmental pollutants and endocrine disruptors: emerging risks and mechanistic insights in maternal, fetal, and child health.
abstract: Exposure to environmental pollutants and endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs) in early life is a critical public health issue because it can alter developmental programming that impacts susceptibility to disease throughout life. The prenatal and early postnatal periods are times of vulnerability when exposure to environmental stressors may impact endocrine signalling, placental function, epigenetic regulation, and metabolic homeostasis. There is increasing evidence that exposure to bisphenols, phthalates, per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), pesticides, heavy metals, and air pollutants has been associated with pregnancy outcomes, neurodevelopmental disorders, metabolic dysfunction, endocrine abnormalities and reproductive impairments. Exposomics, high-resolution mass spectrometry, biomonitoring, and passive sampling technologies have made crucial advances in characterising complex environmental exposures. At the same time, novel methods such as multi-omics, single-cell sequencing, spatial biology and microbiome studies have yielded more detailed mechanistic understanding of how environmental factors can impact developmental processes via epigenetic, inflammatory, oxidative stress, and endocrine pathways. The placenta has emerged as a valuable biomarker matrix for assessing fetal exposure and developmental programming. Exposure routes, biomonitoring methods, placental processes, molecular and epigenetic modifications, and the impacts of early-life environmental exposures on neurodevelopment, metabolism, endocrine function, and reproduction are all summarised in this review. It also emphasises current advancements in exposure assessment, preventive measures, and policy frameworks, highlighting the importance of life-course perspectives and environmental justice. To identify important windows of susceptibility, improve risk assessment, and develop strategies to safeguard maternal and child health, exposomics in conjunction with systems biology and longitudinal epidemiological approaches will be essential.

title: Targeting Nrf2 signaling in Parkinson's disease: Mechanisms, strategies, and therapeutic perspectives.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the selective loss of dopaminergic neurons and the accumulation of α-synuclein. Disease progression is driven by a complex interplay of chronic oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and impaired proteostasis. As a central regulator of the cellular antioxidant response, nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (Nrf2) protects against these cellular insults by driving the expression of various cytoprotective genes. In this review, we summarize the regulatory mechanisms of the Keap1-Nrf2 pathway and evaluate how its activation counteracts core PD pathologies. We also highlight the extensive crosstalk between Nrf2 and other major signaling networks that collectively determine dopaminergic neuronal survival. Finally, we examine the therapeutic potential of current Nrf2 modulators, including natural phytochemicals, clinical-stage candidates, and repurposed drugs, and critically discuss the pharmacokinetic barriers, electrophilic off-target toxicities, and the Nrf2 paradox that must be overcome to successfully translate these compounds into disease-modifying therapies for PD, highlighting the transition toward non-covalent PPI inhibitors.

title: Human-Derived Motor Neuron Progenitor Cell Implantation Rescues Motor Endplates Following Peripheral Nerve Injury.
abstract: PURPOSE: Degradation of motor endplates (MEPs) following peripheral nerve injury (PNI) is a major determinant of functional recovery, as prolonged denervation renders target muscles progressively unreceptive to reinnervation. While prior studies have demonstrated that stem cell-based therapies may provide neurotrophic support following PNI, their potential effects on MEP preservation have not been well studied. We hypothesized that transplantation of human-induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived motor neuron progenitors (MNPs) into chronically denervated muscle would be associated with preservation of MEP architecture. METHODS: With Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee approval, chronic denervation injuries were created in mice via sciatic nerve transection. After 4 months of denervation, when MEPs have consistently degraded in this animal model, the denervated tibialis anterior (TA) was injected with low-dose MNPs (10,000 cells), high-dose MNPs (500,000 cells), or phosphate-buffered saline (negative control). Using a previously established method, hiPSCs were differentiated into functional MNPs prior to injection. At selected time points post-injection, the TA was harvested and immunostained to confirm MNP viability and detect the presence of MEPs. RESULTS: Transplanted MNPs remained viable within host muscle at both evaluated time points. No identifiable MEPs were detected in phosphate-buffered saline-treated chronically denervated muscle. In contrast, MNP-treated muscles demonstrated the presence of MEP-like structures following prolonged denervation. Qualitative differences in MEP density and morphologic complexity were observed between treatment groups, with greater preservation seen in the higher-dose cohort. Contralateral uninjured muscles demonstrated intact native MEP architecture. CONCLUSIONS: Intramuscular transplantation of hiPSC-derived MNPs into chronically denervated muscle was associated with preservation of MEP morphology in this preclinical proof-of-concept model. These preliminary findings suggest that cellular therapies may represent a potential adjunctive strategy to preserve end-organ receptivity following delayed peripheral nerve injury. TYPE OF STUDY/LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Preclinical controlled animal study, Level V.
journal: Journal of hand surgery global online

title: Time-lapse RESOLFT nanoscopy empowered by deep learning.
abstract: Capturing the dynamic interplay of proteins and organelles within cells requires microscopy methods with high spatial and temporal resolution. Reversible Saturable OpticaL Fluorescent Transition (RESOLFT) demonstrated great potential for live cell nanoscopy by using patterned light and reversibly switching fluorescent probes. Despite the latest improvement in both switching probes and optical schemes, the duration and frame rate of the time-lapse are still limited by photobleaching and spatial sampling steps. Here, we present two distinct strategies based on deep learning to restore low signal-to-noise-ratio (SNR) or under-sampled images pushing the experimental boundaries of RESOLFT. We demonstrate the capability of Hierarchical DivNoising (HDN) to restore low-SNR RESOLFT data while maintaining full spatial resolution, both in supervised and unsupervised settings. This allows a 10-fold reduction of light dose per frame, and up to 5 times longer imaging. Then, we present Fast-MoNaLISA, a method that reduces the acquisition time of any point-scanning systems. This allows a 4-fold increase in frame rate, and a reduction of scanning artefacts. Overall, our methods open up possibilities for dynamic data acquisition at the sub-organelle level, such as vesicles budding in and out from intact mitochondria, or the actin meshwork formation and dissociation.

title: KIF1A c.773C > T impairs neural progenitor differentiation and axonal transport in association with dysregulated Wnt/β-catenin-BDNF signaling.
abstract: Pathogenic KIF1A variants are established cause neurodevelopmental and neurodegenerative disorders. However, the mechanisms by which they perturb early human neural development remains undefined. Here, we identified a heterozygous KIF1A c.773C > T (p.T258M) mutation in a Chinese family with hereditary spastic paraplegia and modeled its pathogenicity using patient-derived iPSCs and CRISPR-Cas9-corrected isogenic controls. We found that KIF1A-mutant neural stem cells (NSCs) exhibited hyperproliferation, impaired cell-cycle exit, and defective neuronal differentiation, accompanied by defective neurite outgrowth, neuronal complexity, and calcium activity. Mechanistically, the KIF1A c.773C > T mutation compromised the binding affinity of KIF1A for β-tubulin and thereby impaired microtubule-associated localization of BDNF and synaptophysin. Integrated transcriptomic and biochemical analyses further revealed dysregulation of the Wnt/β-catenin signaling pathway. Notably, pharmacological activation of Wnt signaling restored BDNF expression, whereas exogenous BDNF rescued the proliferative and differentiative defects, indicating a potential functional relationship between BDNF and Wnt/β-catenin signaling. Collectively, these findings suggested that dysregulated Wnt/β-catenin-BDNF signaling may serve as a contributory mechanism linking KIF1A motor dysfunction to aberrant neural stem cell fate.

title: Quantum-sensing-based super-resolution live cell microenvironment imaging.
abstract: Direct monitoring the multifaceted intracellular microenvironment is fundamental for deciphering localized cellular behavior and function. However, performing nanoscale spatiotemporal sensing of the dynamic physiochemical environment within a live cell has remained challenging, mainly limited by the lack of robust, biocompatible method which satisfies the requirements for spatiotemporal resolution, sensitivity, multi-physical sensing capability and long-term viability. Here we present a super-resolution-based quantum biosensing approach, namely Super-resolution Multi-physical field Imaging with Deconvolution, implemented in our custom-built setup which integrates nitrogen vacancy center-based quantum sensing with structured illumination microscopy. This enables quantitative, super-resolved, and long-term tracking of intracellular physical fields, featuring spatial resolution of 136 nm, temporal resolution of 150 ms, and field of view of 180×180 μm2. We further perform super-resolution multimodal imaging in a live cell, revealing the spatially heterogeneous reactive oxygen species dynamics under external stimulation. Our work enables the dynamic assessment of localized physiochemical dynamics under super-resolution quantum biosensing.
authors: Lu Y, Yang Y, Xu K, Mao Z, Yin L, Xu Y, Zhou Z, Wang X, Zhang C, Zhu W
overview: Direct monitoring the multifaceted intracellular microenvironment is fundamental for deciphering localized cellular behavior and function.
main: Our work enables the dynamic assessment of localized physiochemical dynamics under super-resolution quantum biosensing.

title: Multiple motor proteins regulate TDP-43 anterograde axonal transport.
abstract: TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) is an RNA-binding protein essential for RNA metabolism. Under physiological conditions, it predominantly resides in the nucleus but is also expressed in the cytoplasm, where it regulates mRNA trafficking and local translation. In nearly 97% of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) cases, TDP-43 undergoes nuclear depletion and cytoplasmic aggregation. While its nuclear functions are well characterized, its axonal roles remain poorly understood, despite axonal degeneration being a hallmark of ALS pathology. To address this gap, we investigated TDP-43 localization and transport dynamics in axons of H9-derived human neurons. We compared fluorescently labeled TDP-43 with three well-characterized axonal cargoes, ras-related protein Rab5, synaptophysin, and amyloid precursor protein, and examined protein-protein interactions between TDP-43 and the axonal transport machinery. Our analyses revealed that TDP-43 exhibits active anterograde axonal transport and interacts with multiple kinesin motor proteins, including all three KIF5 isoforms, through the adaptor KLC1, and the synaptic vesicles motor KIF1A. This multi-motor engagement suggests a flexible transport system that ensures mRNA delivery to distal axons. In ALS, where TDP-43 accumulates abnormally in the cytoplasm, this flexibility may become compromised, with multiple transport mechanisms simultaneously affected. This could contribute to progressive accumulation of non-functional TDP-43 granules, disrupting mRNA trafficking and local translation. Our findings provide a foundation for understanding how physiological TDP-43 transport mechanisms may be impaired during disease, highlighting axonal TDP-43 transport pathways as potential therapeutic targets.
authors: Feole M, Devoto VMP, Dragišić N, Čarna M, Klosterman K, Limbaek-Stokin C, Forte G, Moya KL, Smith RA, Svendsen CN
overview: TAR DNA-binding protein 43 (TDP-43) is an RNA-binding protein essential for RNA metabolism.
main: Under physiological conditions, it predominantly resides in the nucleus but is also expressed in the cytoplasm, where it regulates mRNA trafficking and local translation.

title: OGT regulates RNA-binding protein nucleocytoplasmic partitioning, but this fails in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
abstract: O-linked N-acetylglucosamine transferase (OGT) catalyzes the O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) modification to proteins and has been implicated in a range of diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a rapidly progressive and currently incurable neurodegenerative disorder. However, the precise mechanisms by which OGT influences ALS pathogenesis remain largely unresolved. In this study, we used human-induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived spinal motor neurons (hiPSC-MNs), the principal cell type that undergoes degeneration in ALS, to systematically reveal that OGT-related mechanisms regulate RNA-binding protein (RBP) nucleocytoplasmic compartmentalization. Using a combination of antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) technology and small molecular pharmacology, we reveal two distinct regulatory mechanisms of RBP compartmentalization, including by intron-retaining transcript-mediated sequestration and O-linked N-acetylglucosaminylation (O-GlcNAcylation)-mediated nuclear transport. We finally examine the tractability of manipulating OGT activity in the ALS context but demonstrate that the OGT-related mechanisms governing RBP localization in healthy hiPSC-MNs are impaired in the context of ALS-causing VCP and TARDBP mutations.

overview: O-linked N-acetylglucosamine transferase (OGT) catalyzes the O-linked β-N-acetylglucosamine (O-GlcNAc) modification to proteins and has been implicated in a range of diseases, including amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), a rapidly progressive and currently incurable neurodegenerative disorder.

title: A comprehensive single-cell transcriptomic atlas of hippocampal microglia in a mouse model of traumatic brain injury.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) triggers microglial activation and disrupts the inflammatory microenvironment in the hippocampus, which are key contributors to neuroinflammation and subsequent secondary brain damage. Nevertheless, the cellular heterogeneity of microglia, their pro-inflammatory activation mechanisms, and microenvironmental regulatory networks have not been fully characterized. METHODS: By integrating multi-source single-cell transcriptomic datasets and establishing a mouse TBI validation model, we constructed a high-resolution cellular atlas of hippocampal microglia. Through comprehensive re-analysis of single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets, bioinformatic approaches, high-dimensional weighted gene co-expression network analysis (hdWGCNA), cell-cell communication profiling, and in vivo behavioral and in vivo pathological evaluations, we thoroughly explored the subpopulation diversity, functional features, and regulatory mechanisms of hippocampal microglia following TBI. RESULTS: TBI elicited extensive phenotypic diversification in hippocampal microglia, and five major subpopulations were identified, among which disease-associated microglia (DAM) were further classified into four distinct subclusters. A distinct inflamed DAM subset (Inflam-DAM) was found to highly express canonical pro-inflammatory signature genes. Transcriptomic profiling revealed enrichment of AP-1 family transcription factors and the IL-17 signaling pathway in this subset, confirming its robust pro-inflammatory phenotype. hdWGCNA demonstrated that the pro-inflammatory state of Inflam-DAM was tightly linked to transcriptional and translational regulation. Cell-cell communication analysis indicated that meningeal macrophages, B cells and fibroblasts acted as upstream regulators and selectively interacted with DAM subclusters in the inflammatory niche. In turn, activated DAM communicated with neurons in an injury-dependent manner, eventually impairing neurogenesis. In vivo experiments validated that TBI mice displayed severe neurological dysfunction, elevated expression of pro-inflammatory microglial markers and signaling molecules in the hippocampus, and fewer newborn mature neurons - all findings consistent with our single-cell data. CONCLUSION: In summary, this work constructs a full-scale single-cell transcriptomic landscape of hippocampal microglia in TBI mice. We systematically delineated the heterogeneity of DAM subsets, the pro-inflammatory regulatory mechanism of Inflam-DAM, and the multi-layered intercellular network within the inflammatory microenvironment. Our results deepen the mechanistic understanding of TBI-associated neuroinflammation and offer valuable clues for the development of targeted anti-inflammatory therapies.

title: TRPML3 and TRPML1/3 differentially regulate unconventional MIF secretion through TMED10 and secretory autophagy.
abstract: The intracellular Ca2+ channel TRPML3 regulates autophagy by multimerization in a phosphoinositide (PIP)-dependent manner; however, its role in other membrane dynamics remains unclear. Here, we report that TRPML3 regulates type III unconventional protein secretion (UcPS) through two distinct pathways: TMED10-channeled UcPS and secretory autophagy. TRPML3 interacted with TMED10 and macrophage migration inhibitory factor (MIF), a signal sequence-lacking pleiotropic cytokine whose secretion mechanism has remained undefined. We found that cytosolic MIF is transported to membrane-enclosed compartments through TMED10-channeled UcPS. Notably, TRPML3, but not TRPML1 or TRPML1/3, promoted TMED10 oligomerization, thereby enhancing MIF secretion in a Ca2+-independent manner. Furthermore, once translocated into vesicular compartments, MIF colocalized with LC3, and its secretion was dependent on secretory autophagy. Mechanistically, we identified PI(3,4)P2 as a key regulator of secretory autophagy, with TRPML1/3 acting downstream of PI(3,4)P2 to mediate Ca2+-dependent MIF secretion. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that MIF is a novel cargo of type III UcPS, operating through TMED10-channeled UcPS and secretory autophagy, which are regulated by TRPML3 in a Ca2+-independent manner and by the PI(3,4)P2-TRPML1/3 axis in a Ca2+-dependent manner, respectively.

title: Mechanism of fluoride-induced neurotoxicity: Dissecting a multi-target organelle signaling network.
abstract: Fluoride is a widely distributed environmental contaminant, and excessive exposure has been associated with adverse neurological outcomes. However, the underlying mechanisms of fluoride-induced neurotoxicity remain incompletely understood. In this review, we integrate current evidence to propose a multilevel, multi-target mechanistic framework of fluoride-induced neurotoxicity. We highlight that fluoride exerts neurotoxic effects not via isolated pathways but through the coordinated disruption of multiple organelles, particularly mitochondria, the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), and lysosomes. Dysfunction of these organelles converges via inter-organelle crosstalk, leading to impaired energy metabolism, calcium dyshomeostasis, defective protein folding, and impaired lysosomal degradation. We further identify oxidative stress as a central integrative relay and amplifier, linking organelle dysfunction to downstream pathological processes, including neuroinflammation, neuronal cell death, and synaptic impairment. Emerging evidence also suggests that epigenetic reprogramming, including aberrant DNA methylation and non-coding RNA network remodeling, contributes to long-term gene expression changes. These molecular and cellular disturbances ultimately converge on impaired neurogenesis, synaptic dysfunction, and cognitive deficits. Finally, we discuss current limitations, including the dependence on high-dose experimental models, and propose future directions emphasizing multi-target strategies to restore organelle homeostasis and redox balance. This integrative framework provides a comprehensive perspective on fluoride-induced neurotoxicity and may facilitate the development of more effective intervention strategies.

title: Convergent molecular mechanisms of chronic heavy metal exposure and repetitive mild traumatic brain injury in neurodegenerative processes.
abstract: Repetitive mild traumatic brain injury (rmTBI) and chronic environmental exposure to heavy metals represent widespread contributors to neurological dysfunction that are typically studied independently. However, emerging evidence indicates that these insults converge on overlapping cellular pathways that disrupt neuronal homeostasis, redox balance, genomic stability and proteostasis, including tau regulation. Notably, environmental metals including mercury, lead, arsenic, cadmium, and hexavalent chromium induce oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neuroinflammatory signaling, processes that are also central to rmTBI pathophysiology. In this review, we synthesize mechanistic and clinical evidence linking chronic heavy metal exposure and rmTBI and examine how their interaction may influence long-term vulnerability to neurodegeneration. To our knowledge, this is the first review to integrate these two domains within a unified mechanistic framework. We first summarize shared and metal-specific mechanisms of heavy metal neurotoxicity and integrate these findings with the cellular and systemic consequences of rmTBI. Attention is given to higher-order convergent processes, including disruption of the blood-brain barrier, dysregulation of the gut-brain axis, protein misfolding and tau pathology, ferroptosis, and impairment of proteostatic and autophagic pathways. We also discuss emerging biomarker signatures and therapeutic targets relevant to combined environmental and traumatic exposures. Collectively, current evidence supports a model in which chronic heavy metal burden may diminish neural resilience and could increase vulnerability to the cumulative effects of rmTBI. Although direct evidence of their interaction remains limited, the substantial mechanistic overlap provides a framework for future studies investigating environmental contributions to post-traumatic neurodegeneration, biomarker discovery, and potential therapeutic strategies.

title: Intermittent fasting as a therapeutic strategy in Alzheimer's disease: Understanding of brain-derived neurotrophic factor modulation.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease with amyloid-beta (Aβ) plaques, tau tangles, neuroinflammation, and oxidative stress, and it causes cognitive impairment and neuronal loss. The pharmacological treatment is of limited effectiveness, therefore the interest in novel approaches such as intermittent fasting (IF). IF, a nutritional regimen of periodic caloric restriction, has shown a potential to modulate neurodegenerative alterations by metabolic and molecular mechanisms. This review presents the implications of IF in the etiopathogenesis of AD, specifically in controlling brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF). BDNF is a major neurotrophin that plays a key role in synaptic plasticity, neuronal survival, and cognition. Evidence indicates that BDNF is drastically decreased in AD, therefore enhancing disease progression. IF enhances BDNF expression via mechanisms such as improved mitochondrial function, increased ketone body production, and reduced systemic inflammation. Preclinical studies indicate that IF not only upregulates BDNF but also alleviates key AD pathologies, including Aβ deposition and tau hyperphosphorylation. Additionally, clinical data highlight the cognitive benefits of IF and its role in modulating metabolic health, although studies specifically linking IF, BDNF and AD in humans remain limited. This review underscores the need for further research to determine optimal IF protocols and clarify its long-term impact on AD progression. IF's ability to modulate BDNF and other neuroprotective pathways positions it as a promising non-pharmacological intervention for AD management. By bridging metabolic health and neuroprotection, IF offers potential therapeutic synergy for mitigating AD's complex etiopathogenesis.

title: Autolysosomal enhancer GHF201 attenuates pathophysiology in a mucopolysaccharidosis type I mouse model.
abstract: Mucopolysaccharidosis type I (MPS-I) is a hereditary lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency in the lysosomal enzyme α-L-iduronidase (IDUA) leading to pathogenic over-accumulation of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), major constituent of connective tissue and mediators of cell signaling. We tested the therapeutic efficacy of the autolysosomal activator GHF201 in the Idua -/- mouse model of MPS-I. We show that GHF201 reduced GAGs and increased cathepsin activity in Idua -/- mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) and brain cells. In vivo GHF201 improved aberrant locomotion and behavior, reduced interstitial cathepsins in joints and liver, increased systemic catabolism, corrected bone dysplasia, increased autophagic flux, and ameliorated CNS neurodegeneration and neuroinflammation. GHF201 also reduced brain N-glycans, which are degraded in lysosomes. In conclusion, the lysosomal and autophagic activator GHF201 was demonstrated to improve various pathophysiological parameters in MPS-I-modeling Idua -/- female mice. Our results suggest that GHF201 can complement the inadequate Aldurazyme enzyme replacement therapy as an add-on therapy.

title: Paeonol alleviates oxidative stress and brain injury in hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy by activating the PI3K/Akt/Nrf2 signaling pathway.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy (HIE) is a severe neonatal neurological disorder, in which oxidative stress serves as a central mediator of brain injury. Paeonol (Pae), a phenolic compound with established anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties, remains underexplored as a therapeutic strategy for HIE. This study investigated the neuroprotective effects of Pae against HIE-induced brain injury and explored whether its protective effects involves attenuation of oxidative stress through activation of the PI3K/Akt/Nrf2 signaling pathway. METHODS: A neonatal rat HIE model was established using the modified Rice-Vannucci method. Brain injury, oxidative stress markers, and neurological function were assessed through histological staining and behavioral testing. Network pharmacology, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations were used to identify and validate potential targets. An H2O2-induced oxidative stress model in PC12 cells was employed for mechanistic validation, with PI3K and Nrf2 pharmacologically inhibited using LY294002 and ML385, respectively. RESULTS: Pae significantly reduced cerebral infarct volume and histopathological alterations, attenuated oxidative stress, and improved motor and cognitive performance in HIE rats. Network pharmacology identified the PI3K/Akt as a key target pathway, while molecular docking revealed a strong binding affinity between Pae and AKT1. Consistently, Pae activated the PI3K/Akt pathway, promoted Nrf2 nuclear translocation, and upregulated HO-1 expression in both in vivo and in vitro experiments; these effects were substantially reversed by LY294002 and ML385. CONCLUSION: Pae ameliorates HIE-induced brain injury and neurological deficits via activation of the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway and reinforcement of Nrf2-mediated antioxidant defenses. These findings identify Pae as a preclinical neuroprotective candidate worthy of further exploration.
authors: Hu D, Li J, Ye L, Yan J, Lei S, Zhang G, Lin L, Lin Q

title: Celastrol attenuates testosterone-induced benign prostatic hyperplasia by modulating the PTEN/PI3K/AKT pathway.
abstract: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) represents a prevalent urological disease observed primarily among aging men. Celastrol (CELA) is an active natural compound with diverse pharmacological properties. The primary aim of this research is to assess the potential protective activity of CELA in testosterone (TEST)-induced BPH in rats. Male Wistar rats were allocated into six distinct groups for treatment: group 1 acted as the control and was given the vehicle; group 2 received only CELA (2 mg/kg, orally); group 3 was administered TEST alone (3 mg/kg, subcutaneously); groups 4 and 5 were administered the combination of TEST (3 mg/kg, subcutaneously) and CELA (1 or 2 mg/kg, orally); and group 6 received a combination of TEST (3 mg/kg, subcutaneously) and finasteride (FINA) (0.5 mg/kg, orally). Over a period of four weeks, CELA at doses of 1 or 2 mg/kg effectively inhibited the increase in both the prostate index and weight when compared to rats treated with TEST. CELA mitigated pathological alterations in prostate architecture, reduced the proliferation markers and modulated the expression of apoptosis markers compared to TEST-treated rats. Furthermore, CELA exhibited antioxidant properties by mitigating the TEST-induced increase in lipid peroxide levels and the depletion of superoxide dismutase and catalase activities. Moreover, CELA exhibited anti-inflammatory activity by significantly downregulating tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin-6, and nuclear factor-κB expression. In addition, CELA elevated phosphatase and tensin homolog (PTEN) and reduced phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) and AKT expression compared with the TEST group. In addition, CELA inhibited TEST-induced enhancement of mRNA expression of 5α-reductase type 2, androgen receptor and fibroblast growth factor 2. Overall, CELA partially alleviates TEST-induced BPH in rats, an effect that is associated with modulation of PTEN/PI3K/AKT axis.

title: Volume electron microscopy reveals oligodendrocyte axon selection patterns and spatial assembly of myelin and nodes.
abstract: Oligodendrocytes myelinate multiple axons, requiring single cells to coordinate target selection, sheath growth, and node formation across complex cortical geometry. We combined serial block-face electron microscopy, complete segmentation, and three-dimensional reconstruction to analyze early-myelinating oligodendrocytes in the somatosensory cortex of a postnatal day 14 rat at single-cell and nanoscale resolution. Individual oligodendrocytes initiated myelination across all contacted axons, while early ensheathment decreased with increasing process distance from the soma. Each oligodendrocyte also contacted axons within a restricted caliber range, independently of wrapping progression. At prospective nodes of Ranvier, transient cytoplasmic projections extended into axonal domains from adjacent oligodendrocytes and converged near presumptive paranodes. These observations support a structural model in which oligodendrocyte geometry, cell-specific axon selection, and intercellular interactions jointly organize early cortical myelination and nodal assembly, providing testable hypotheses for developmental myelination and repair after demyelination.

title: MIMAS: An open-source microlens-array miniature microscope for accessible large-field cortical imaging in freely behaving mice.
abstract: Large-scale cortical dynamics during natural behavior are difficult to measure because head-mounted imaging systems must balance field of view, spatial resolution, weight, and optical complexity. Existing wide-field miniature microscopes often rely on compound or custom-corrected optical assemblies, which increase device complexity and limit accessibility for laboratories without specialized optics expertise. Here, we present the Miniature Integrated Microlens Array System (MIMAS), an open-source head-mounted fluorescence microscope that replaces conventional multi-element optics with a 4 × 5 microlens array as its sole imaging element. By combining modular subfield acquisition with computational registration and stitching, MIMAS achieves cellular-resolution imaging across an approximately 4 × 4.5 mm2 field of view while weighing only 2.31 g. In freely behaving mice with sparse labeling of layer 2/3 cortical neurons, MIMAS enabled simultaneous calcium imaging across multiple dorsal cortical regions, with signals extracted from thousands of neurons. This broad sampling captured distributed cortical activity related to locomotor state and sparse position-modulated responses during open-field exploration without detectable disruption of locomotion or loss of signal quality over 30 min of recording. Beyond neuronal imaging, MIMAS also supported wide-field vascular imaging and resolved vessel caliber-dependent hemodynamic responses to isoflurane. These results establish MIMAS as a lightweight, accessible, and versatile platform for large-scale fluorescence imaging in freely behaving mice and demonstrate an alternative strategy for wide-field cortical imaging that lowers the optical complexity barrier for individual laboratories.

title: Dorsal horn mapping: a Fiji toolbox for standardized laminar registration and transparent reporting of spinal cord imaging data from adult C57Bl/6 mice.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Rexed's laminae provide the anatomical framework for interpreting the spatial organization of neuronal populations within the spinal dorsal horn and are therefore widely used to describe immunohistochemical, in situ hybridization, and functional imaging data. However, despite their widespread use, no standardized approach for assigning cells to individual laminae has been established, limiting reproducibility and direct comparison of datasets across studies. METHODS: We developed Dorsal Horn Mapping, an open-source Fiji toolbox that implements a standardized workflow for laminar registration in transverse mouse spinal cord sections. The toolbox aligns segment-specific reference maps to experimental images using user-guided rigid transformations and independent scaling, assigns labeled cells to Rexed's laminae, and transforms their positions into a common spatial reference frame. In addition, it provides tools for quantitative laminar analysis and visualization of pooled datasets as composite reference maps. RESULTS: Validation experiments demonstrated high inter-user reproducibility of template alignment and laminar assignment across users with different levels of anatomical expertise. Registrations showed good agreement with established laminar markers and resulted in highly consistent assignment of neuronal populations to individual laminae. Thus, 81% of IB4-pos pixels were mapped to lamina II (95% CI: 68.4-86.2%) and the estimated difference in cell counts averaged across all users, segments and laminae was 0.08 cells (95% CI: -0.68 to 0.83; P = 0.843). Analysis of representative multichannel immunohistochemical datasets further demonstrated the utility of the workflow for standardized visualization and quantitative analysis of cellular localization. CONCLUSION: Dorsal Horn Mapping provides an accessible framework for standardized laminar registration and transparent spatial reporting of spinal cord imaging data from adult C57BL/6 mice. By introducing a common spatial reference system for dorsal horn anatomy, the toolbox facilitates direct comparison of cellular localization across experiments and laboratories and has the potential to improve reproducibility, comparability, and reporting standards in pain and spinal cord research.

title: EasyQuant: A machine-learning-assisted imaging-based tool for quantifying neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs).
abstract: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) play a crucial role in host defense, yet their dysregulation is associated with inflammation and tissue damage. Consequently, researching NETs in vitro is essential for understanding their role in both health and disease. However, accurate quantification of NETs in vitro remains a challenge due to limitations in manual methods and semi-automated tools, which often require extensive user input and/or are time-consuming. Moreover, some methods identify neutrophils and NETs based on a single fixed parameter, such as size, which may lead to inaccuracies in recognizing neutrophils due to the cells' biological complexity. In this study, we developed a user-friendly framework for NET quantification using LABKIT, an ImageJ plugin, together with a custom Jython-based script that streamlines image processing and NET classification. By combining fluorescence microscopy with a machine learning tool, this approach enables rapid, scalable analysis of large multi-dimensional datasets with improved flexibility, reliability, and accessibility. Leveraging LABKIT for quantification ensures objective and consistent segmentation of NETs and neutrophils, reducing user bias and processing time while supporting reproducible data curation. Overall, EasyQuant provides a foundation for a freely accessible pipeline that can be integrated into diverse research workflows, herein specifically applied to improve the accuracy and throughput of neutrophil quantification.

title: BVLab-analyzer: a unified visual toolbox for terabyte-scale whole-brain cell detection, neuron reconstruction, and vascular network extraction.
abstract: BVLab-Analyzer is a standalone graphical software tool for end-to-end analysis of terabyte-scale whole-brain microscopy images. Operating through a zero-code interface, it handles data import (TIFF, BioImageVision, OME-Zarr), deep learning-based semantic segmentation, 3D skeleton reconstruction, and morphological statistical analysis within a unified pipeline. The software supports three target structures-cells, neurons and vasculature-and exports their morphological reconstructions in standard SWC format. To accelerate training data preparation, Smart Annotation tools provide sub-volume interference isolation, coarse-vessel ray tracing, and skeleton auto-interpolation. For inference, optimized block-wise strategies enable a standard 3D U-Net to predict whole-brain volumes up to 12 TB on a single consumer-grade GPU, while an interrupt-and-resume engine ensures fault tolerance during extended computations. By integrating these features, BVLab-Analyzer lowers the hardware barrier for whole-brain analysis and unifies previously fragmented toolchains-from annotation and segmentation to reconstruction and quantification-into a single, accessible software environment.

title: Emerging role of cGAS-STING in the pathogenesis of allergic diseases.
abstract: The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase-stimulator of interferon genes (cGAS-STING) signaling pathway, classically recognized as a crucial cytosolic DNA-sensing mechanism in innate antiviral immunity, is now emerging as a pivotal regulator of sterile inflammation and immune dysregulation. Recent evidence has shifted the paradigm, revealing its significant involvement in the pathogenesis of various allergic diseases, including asthma, atopic dermatitis, and allergic rhinitis. Beyond its canonical role in infection, aberrant activation of cGAS by endogenous DNA from mitochondrial stress, cellular damage, or neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) can drive pro-inflammatory cytokine responses and, depending on context, type I interferon responses; however, stimulus-induced type I interferon production is impaired in asthmatic airway epithelium and is further suppressed by type 2 inflammatory mediators. This review synthesizes current findings on how dysregulated cGAS-STING signaling contributes to allergic inflammation by amplifying Th2 responses, promoting airway remodeling, enhancing epithelial barrier dysfunction, and modulating the activity of key immune cells such as eosinophils, macrophages, mast cells, dendritic cells, and fibroblasts. We further explore the interplay between this pathway and other allergic signaling cascades, highlighting its role as an innate immune amplifier of allergic sensitization and chronicity Finally, we discuss the translational potential of targeting the cGAS-STING axis as an emerging therapeutic strategy for managing severe, steroid-resistant, or type-2-low allergic endotypes, while emphasizing the need for further validation, particularly in settings where type I interferon responses are impaired and where direct evidence for type-2-low endotypes remains limited.Understanding the emerging role of cGAS-STING provides critical insights into the complex immunobiology of allergic diseases and opens new avenues for intervention.

title: Maternal circulating cytokine and chemokine levels during pregnancy and risk of autism spectrum disorder in offspring: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Maternal immune activation (MIA) during pregnancy has been implicated in offspring neurodevelopment, but evidence linking maternal gestational immune mediators with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) remains heterogeneous. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated whether maternal circulating cytokine and chemokine levels during pregnancy are associated with autism in offspring. METHODS: Five databases were searched for human observational studies measuring maternal blood cytokines or chemokines during pregnancy and reporting autism outcomes in offspring. Eligible studies included autism versus control comparisons using maternal serum or plasma samples. Random-effects meta-analyses were conducted using odds ratios (ORs) as the primary effect measure. Standardised mean differences (SMDs) were also analysed where group-level concentration data were available. Heterogeneity was assessed using I² statistics, and small-study effects were explored using Egger's test where estimable. RESULTS: Seven studies met the eligibility criteria. In OR-based analyses, nominal associations with autism were observed for IL-10 (OR 1.34, 95% CI 1.06-1.69), CXCL10 (OR 1.62, 95% CI 1.24-2.11), IL-1α (OR 1.42, 95% CI 1.23-1.65), IL-5 (OR 1.49, 95% CI 1.18-1.89), and IL-17A (OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.70-0.94). CCL4 showed a borderline association. Supportive SMD analyses indicated higher IL-6 and lower IL-1β concentrations in autism-associated pregnancies. Heterogeneity varied across analytes and was substantial for IL-10 and CCL4. CONCLUSION: Maternal gestational immune profiles may differ in pregnancies later associated with autism, but current evidence does not support a single robust cytokine biomarker. Progress requires larger prospective cohorts with repeated sampling, harmonised assays, pathway-level analyses, and integrated placental-foetal neurodevelopmental phenotyping.
